title: 07 — Formal Power Series
text:
2. Newton inversion
Suppose \(B\) is an inverse approximation: \(AB\equiv1\pmod{x^{m}}\). The error \(E=1-AB\) has no terms below degree \(m\). Rather than solve missing coefficients individually, correct all of them in one multiplication: \[
B_{new}=B(2-AB)\pmod{x^{2m}}.
\] Indeed \(AB_{new}=AB(2-AB)=(1-E)(1+E)=1-E^2\). Thus the old error is squared; if \(E\) starts at degree \(m\), the new error starts at degree \(2m\). Precision doubles, and the total cost over lengths \(1,2,4,\ldots,n\) is \(O(M(n))\).
For \(A=1-x-x^2\), start \(B=1\). The first update modulo \(x^2\) gives \(1+x\). Using that prefix, \(AB=1-2x^2-x^3\), so the next correction is \((1+x)(1+2x^2+x^3)=1+x+2x^2+3x^3\pmod{x^4}\). The invariant is \(AB\equiv1\) at the current precision; no coefficient is guessed from a numerical approximation. At the final step use \(\min(2m,n)\), so a non-power-of-two request has exact boundaries too.
Precision doubling should operate on a truncated copy so that a caller’s longer series is not accidentally destroyed.

title: 07 — Formal Power Series
text:
3. Logarithm and exponential
For a unit series with constant coefficient \(1\), define the logarithm to be the unique zero-constant series whose derivative is \(A'/A\):
\[
\log A=\int A'A^{-1}\,dx,
\]
in \(O(M(n))\). More generally \(A'/A\) makes sense whenever \(A[0]\) is a unit, but the integral above deliberately discards the scalar factor \(A[0]\): it is a normalized logarithm with constant term zero. Thus \(\exp(\log A)=A\) only under the clean contract \(A[0]=1\); otherwise it equals \(A/A[0]\). The divisions from integration also require \(1,\ldots,n-1\) to be units at precision \(n\).
For exponential, the desired identity is \(\log B=A\). If \(B\) is already correct in degrees below \(m\), then \(A-\log B\) begins at degree \(m\), so multiplying by \(1+A-\log B\) corrects only unknown coefficients: \[
B_{new}=B(1+A-\log B)\pmod{x^{2m}}.
\]
The bracket is \(1 \bmod x^{m}\), so known coefficients remain unchanged. Standard implementations are \(O(M(n))\), though careless repeated inversions may add a constant or logarithmic factor.
To prove the improvement, set \(E=A-\log B\), so \(v(E)\ge m\). At precision \(2m\), all powers \(E^j\) for \(j\ge2\) vanish, hence \(\log(1+E)\equiv E\). Therefore \(\log(B(1+E))\equiv\log B+E=A\pmod{x^{2m}}\). The logarithm product identity follows by differentiating both sides and matching zero constants; the required integers through the working degree must be units. This proves both preservation and correction.
For example, over the rationals, \(\exp(x+x^2)\) begins \(1+x+\tfrac32x^2+\tfrac76x^3\). From \(B'= (1+2x)B\) we get \(b_1=1\), \(2b_2=b_1+2b_0=3\), and \(3b_3=b_2+2b_1=7/2\). Over \(\mathbb F_5\) the same prefix is \((1,1,4,2)\). At degree five the usual division recurrence cannot continue: \(5b_5\) loses information.

title: 07 — Formal Power Series
text:
4. Powers and square roots
When the logarithm and exponential contracts above hold, \(A(0)=1\) gives \(A^{k}=\exp(k\log A)\) because logarithm turns multiplication into addition. Here \(k=0\) is the separate identity case \(A^0=1\). For nonnegative \(k\) and a nonzero series whose leading coefficient is a unit, find the first nonzero term \(a_tx^{t}\). A nonzero field coefficient is sufficient; a nonzero coefficient in a general ring need not be. Under this additional condition:
\[
A^k=x^{tk}a_t^k
\exp\!\left(k\log\frac{A}{a_tx^t}\right).
\]
If \(tk \ge  n\), the truncated answer is zero. This handles huge nonnegative \(k\) without reducing \(k\) when computing the shift; only the scalar \(k\) multiplying \(\log A\) is reduced in the coefficient field. Negative powers require a unit series and are a different contract.
Over a field of odd characteristic, solve \(B^2-A=0\). For a unit series, the ordinary Newton correction \(B-(B^2-A)/(2B)\) simplifies to \[
B_{new}=\frac12(B+A/B).
\] Start with a square root of the constant coefficient. For a nonunit \(A\), first strip an even valuation \(2t\) and solve for the remaining unit series; an odd finite valuation makes a root impossible. Tonelli–Shanks supplies the initial scalar root over an odd prime field. A unit series over an odd prime field has roots exactly when its constant coefficient is a quadratic residue; then it has exactly two, differing by sign. For a positive even valuation, shifting either unit root gives two canonical roots when the unused high coefficients are set to zero. Coefficients of \(B\) in degrees at least \(n-t\) are invisible in \(B^2\bmod x^n\) and may be arbitrary. Thus a nonunit truncated series can have more than two roots. The zero series modulo \(x^n\) is another non-unique case; choose the all-zero root unless the problem states a different normalization. Problems must specify a canonical root or accept any valid one.

Worked failure: counting roots of a truncated nonunit
Over \(\mathbb F_5\), let \(A=x^2\pmod{x^5}\). Write \(B=b_1x+b_2x^2+b_3x^3+b_4x^4\). Comparing degrees two, three, and four gives \(b_1^2=1\), \(2b_1b_2=0\), and \(b_2^2+2b_1b_3=0\). Thus \(b_1=\pm1\), \(b_2=b_3=0\), while \(b_4\) is arbitrary: there are ten roots \(B=\pm x+cx^4\). In the infinite series ring the exact equation \(B^2=x^2\) has only \(B=\pm x\). Confusing exact equality with a truncated congruence causes the erroneous “exactly two roots” conclusion.

title: 07 — Formal Power Series
text:
5. Composition
Naive composition computes powers \(1,B,B^{2},\ldots\) in \(O(nM(n))\). Brent–Kung baby-step/giant-step chooses \(k\approx\sqrt n\):
\[
A(B)=\sum_q B^{qk}\left(\sum_{r<k}a_{qk+r}B^r\right).
\]
Precompute baby powers \(B^{r}\), form each block polynomial, then combine by Horner in \(B^{k}\). Merely forming every dense block as a separate linear combination can still cost \(O(n^2)\). The full Brent–Kung algorithm batches those combinations with rectangular matrix multiplication; its classical FFT bound is \(O((n\log n)^{3/2})\) field operations. Exact practical complexity and memory depend on the polynomial- and matrix-multiplication routines. The block decomposition is the conceptual step; it is not by itself a proof of an \(O(M(n)\sqrt n)\) implementation.
The condition \(B[0]=0\) is about information flow: \(B(x)^r\) then starts at degree \(r\), so a coefficient below \(n\) can only use \(a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1}\). With a nonzero constant term, arbitrarily high powers of \(B\) can influence the constant coefficient, so a finite prefix does not generally determine the composition.

title: 07 — Formal Power Series
text:
6. Compositional inverse (reversion)
For \(A(0)=0\) and \(A'(0)\) a unit, there is one series \(B\) beginning with \(x/A'(0)\) that satisfies \(A(B)=x\). Newton solves the equation \(A(B)-x=0\) by the familiar tangent correction:
\[
B_{new}=B-\frac{A(B)-x}{A'(B)}\pmod{x^{2m}}.
\]
This needs composition plus multiplicative inversion and has the same asymptotic bottleneck as the chosen composition routine. If only one or a structured set of coefficients is needed, Lagrange inversion is usually better:
For integers \(1\le k\le n\),
\[
[x^n]B(x)^k=\frac{k}{n}[t^{n-k}]\left(\frac{t}{A(t)}\right)^n.
\]
This divided form requires \(n\) to be invertible in the coefficient field; in small characteristic, use a division-free identity or a method designed for that characteristic.
For \(A=x+x^2\), write \(B=x+b_2x^2+b_3x^3+\cdots\). The condition \(B+B^2=x\) first gives \(b_2=-1\), then \(b_3+2b_2=0\), so \(b_3=2\). Thus \(B=x-x^2+2x^3+\cdots\). The derivative in the Newton denominator has constant term \(A'(0)\), so it remains a unit throughout. Composition is the expensive step; reversion should not be billed at ordinary multiplication cost.

title: 07 — Formal Power Series
text:
7. Sparse series
Dense NTT is wasteful when only \(K\) coefficients of the defining series are nonzero. Coefficient recurrences from derivatives often give \(O(nK)\): for \(B=\exp(A)\), \(B'=A'B\), hence
\[
nb_n=\sum_{i=1}^n i a_i b_{n-i}.
\]
Similarly, after \(b_0=a_0^{-1}\), \(B=A^{-1}\) uses \(b_n=-a_0^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_{n-i}\) for \(n\ge1\). The exponential recurrence additionally divides by \(n\), so it is valid only while each \(1,\ldots,n\) is a unit (for example \(n<MOD\) over \(\mathbb F_{MOD}\)). Choose sparse versus dense by estimated work, not merely by degree.

title: 07 — Formal Power Series
07 — Formal Power Series
text:
9. Contest checklist and reference
Before selecting an operation, specify output indices \(0,\ldots,n-1\), coefficient ring, constant normalization, valuation, and required integer divisions. For powers, test \(k=0\) and the zero input before finding a leading coefficient. For logarithms distinguish \(A\) from \(A/A(0)\). For composition, distinguish a finite outer polynomial from an unknown infinite outer series: only the latter generally requires inner constant zero for finite-prefix data.

title: 06 — Fast Polynomial Algorithms
text: A polynomial is a finite coefficient array, but it is useful to think of it as a compact description of size-indexed choices: \([x^k]A(x)\) is the answer for total size \(k\). This chapter explains why the fast operations work and when their algebraic preconditions hold. It assumes your library already supplies tested convolution and basic polynomial operations.

title: 06 — Fast Polynomial Algorithms
text:
Prerequisites, notation, and learning objectives
Read fields and modular units and counting products. You should learn to justify transform multiplication, prove the division/remainder invariant, recover a polynomial from samples, and recognize correlations and shifts.
Write \(A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{a}a_ix^i\), where \(x\) is an indeterminate and \(a_i\) belong to a commutative coefficient ring \(R\). The degree is the largest index with nonzero coefficient; the zero polynomial has no ordinary finite degree. We use \(\deg0=-\infty\) when comparing degrees. A polynomial equality means coefficientwise equality; it need not mean equality as functions on a finite field (for example \(x^p-x\) vanishes everywhere in \(\mathbb F_p\)).
Let \(M(n)\) be the arithmetic-operation cost of multiplying polynomials with at most \(n\) coefficients. For FFT-compatible lengths, \(M(n)=O(n\log n)\). Complexity estimates assume \(M(n)/n\) is nondecreasing and costs over doubling sizes sum to \(O(M(n))\), as with schoolbook or FFT multiplication. Field operations have unit cost here; integer bit complexity is a separate cost.

title: 06 — Fast Polynomial Algorithms
text:
1. Multiplication is adding independent sizes
For \(C(x)=A(x)B(x)\),
\[c_k=\sum_{i+j=k}a_ib_j. \tag{1}\]
Each summand chooses an \(i\)-sized object from \(A\) and a \((k-i)\)-sized object from \(B\). This “split a total” meaning is why convolution occurs in counting, DP merging, and formal power series.
The transform idea is simple: evaluate polynomials at a specially chosen set of points. At every point \(z\), \((AB)(z)=A(z)B(z)\), so multiplication becomes pointwise. An FFT uses complex roots of unity; an NTT uses roots of unity in a finite field. Interpolation returns to coefficient form.

Why evaluation at roots is invertible and fast
Work over a field containing a primitive \(L\)th root \(w\), with \(L\) invertible. Primitive means \(w^L=1\) and \(w^d\ne1\) for \(1\le d<L\). For an integer \(t\),
\[\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}w^{jt}=\begin{cases}L,&L\mid t,\\0,&L\nmid t.\end{cases}\]
In the second case multiplication of the sum by \(1-w^t\) telescopes to \(1-w^{Lt}=0\); its multiplier is a nonzero field element and hence invertible. If \(\widehat a_j=A(w^j)\) and \(\deg A<L\), this proves
\[\frac1L\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}\widehat a_jw^{-jk}
=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}a_i\frac1L\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}w^{j(i-k)}=a_k,
\qquad 0\le k<L.\]
Each coefficient survives only its matching frequency sum. To evaluate fast when \(L\) is a power of two, split even and odd coefficient indices: \(A(x)=A_e(x^2)+xA_o(x^2)\). The point squares \(w^{2j}\) have only \(L/2\) distinct values, and the pair \(w^j,w^{j+L/2}\) combines the same two recursive values with opposite signs. At each stage every coefficient is in exactly one even or odd child. Thus \(T(L)=2T(L/2)+O(L)=O(L\log L)\); inverse evaluation uses the same recursion with \(w^{-1}\) and final scaling by \(L^{-1}\).
For example, over \(\mathbb F_{17}\), \(w=4\) has order four. The values of \(1+2x\) at \(1,4,16,13\) are \(3,9,16,10\). The inverse formula recovers coefficients \((1,2,0,0)\). This is exact finite-field arithmetic, unlike FFT rounding over complex numbers.


Transform contract
For an NTT of length \(L=2^s\) modulo prime \(p\), we need \(L\mid p-1\) so the field has a primitive \(L\)th root of unity. The result length must cover every possible degree, so \(L\ge |A|+|B|-1\). For example, \(998244353=119\cdot2^{23}+1\) supports powers of two through \(2^{23}\).
If the answer is modulo an arbitrary \(m\), do not pretend one NTT prime computes it. Convolve under one or more NTT-friendly primes, reconstruct the integer coefficient by CRT (or use Garner to perform the same reconstruction directly modulo \(m\) when the bounded coefficients are nonnegative), then reduce. Garner avoids storing a huge reconstructed integer; it does not remove the reconstruction-range requirement. For signed coefficients, centered CRT must also determine whether the representative means \(c\) or \(c-P\), where \(P\) is the product of auxiliary primes; a direct Garner residue needs the corresponding sign correction modulo \(m\). The number of primes is determined by a proved bound on the integer coefficients: for a signed coefficient of absolute value at most \(B\), centered CRT needs a product of moduli greater than \(2B\). Three primes are a convention, not a proof. Complex FFT instead needs coefficient splitting and a rounding-error bound.


Worked failure: insufficient padding
For \(A=B=1+x\), the true product is \(1+2x+x^2\). A length-two transform knows only values at roots of \(x^2=1\), so it recovers \(2+2x\): the \(x^2\) coefficient wraps into the constant term. Evaluation multiplies in \(R[x]/(x^L-1)\). Padding until \(\deg(AB)<L\) makes this cyclic product equal the desired ordinary product. Empty arrays should return the zero polynomial before choosing \(L\).

title: 06 — Fast Polynomial Algorithms
section: 2. Division: turn the high-degree end into a series inverse
text:
2. Division: turn the high-degree end into a series inverse
Assume \(B\ne0\) and its leading coefficient is a unit. The zero dividend has quotient and remainder zero; a unit constant divisor has zero remainder.
Given \(A=BQ+R\) with \(\deg R<\deg B\), ordinary long division removes the highest remaining term one at a time. Reversal makes those highest terms become the low-degree terms of a formal power series, where inversion is fast. If \(\deg A<\deg B\), there is nothing to divide: return \(Q=0,R=A\).
Let \(k=\deg A-\deg B+1\). Define \(\operatorname{rev}_k(F)\) by reading from \(F\)’s actual leading coefficient downward, retaining \(k\) coefficients and padding with zeros only after its constant term. Then
\[
\operatorname{rev}_k(Q)
\equiv \operatorname{rev}_k(A)\operatorname{rev}_k(B)^{-1}\pmod{x^k}. \tag{2}
\]
Why is this legal? The leading coefficient of \(B\) becomes the constant coefficient of \(\operatorname{rev}_k(B)\); it can be inverted precisely when the leading coefficient is a unit (equivalently nonzero over a field). Terms from \(R\) land beyond the first \(k\) reversed coefficients and disappear modulo \(x^k\). Reverse the quotient back, then compute \(R=A-BQ\).
For example, \(A=x^3+2x+1\) and \(B=x+1\) give \(k=3\). Their reversed prefixes are \(1+2x^2\) and \(1+x\). Modulo \(x^3\), \((1+x)^{-1}=1-x+x^2\), so the reversed quotient is \(1-x+3x^2\). Reversing yields \(Q=x^2-x+3\) and \(R=-2\). Multiplying \(BQ+R\) recovers \(A\). The inverse used here follows from the geometric series; general fast inversion is derived in formal power series.
This costs \(O(M(n))\) with fast multiplication. Over a general ring it requires the leading coefficient of \(B\) to be a unit. In particular, modulo a composite number a nonzero leading coefficient might not be invertible, so this division contract can fail.

title: 06 — Fast Polynomial Algorithms
text:
3. Product trees and multipoint evaluation
To evaluate \(f\) at points \(x_0,\ldots,x_{m-1}\), build a balanced tree. A leaf stores \(x-x_i\); an internal node stores the product of its children:
\[P_v(x)=\prod_{i\text{ below }v}(x-x_i).\]
At the root, replace \(f\) by its remainder modulo \(P_{root}\). A polynomial remainder modulo \(x-x_i\) is its value at \(x_i\), so recursively passing the remainder modulo each child reaches \(f(x_i)\) at every leaf. This is the same divide-and-conquer idea as a segment tree: a node stores the polynomial that vanishes at all points in its interval.
If \(\deg f=O(m)\), fast division at each level costs \(O(M(m)\log m)\) in the balanced case. For a higher-degree \(f\), first reducing it modulo \(P_{root}\) adds the cost of that division. For a small number of points, Horner’s rule is simpler and often faster; use a product tree only when the asymptotic saving matters.

title: 06 — Fast Polynomial Algorithms
text:
4. Interpolation reverses evaluation
Given \(m\) samples, we seek a polynomial of degree less than \(m\). This bound is essential: adding any multiple of \(\prod_i(x-x_i)\) preserves all samples.
Now suppose the points \(x_i\) are pairwise distinct in the coefficient field and the desired values \(y_i\) are known. Let
\[P(x)=\prod_i(x-x_i).\]
The polynomial \(P(x)/(x-x_i)\) vanishes at every \(x_j\) except \(x_i\). Dividing it by its value there, \(P'(x_i)\), creates a basis polynomial that is \(1\) at \(x_i\) and \(0\) at every other sample. Therefore
\[f(x)=\sum_i y_i\frac{P(x)}{(x-x_i)P'(x_i)}. \tag{3}\]
This formula is not magic: each summand is responsible for exactly one sample. Evaluate \(P'\) at all points via the product tree, place \(w_i=y_i/P'(x_i)\) at leaves, and merge children as
\[F_v=F_LP_R+F_RP_L.\]
The merge invariant is that \(F_v\) is the sum of all leaf terms \(w_i\prod_{j\text{ below }v,j\ne i}(x-x_j)\). Left terms need exactly the missing right product and vice versa, so no leaf is lost or repeated.
At the root this is (3), in \(O(M(n)\log n)\). If points repeat, \(P'(x_i)=0\) and this formula is undefined. Repeated samples with identical values can be deduplicated; contradictory values admit no solution. Hermite interpolation adds derivative data at repeated points and is a different contract. For distinct points over a field, a nonzero polynomial of degree below \(m\) cannot have \(m\) roots: division by each root factor would force its degree to be at least \(m\). Thus the formula gives the unique permitted polynomial. Over a general ring, require every difference \(x_i-x_j\) to be a unit.
For values at the \(n+1\) consecutive points \(0,\ldots,n\), the denominators simplify to \(i!(-1)^{n-i}(n-i)!\). Prefix and suffix products of \((t-j)\) evaluate (3) at one arbitrary \(t\) in \(O(n)\). Factorials must be invertible, so normally \(n<MOD\).

title: 06 — Fast Polynomial Algorithms
section: 5. Taylor shift: substitute \(x+c\) in one convolution
text:
5. Taylor shift: substitute \(x+c\) in one convolution
We want the coefficients of \(f(x+c)\), not just its value at one point. Expanding each monomial gives
\[[x^k]f(x+c)=\sum_{i\ge k}a_i\binom ikc^{i-k}. \tag{4}\]
This says degree \(i\) contributes to every lower degree \(k\). Expand the binomial coefficient and reverse the \(a_i i!\) array; (4) becomes one convolution with the array \(c^j/j!\), followed by division by \(k!\). If \(n=\deg f\), put \(u_{n-i}=a_i i!\) and \(v_j=c^j/j!\). Then
\[\frac{(u*v)_{n-k}}{k!}=
\sum_{i\ge k}a_i\binom ikc^{i-k},\]
so \((u*v)_{n-k}\) is \(k!\) times the shifted coefficient of \(x^k\); the final division by \(k!\) is essential. For example, if \(f(x)=x^2\) and \(c=1\), then the convolution entries at indices \(2,1,0\) are \(1,2,2\), and division by \(0!,1!,2!\) gives the coefficients \(1,2,1\) of \((x+1)^2\). The reversal lines up \(i-k\) as a convolution index. As with binomial transforms, this needs the factorials through the working degree to be units; it is normally used over a prime modulus larger than that degree.
The arrays in the shift have indices \(0,\ldots,n\). For output index \(0\le k\le n\), only convolution terms with \(u_{n-i}\) and \(v_{i-k}\), \(k\le i\le n\), enter index \(n-k\). For \(f=1+3x+2x^2\) and \(c=2\), the shifted polynomial is \(15+11x+2x^2\).

title: 06 — Fast Polynomial Algorithms
section: 6. Many factors: keep merge sizes balanced
text:
6. Many factors: keep merge sizes balanced
For \(\prod_i A_i(x)\), multiplying factors one after another repeatedly makes a large polynomial absorb a tiny one. A divide-and-conquer product tree, or a priority queue that merges the two smallest degrees, keeps products balanced. For \(k\) positive-degree factors of total degree \(N\), a product tree balanced by number of factors has at most \(\lceil\log_2 k\rceil\) levels; total degrees per level are at most \(N\). Under the multiplication assumptions above, it costs \(O(M(N)\log(k+1))\). Degree-balanced merging is often faster when sizes vary widely. Absorb constants separately in \(O(k)\) operations and stop if a factor is zero; arbitrarily many constants still incur input cost.
If the question only asks through degree \(D\), truncate after each merge. In a knapsack-style product such as \(\prod_i(1+x^{w_i})\), coefficients above \(D\) can never influence lower coefficients later, so retaining them only wastes time and memory.

title: 06 — Fast Polynomial Algorithms
section: 7. Worked contest translation: all string alignments
text:
7. Worked contest translation: all string alignments
Let a binary text have length \(n\) and a pattern length \(m\le n\). We want the Hamming distance at every start \(0\le s\le n-m\). Define text indicator \(a_i=[\text{text}_i=1]\) and reversed pattern indicator \(b_{m-1-j}=[\text{pattern}_j=1]\). Then
\[[x^{s+m-1}]A(x)B(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}a_{s+j}[\text{pattern}_j=1].\]
This counts aligned pairs of ones: \(i+(m-1-j)=s+m-1\) forces \(i=s+j\). If \(u_s\) and \(v\) count ones in the text window and pattern, mismatches equal \(u_s+v-2[x^{s+m-1}]AB\). Prefix sums give all \(u_s\) in linear time and one convolution gives all correlations. For text 10110 and pattern 110, the one-one correlations are \((1,1,2)\) and the distances are \((2,2,0)\). The pattern reversal is justified by the index equation. Complexity is \(O(M(n+m))\) and linear storage; exact convolution needs coefficient range through at least \(m\).

title: 06 — Fast Polynomial Algorithms
text:
8. Failure checklist and reference

Before an NTT, verify both the required length and the root-of-unity condition.
Before a polynomial inverse, verify a nonzero/invertible constant term; before division, verify the leading coefficient condition instead.
Normalize negative coefficients in the target ring.
For CRT convolution, prove the reconstruction range covers a coefficient.
Interpolation requires distinct sample points; consecutive-point formulas additionally need nonzero factorial denominators.
Check a small product, quotient/remainder identity, and interpolation samples independently of the fast routine.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
text: Symmetry problems ask when two drawings, colorings, or arrangements should be considered the same after an allowed move. They are not “divide by the number of symmetries” problems: one object can be fixed by several moves while another is fixed only by doing nothing. This chapter develops the averaging rule that accounts for that difference.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
text:
Prerequisites and learning objectives
Use bijections and double counting, inclusion–exclusion, and modular units. Weighted inventories use coefficient extraction; its meaning is introduced locally below. You should finish able to specify the exact symmetry group, prove the averaging rule, derive position cycles, count constrained fixed objects, and explain why division by the number of moves is or is not legal.
All sets and groups used for ordinary counting are finite. The notation \(X/G\) means the set of orbits, not numerical division. A permutation is a bijection of positions; its cycles follow repeated application until returning to the starting position. Different cycles share no position.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
section: 1. From an equivalence relation to an action
text:
1. From an equivalence relation to an action
A finite group \(G\) is a set of allowed moves with an associative composition, an identity move, and an inverse for every move. It acts on a set \(X\) of objects when every \(g\in G\) gives a map \(x\mapsto g\cdot x\), the identity fixes every object, and \(g\cdot(h\cdot x)=(gh)\cdot x\). This last law says that group multiplication and applying moves in sequence use the same convention.
The orbit \(Gx\) is every version of \(x\) reachable by allowed moves. Thus an orbit is one object “up to symmetry.” The stabilizer \(G_x\) is the set of moves leaving \(x\) visually unchanged. They satisfy
\[|Gx|\,|G_x|=|G|. \tag{1}\]
Map each move \(g\) to \(g\cdot x\). If \(h\cdot x=y\), all moves reaching \(y\) are exactly \(hs\) with \(s\in G_x\): \(hs\cdot x=h\cdot x\), and \(g\cdot x=h\cdot x\) implies \(h^{-1}g\in G_x\). Thus every reachable object has exactly \(|G_x|\) preimages. Partitioning the \(|G|\) moves into these equal fibers proves (1). Such a fiber is called a coset of the stabilizer.
This immediately explains why naive division fails. Under rotation, the three-bead coloring AAA has orbit size \(1\), while AAB has orbit size \(3\). The raw colorings cannot all be assigned weight \(1/3\).
Recognition. First write the actual move set.

necklaces use rotations \(C_n\);
bracelets use rotations and reflections \(D_n\);
a square grid under quarter turns uses a small geometric permutation group;
interchangeable colors introduce another action, usually handled through cycle types or another Burnside layer.

The moves must preserve the problem’s validity condition. If they do not, their orbits are irrelevant to the requested count.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
section: 2. Burnside’s lemma: average fixed objects, not raw objects
text:
2. Burnside’s lemma: average fixed objects, not raw objects
Assume here that both \(G\) and the object set \(X\) are finite. For a move \(g\), let \(\operatorname{Fix}(g)=\{x:g\cdot x=x\}\) be the objects unchanged by that move. Burnside’s lemma says
\[\boxed{|X/G|={1\over|G|}\sum_{g\in G}|\operatorname{Fix}(g)|}. \tag{2}\]
It looks surprising because it counts a different quantity for every move. Here is the proof and the meaning. Count pairs \((g,x)\) such that \(gx=x\). Counting by \(g\) gives the numerator. Now look at one orbit \(O\). By (1), each object in \(O\) has \(|G|/|O|\) fixing moves, so the objects of that orbit contribute
\[|O|\cdot {|G|\over|O|}=|G|\]
pairs. Every orbit contributes exactly \(|G|\); dividing by \(|G|\) counts one per orbit.
For a coloring with \(c\) available colors, a move permutes positions into cycles. A fixed coloring must be constant along one cycle, and each cycle independently chooses a color. Thus a move with \(z(g)\) cycles fixes exactly \(c^{z(g)}\) unrestricted colorings.

Example: necklaces
For \(n\ge1\), rotation by \(r\) on \(n\) positions repeatedly jumps by \(r\). Starting at one position, it returns after \(n/\gcd(n,r)\) jumps, so there are \(\gcd(n,r)\) cycles. Applying (2) gives
\[
N(n,c)={1\over n}\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}c^{\gcd(n,r)}
={1\over n}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(n/d)c^d. \tag{3}
\]
For \(n=3,c=2\), the identity fixes \(2^3=8\) colorings and each nontrivial rotation fixes the two constant colorings. Hence there are \((8+2+2)/3=4\) binary necklaces. The divisor form groups rotations with the same cycle count; it is normally preferable after factoring \(n\).
To justify the regrouping, write \(r=du\) and \(n=dv\) for rotations with \(\gcd(n,r)=d\). Then \(0\le u<v\) and \(\gcd(u,v)=1\), giving \(\varphi(v)\) rotations. The \(d=n\) identity case uses \(\varphi(1)=1\).
For bracelets, include reflections too. Derive their cycles from the axis: if \(n\) is odd, each reflection has one fixed position and \((n-1)/2\) pairs. If \(n\) is even, half have two fixed positions and \((n-2)/2\) pairs, while half have no fixed positions and \(n/2\) pairs. This parity split is why a memorized necklace formula does not automatically answer a bracelet task.
For \(n=4,c=2\), rotations contribute \(16+2+4+2=24\). Two reflections have three cycles and two have two cycles, adding \(2\cdot8+2\cdot4=24\). The bracelet count is \(48/8=6\), while the necklace count is \(24/4=6\). Equality happens here; it is not a general identity. For \(n=6,c=2\), rotations give \(84/6=14\) necklaces, while reflections add \(3\cdot16+3\cdot8=72\), giving \((84+72)/12=13\) bracelets.
We use the dihedral group of \(2n\) formal moves, even for \(n=1,2\) when several moves induce the same permutation of bead positions. Burnside remains valid for this nonfaithful action: every distinct induced move occurs equally often.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
section: 3. Pólya: remember color counts while averaging
text:
3. Pólya: remember color counts while averaging
Burnside with \(c^{z(g)}\) only counts all colors as freely available. To require, say, exactly three red and two blue beads, attach a marker \(y_i\) to color \(i\). A length-\(j\) cycle painted color \(i\) contributes \(y_i^j\), because that choice uses color \(i\) exactly \(j\) times.
The cycle index records this for every group element:
\[
Z_G(s_1,s_2,\ldots)={1\over|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\prod_{j\ge1}s_j^{c_j(g)}, \tag{4}
\]
where \(c_j(g)\) is the number of length-\(j\) cycles. Substitute
\[s_j\leftarrow y_1^j+\cdots+y_c^j.\]
Then the coefficient of \(y_1^{a_1}\cdots y_c^{a_c}\) is the number of symmetry classes using exactly \(a_i\) positions of color \(i\). For a two-position segment under reflection, the cycle index is
\[\frac12(s_1^2+s_2).\]
After substitution it becomes \(\tfrac12((y_1+y_2)^2+y_1^2+y_2^2)\). The coefficient of \(y_1y_2\) is \(1\): the two raw mixed colorings form one reflection class. The swap itself fixes no mixed coloring, which is why its term is \(y_1^2+y_2^2\) rather than \((y_1+y_2)^2\).
For weighted states with inventory \(A(x)=\sum_w a_wx^w\), where \(a_w\) counts the available states of weight \(w\), use \(s_j\leftarrow A(x^j)\). A cycle of length \(j\) repeats the chosen component \(j\) times, which is exactly why its weight variable becomes \(x^j\). Truncate to the requested total weight throughout.
Assume weights are nonnegative integers and each \(a_w\) is finite. For a fixed finite number of positions, every coefficient then counts finitely many assignments. The notation \([x^s]\) selects assignments of total weight \(s\). For example, a swapped pair with positive integer states has inventory \(x^2+x^4+\cdots=x^2/(1-x^2)\), because both positions receive the same value.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
section: 4. Constraints belong inside the fixed-point count

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
text:
5. Symmetric groups and conjugacy classes
For \(S_n\), listing all \(n!\) vertex relabelings is impossible. In problems whose fixed count depends only on cycle lengths, all permutations with the same cycle type behave alike. A type \(1^{m_1}2^{m_2}\cdots\) with \(\sum_i i m_i=n\) has class size
\[\frac{n!}{\prod_i i^{m_i}m_i!}. \tag{5}\]
The denominator has a concrete purpose: rotating a cycle of length \(i\) does not change the cycle, and permuting the \(m_i\) equal-length cycles does not change the permutation. Burnside can therefore sum over integer partitions of \(n\), not over \(n!\) permutations. For each type, construct the induced action on the objects of interest (for unlabeled graphs, on unordered vertex pairs), count its cycles, and multiply by (5). If vertices are colored as well as joined by edges, there are two induced actions: a fixed coloring is constant on each vertex cycle, while a fixed edge set is constant on each unordered-pair cycle. Enforce a requirement such as “every color is used” inside that fixed count, for example by inclusion–exclusion over missing colors.

Induced pair cycles, derived
Two permutations are conjugate if one is \(hgh^{-1}\) for a relabelling \(h\). Conjugation only renames the entries of cycles, so cycle type determines a conjugacy class in \(S_n\). Formula (5) starts with all \(n!\) linear orderings, cuts them into cycles of prescribed lengths, and removes rotations within each cycle and reorderings among equally long cycles.
For simple undirected graphs, a vertex permutation acts on unordered pairs. Consider two different vertex cycles of lengths \(a,b\). A pair with one endpoint in each returns after \(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\) steps. The \(ab\) pairs therefore form \(\gcd(a,b)\) edge cycles. Inside one length-\(a\) vertex cycle, pairs are classified by circular distance \(1,\ldots,\lfloor a/2\rfloor\). Each distance is one orbit; when \(a\) is even, opposite pairs have orbit size \(a/2\) instead of \(a\). Hence the number of induced pair cycles for lengths \(a_1,\ldots,a_r\) is
\[e=\sum_{i=1}^r\lfloor a_i/2\rfloor+
\sum_{1\le i<j\le r}\gcd(a_i,a_j).\]
A fixed simple graph independently includes or excludes each entire edge cycle, giving \(2^e\). For type \((2,1)\) on three vertices, \(e=1+1=2\): the edge inside the swapped pair is fixed, and its two edges to the remaining vertex form one orbit. There are four invariant graphs. Over \(S_3\), the three types contribute \(1\cdot8+3\cdot4+2\cdot2=24\), so there are four unlabelled simple graphs on three vertices: zero, one, two, or three edges.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
text:
6. Arithmetic and modelling checks

Division by \(|G|\) modulo prime \(p\) requires \(p\nmid |G|\). Otherwise divide exactly before reduction, or use a problem-specific integral rearrangement.
A reflection and a rotation with the same order need not have the same cycles.
If colors are themselves indistinguishable, ordinary position Burnside still treats color names as distinct; model the color symmetry too.
Exact multiplicities require coefficient extraction from (4), not simply colors ^ cycles.
On a two- or three-position toy case, enumerate raw objects, group their orbits by hand, and compare with the Burnside numerator before coding.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
text:
7. Algorithm selection and reference
For an explicitly listed group acting on \(v\) positions, cycle decomposition costs \(O(v)\) per element. The total is \(O(|G|v)\) plus fixed-object counting. Necklace divisor grouping uses one modular exponentiation per divisor after factorization. Enumerating cycle types of \(S_n\) visits the integer partitions of \(n\); the edge-cycle formula above takes \(O(n^2)\) gcd operations per type as a simple bound. Partition enumeration itself is a serious limit, not a polynomial-time solution for arbitrary \(n\).
If a Burnside numerator \(A\) is divisible by \(g=|G|\), computing \(A\bmod gm\) is enough to recover \((A/g)\bmod m\): write \(A=qgm+r\) with \(0\le r<gm\), then \(g\mid r\) and \(A/g\equiv r/g\pmod m\). This avoids an illegal inverse when \(g\) is not a unit, provided the fixed-count algorithm works modulo \(gm\) and the larger modulus fits the arithmetic model.
Before implementing, identify positions, moves, valid objects, fixed-cycle constraints, and the ring for the final division. Test a nontrivial stabilizer.

title: 04 — Advanced Combinatorics
text:
Combinatorics is not primarily a collection of formulas. It is the job of describing exactly what one valid object is, then counting those objects without losing or duplicating any of them. This chapter starts from that description. It assumes that factorials and binomial coefficients are already in your library, but it does not assume that you have previously seen the counting models below.
Before doing algebra, write four answers on paper:
Those answers prevent most wrong applications of a correct formula.

title: 04 — Advanced Combinatorics
text:
Prerequisites and learning objectives
Read proofs and counting arguments and units in modular algebra. After this chapter you should be able to derive an inclusion–exclusion sum, distinguish labelled assignments from unlabelled partitions, identify a unique recursive split, and expose convolution inside a binomial sum.
Throughout, \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) for an integer \(n\ge0\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). An empty product is \(1\). We use \(\binom nk=0\) for \(k<0\) or \(k>n\) when \(n\ge0\). The value \(0^0=1\) in a counting formula represents the unique empty function. Binomial coefficients count subsets; factorials count linear orders of distinct objects. Neither definition requires division in a coefficient ring.

title: 04 — Advanced Combinatorics
text:
1. Recognition map

For example, “put \(n\) students into \(k\) nonempty teams” has labelled students but unlabelled teams. “Assign every student one of \(k\) named rooms” has labelled rooms. The two answers differ by a factor of \(k!\); it is not a minor implementation detail.

title: 04 — Advanced Combinatorics
text:
2. Inclusion–exclusion: correcting overcounting
Suppose \(U\) is the set of all candidate objects and \(E_i\) is the set of objects violating requirement \(i\). We want objects in none of the bad sets:
\[|U\setminus(E_1\cup\cdots\cup E_m)|.\]
The easy count \(|U|\) includes bad objects. Subtracting every \(|E_i|\) removes an object that violates two requirements twice, so it is now missing once too many. Add pair intersections back; then three-way intersections are too large again; and so on. The resulting formula is
\[
|U\setminus\textstyle\bigcup_i E_i|
=\sum_{S\subseteq[m]}(-1)^{|S|}\left|\bigcap_{i\in S}E_i\right|. \tag{IE}
\]
The empty intersection is \(U\). Formula (IE) is safest when understood per object: if a particular object violates exactly \(t\) requirements, it occurs in \(\binom{t}{j}\) intersections of size \(j\), so its total coefficient is
\[\sum_{j=0}^{t}(-1)^j\binom tj=(1-1)^t.\]
It is \(1\) for a valid object (\(t=0\)) and \(0\) otherwise. This tells us exactly what IE is calculating: it filters all candidates down to candidates with no bad property.

Example: functions that use every target
How many functions from \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) to \([k]\) use every one of the \(k\) targets? There are \(k^n\) unrestricted functions. Let \(E_j\) mean “target \(j\) is unused.” If we insist that a chosen set \(S\) of \(i\) targets is unused, each input has only \(k-i\) possible images, so the intersection has \((k-i)^n\) functions. There are \(\binom ki\) choices of \(S\). Thus
\[\#\text{surjections}=\sum_{i=0}^{k}(-1)^i\binom ki(k-i)^n. \tag{1}\]
Notice the separate meaning of every factor: choose which forbidden targets are absent, then count functions that avoid all of them. IE is useful here because intersections are simpler than “uses every target” directly.


Exactly \(r\) satisfied conditions
Sometimes the target is not “none of the bad events.” Let \(a_j\) be the number of objects satisfying exactly \(j\) of \(m\) conditions. Let \(b_k\) count pairs
\[\bigl(\text{object},\ \text{a chosen set of $k$ conditions it satisfies}\bigr).\]
An object satisfying exactly \(j\) conditions contributes \(\binom jk\) such pairs, so double counting gives
\[b_k=\sum_{j\ge k}\binom jk a_j. \tag{2}\]
Binomial inversion undoes that “choose \(k\) among \(j\)” operation:
\[a_r=\sum_{k=r}^{m}(-1)^{k-r}\binom kr b_k. \tag{3}\]
To verify this inverse, fix an object satisfying \(j\) conditions. Its coefficient on the right is
\[
\sum_{k=r}^j(-1)^{k-r}\binom kr\binom jk
=\binom jr\sum_{k=r}^j(-1)^{k-r}\binom{j-r}{k-r}
=\binom jr(1-1)^{j-r}.
\]
The first equality chooses the \(r\) distinguished conditions first, then the other \(k-r\) selected conditions. This weight is one when \(j=r\) and zero otherwise, which proves (3). Notice that \(b_k\) counts marked pairs, not simply the objects satisfying at least \(k\) conditions.
For example, take all subsets of \(\{1,2\}\) and let condition \(i\) be membership of \(i\). Then \((a_0,a_1,a_2)=(1,2,1)\) and \((b_0,b_1,b_2)=(4,4,1)\): the full subset contributes twice to \(b_1\). Formula (3) gives \(a_1=b_1-2b_2=2\). Treating \(b_1\) as the three nonempty subsets would instead give \(1\), exposing the mistaken interpretation.
Use (2) to derive the quantity you can count, and (3) only after you know what \(b_k\) means. This prevents the common mistake of alternating signs without a defined universe.

title: 04 — Advanced Combinatorics
text:
3. Three recurring object families

Stirling numbers: partitions and permutation cycles
The second-kind Stirling number \(\left\{ {n\atop k}\right\}\) is the number of ways to split \(n\) labelled elements into \(k\) nonempty unlabelled blocks. Consider where label \(n\) goes. Either it joins one of the existing \(k\) blocks of a partition of \([n-1]\), or it forms its own block beside a partition into \(k-1\) blocks. Therefore
\[
\left\{ {n\atop k}\right\}
=k\left\{ {n-1\atop k}\right\}
+\left\{ {n-1\atop k-1}\right\}. \tag{4}
\]
For instance, \(\left\{ {3\atop2}\right\}=3\): the singleton can be \(1\), \(2\), or \(3\). If the \(k\) blocks are then assigned to \(k\) named targets, there are \(k!\left\{ {n\atop k}\right\}\) functions using every target. Comparing this with (1) explains, rather than merely states,
\[\left\{ {n\atop k}\right\}={1\over k!}\sum_{i=0}^k(-1)^{k-i}\binom ki i^n.\]
This is first an identity of integers. If it is evaluated by dividing in a coefficient ring, \(k!\) must be a unit; over \(\mathbb F_p\) the usual factorial-inverse route therefore requires \(k<p\).
The unsigned first-kind number \(\left[ {n\atop k}\right]\) counts permutations of \([n]\) having \(k\) cycles. To add label \(n\), either make it a one-element cycle, or insert it immediately after any of the \(n-1\) existing labels in a cycle. This gives
\[
\left[ {n\atop k}\right]
=(n-1)\left[ {n-1\atop k}\right]
+\left[ {n-1\atop k-1}\right]. \tag{5}
\]
Both triangles begin with value \(1\) at \((n,k)=(0,0)\) and zero outside \(0\le k\le n\); entries with \(k=0<n\) are zero. For \(n=3\), the cycle counts for \(k=1,2,3\) are \(2,3,1\): the two directed three-cycles, the three choices of a transposition, and the identity. These sum to \(3!=6\).
The second-kind triangle also changes polynomial bases. Let \(x^{\underline j}=x(x-1)\cdots(x-j+1)\), with \(x^{\underline0}=1\). Counting functions from \([K]\) to \([x]\) by the partition of inputs with equal images gives
\[x^K=\sum_{j=0}^K\left\{{K\atop j}\right\}x^{\underline j}.\]
Each summand first partitions the inputs into \(j\) nonempty fibers, then assigns distinct target names to those fibers. The proof holds for all nonnegative integer \(x\), hence gives a polynomial identity over the integers. For \(K=3\), \(x^3=x^{\underline3}+3x^{\underline2}+x\).


Catalan objects: an independent first split
Catalan numbers count many objects because those objects have the same decomposition. A balanced-parenthesis string is either empty, or has the form
( a balanced string ) another balanced string. The first matching ) creates this split uniquely. If \(C_n\) counts strings with \(n\) pairs, choosing \(i\) pairs inside the first pair leaves \(n-1-i\) pairs after it, so
\[C_0=1,\qquad C_n=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}C_iC_{n-1-i}. \tag{6}\]
The product appears because the two pieces can be chosen independently. With \(C(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}C_nx^n\), (6) becomes \(C(x)=1+xC(x)^2\), from which
\[C_n={1\over n+1}\binom{2n}{n}.\]
One direct derivation views a parenthesis string as a path with an up-step for ( and a down-step for ). There are \(\binom{2n}{n}\) paths ending at height zero. Reflect the prefix through the first step below zero; this bijects the bad paths with paths having \(n+1\) up-steps and \(n-1\) down-steps, of which there are \(\binom{2n}{n+1}=\binom{2n}{n-1}\). Therefore
\[
C_n=\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n-1}
=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
This quotient is an integer combinatorially; when evaluating it in a field, also require \(n+1\) to be invertible (or compute it as an integer before reducing). Computing the binomial by inverse factorials additionally requires factorials through \(2n\) to be units; over \(\mathbb F_p\), \(2n<p\) suffices. When those factorials vanish, the integer identity still holds but this implementation does not; see modular combinatorics. Do not apply the formula merely because parentheses or trees appear: verify the unique, independent split first.


Integer partitions: choose a multiplicity for each part size
An integer partition ignores the order of parts. For a part size \(j\), we may use it zero, one, two, … times, contributing the size-marking series
\[1+x^j+x^{2j}+\cdots={1\over1-x^j}.\]
Here \([x^n]F(x)\) means the coefficient of \(x^n\) in \(F\). Multiplication adds exponents, so it adds sizes. The displayed inverse is formal: multiplying the series by \(1-x^j\) cancels every positive-degree term and leaves \(1\). There is no claim about substituting a real number into an infinite sum.
Choices for different sizes are independent, so multiply them:
\[P(x)=\prod_{j\ge1}{1\over1-x^j}. \tag{7}\]
This infinite product is formal: to determine \([x^n]P\), factors with \(j>n\) can be replaced by \(1\), so every requested coefficient depends on only finitely many choices.
For \(n=4\), the coefficient of \(x^4\) represents \(4\), \(3+1\), \(2+2\), \(2+1+1\), and \(1+1+1+1\). If each size can be used once, replace the relevant factor by \(1+x^j\); if only some sizes are allowed, omit the others. The product comes from a modelling decision, not from a pattern to memorise.

title: 04 — Advanced Combinatorics
section: 4. Fast binomial transforms by factorial scaling
text:
4. Fast binomial transforms by factorial scaling
The binomial transform
\[b_n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk a_k\]
looks quadratic for all \(n\). Expand the binomial coefficient:
\[
b_n=n!\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{a_k}{k!}\frac1{(n-k)!}. \tag{8}
\]
The right side is the coefficient of \(x^n\) in the product of the two ordinary polynomials whose coefficients are \(a_k/k!\) and \(1/k!\). Thus one convolution, followed by multiplying coefficient \(n\) by \(n!\), computes all \(b_n\).
This is a change of representation: labelled choices produce \(\binom nk\); dividing by factorials changes “choose labels” into ordinary convolution. It requires the factorials through the desired degree to be invertible, normally a prime modulus larger than that degree. See Chapter 06 for the convolution contract.

title: 04 — Advanced Combinatorics
section: 5. Rook polynomials: IE for forbidden permutations
text:
5. Rook polynomials: IE for forbidden permutations
There are \(n\) people and \(n\) jobs. A permutation \(\pi\) is a complete assignment: person \(i\) receives job \(\pi(i)\), with every job used once. Draw an \(n\times n\) board. Row \(i\), column \(j\) is a forbidden cell when person \(i\) may not receive job \(j\). We want the number of permutations that avoid every forbidden cell.
For each forbidden cell \((i,j)\), define the bad event
\[E_{i,j}=\{\pi:\pi(i)=j\}.\]
IE says to sum over sets \(S\) of forbidden assignments that are all forced to happen. But an intersection is impossible if \(S\) asks one person to take two jobs, or two people to take one job. The possible sets are exactly placements of nonattacking rooks on forbidden cells: no two share a row or a column.
Let \(r_k\) be the number of ways to place \(k\) such rooks. Fix one placement. It forces \(k\) person–job pairs, and the remaining \(n-k\) people can be matched to the remaining \(n-k\) jobs in exactly \((n-k)!\) ways. Every placement with \(k\) rooks therefore contributes the same intersection size. Grouping IE terms by \(k\) gives
\[
\boxed{\#\text{valid assignments}
=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k r_k(n-k)!}. \tag{9}
\]
So IE in (9) is calculating the number of complete assignments that use no forbidden cell. \(r_k\) is not the number of assignments; it counts the compatible ways to force \(k\) forbidden assignments while performing IE.

Small example
Suppose \(n=3\) and the forbidden cells are \((1,1)\) and \((2,2)\). The rook counts are \(r_0=1\), \(r_1=2\), \(r_2=1\): place no rook; choose either cell; or choose both cells, which do not share a row or column. Formula (9) gives
\[3!-2\cdot2!+1\cdot1!=6-4+1=3.\]
Indeed the valid permutations are \((2,1,3)\), \((2,3,1)\), and \((3,1,2)\).
Package the rook counts as a polynomial
\[R_B(z)=\sum_{k\ge0}r_kz^k,\]
where \(B\) is the forbidden board. If the forbidden cells split into two parts using disjoint sets of rows and columns, a nonattacking placement is an independent placement in each part. Consequently
\[R_{B_1\cup B_2}(z)=R_{B_1}(z)R_{B_2}(z).\]
For example, \(t\) isolated forbidden cells in distinct rows and columns have \(R_B(z)=(1+z)^t\). This product rule is valuable only after checking that the components share neither a person nor a job; disconnected-looking cells that share a row are not independent.

title: 04 — Advanced Combinatorics
section: 6. A derivation habit and failure checks

title: 04 — Advanced Combinatorics
section: 7. From a count to an algorithm
text:
7. From a count to an algorithm

Worked reduction: a binomially weighted power
Suppose we want \(\sum_{s=0}^N\binom Ns s^K\) for small \(K\) but huge \(N\). An object is a chosen subset \(S\subseteq[N]\) together with a function from \([K]\) into \(S\). Group functions by their \(j\) distinct used targets:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{s=0}^N\binom Ns s^K
&=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(K,N)}\left\{{K\atop j}\right\}
  \sum_{s=j}^N\binom Ns s^{\underline j}\\
&=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(K,N)}\left\{{K\atop j}\right\}
  N^{\underline j}\sum_{s=j}^N\binom{N-j}{s-j}\\
&=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(K,N)}\left\{{K\atop j}\right\}
  N^{\underline j}2^{N-j}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The used targets are distinct and ordered by their fiber blocks; every unused target independently joins \(S\) or stays outside. For \(N=3,K=2\), the original sum is \(0+3+12+9=24\). The transformed sum is \(3\cdot4+6\cdot2=24\). Compute the Stirling row in \(O(K^2)\) ring operations and the falling factorials in \(O(K)\). Binary exponentiation for each power is a safe \(O(K\log N)\) route even when \(2\) is not a unit; division by two to update powers needs a unit.


Worked failure: visually separated forbidden cells
For \(n=3\), forbid \((1,1)\) and \((1,2)\). They share a row, so \(R_B(z)=1+2z\), not \((1+z)^2\). There are \(6-2\cdot2=2\) valid assignments: person 1 must take job 3, then the other two people may swap jobs 1 and 2. The tempting product would add a nonexistent two-rook placement and incorrectly return \(3\).
General IE on \(m\) bad events costs \(2^m\) intersection counts. Stirling or Catalan recurrence tables cost \(O(n^2)\) arithmetic operations through size \(n\). The partition coefficients through \(n\) can use part-size DP in \(O(n^2)\) time and \(O(n)\) space; its invariant fixes multiplicities for the part sizes already processed. A factorial-scaled binomial transform costs one convolution plus \(O(n)\) scaling, under its unit assumptions. Rook IE is fast only if the rook numbers can themselves be obtained efficiently; an arbitrary forbidden board has no promised polynomial-time counting algorithm here.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory

The formulas are less important than the objects they regroup. Each section says what a new coordinate represents, so that it can be re-derived when the statement changes slightly.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
Prerequisites and learning objectives
Use unique factorization and double counting and modular fields and valuations. After reading, you should be able to derive a function from its prime-power values, prove divisor inversion, convert gcd restrictions to frequency sums, and choose between a sieve over a bounded domain and factorization of sparse values.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
Definitions and notation
An arithmetic function assigns a coefficient to each positive integer. Coefficients lie in the integers or a stated commutative ring; no division is assumed unless a unit condition is stated. The function \(\mathbf1(n)=1\) is constant one, \(\operatorname{id}(n)=n\), and \(\varepsilon\) is one at \(n=1\) and zero elsewhere. Products of function values differ from Dirichlet convolution, denoted \(*\) below. The prime factorization \(n=\prod_p p^{e_p}\) has only finitely many nonzero exponents; \(1\) is the empty product. Zero is outside the divisor-transform domain.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
1. Reliable 64-bit primality and factorization
Factorization is useful because most arithmetic functions are determined by a number’s prime powers. Trial division asks every small prime whether it divides \(n\), which becomes too slow for large 64-bit inputs. For arbitrary unsigned 64-bit integers, use deterministic Miller–Rabin to tell primes from composites and Pollard–Rho to split composites.

Miller–Rabin
For odd \(n\), write \(n-1=d\cdot2^{s}\) with \(d\) odd. If \(n\) is prime and \(a\not\equiv0\pmod n\), set \(x=a^d\). Because \(x^{2^s}=1\) and a field has only the two square roots \(\pm1\) of \(1\), the squaring chain must either start at \(1\) or reach \(-1\) before it reaches \(1\). A base that does neither is a witness that \(n\) is composite. A base that passes is only evidence, which is why several bases are tested. After handling \(n<4\) and reducing every base modulo \(n\), testing bases
\[\{2,\ 325,\ 9375,\ 28178,\ 450775,\ 9780504,\ 1795265022\}\]
is deterministic for \(0\le n<2^{64}\) with the usual small/even branches. A base that reduces to zero is skipped, not treated as a compositeness witness; other bases must still be tested. The finite-range certificate is recorded in the SPRP base database. Complexity is \(O(\log n)\) modular multiplications per base.
For example, \(n=21\) has \(n-1=5\cdot4\). For base \(2\), the chain starts \(2^5=11\bmod21\), then squares to \(16\), then \(4\); it neither starts at one nor reaches \(-1=20\). Thus \(2\) witnesses compositeness. Passing one base is weaker: \(2047=23\cdot89\) passes base two.


Pollard–Rho
Iterate a pseudo-random polynomial \(f(x)=x²+c \bmod n\). Although the sequence is not visibly periodic modulo \(n\), it eventually cycles modulo an unknown factor \(p\). If two iterates \(x,y\) agree modulo \(p\), then \(p\mid(x-y)\), and \(\gcd(|x-y|,n)\) can reveal a nontrivial divisor without knowing \(p\) first. Floyd/Brent cycle detection and batched gcds make this fast in practice. It is randomized with heuristic expected time about \(O(p^{1/2})\) for a factor \(p\), often described as \(O(n^{1/4})\) for balanced semiprimes.
Pitfalls. Handle \(n<2\); use unsigned 128-bit multiplication; restart Rho when it returns \(n\); recursion receives prime powers as well as semiprimes; randomized runtime has no strict worst-case guarantee.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
section: 2. Multiplicative functions and the linear sieve
text:
2. Multiplicative functions and the linear sieve
\(f\) is multiplicative when \(f(1)=1\) and \(f(ab)=f(a)f(b)\) for coprime \(a,b\). Prime factorization then says that \(f(n)\) is the product of its values on the prime-power factors of \(n\). It does not say \(f(ab)=f(a)f(b)\) when \(a,b\) share a prime. For example \(\varphi(2)\varphi(2)=1\) but \(\varphi(4)=2\). Central examples are:



\(f(n)\)
prime-power value \(f(p^{e})\)
interpretation




\(\varphi\)
\(p^{e}-p^{e-1}\)
units modulo \(n\)


\(\mu\)
\(-1\) if \(e=1\), else \(0\)
inverse of constant-one function


\(τ\)
\(e+1\)
number of divisors


\(\sigma_k\)
\(1+p^{k}+…+p^{ek}\)
sum of kth powers of divisors



The totient prime-power formula follows by deleting the \(p^{e-1}\) multiples of \(p\) among \(p^e\) residues. CRT pairs independent unit choices for coprime moduli, proving multiplicativity of \(\varphi\). Divisor counts and sums factor because a divisor independently chooses each exponent \(0,\ldots,e_p\). For \(\mu\), define \(\mu(1)=1\), \(\mu(n)=0\) when any exponent exceeds one, and \(\mu(n)=(-1)^r\) for a product of \(r\) distinct primes. This is also multiplicative by independent prime choices.
The Euler/linear sieve visits each composite exactly once as \(i\cdot p\), where \(p\) is its least prime factor. The “stop when \(p\) divides \(i\)” rule is what makes that representation unique. Keep enough information about the exponent of the least prime to distinguish, for example, whether adding another \(p\) makes \(\mu\) zero or changes \(\varphi(p^e)\) to \(\varphi(p^{e+1})\). It computes primes, \(\mu\), and \(\varphi\) through \(N\) in \(O(N)\) time and memory. More precisely, process \(i=2,\ldots,N\) and primes \(p\le\operatorname{lpf}(i)\) while \(ip\le N\), where \(\operatorname{lpf}(i)\) is the least prime factor. Every composite \(x\) appears at \(p=\operatorname{lpf}(x),i=x/p\) because \(\operatorname{lpf}(i)\ge p\). Any other emitted representation would have a different least prime factor. If \(p\nmid i\), then \(\mu(ip)=-\mu(i)\) and \(\varphi(ip)=(p-1)\varphi(i)\); if \(p\mid i\), then \(\mu(ip)=0\) and \(\varphi(ip)=p\varphi(i)\). These follow directly from the local table.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
3. Dirichlet convolution and Möbius inversion
For arithmetic functions, Dirichlet convolution combines two functions by splitting an integer into an ordered pair of divisors:
\[ (f*g)(n)=\sum_{d\mid n} f(d)g(n/d). \]
For example \((1*1)(6)\) counts the divisors of \(6\), because each divisor \(d\) chooses the factorization \(6=d\cdot(6/d)\). It is associative and commutative, with identity \(ε(1)=1\), \(ε(n>1)=0\). Convolution preserves multiplicativity. Let \(1(n)=1\); since \(1*\mu=ε\),
\[F(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}f(d)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)F(n/d).\]
This is not a formula to memorize in isolation. \(F(n)\) is the sum of \(f\) over divisors of \(n\), so it says \(F=f*1\); convolving both sides with \(\mu\) cancels \(1\) and recovers \(f\). Useful identities follow immediately:
\[1*\varphi=\operatorname{id},\qquad \mu*\operatorname{id}=\varphi,
\qquad 1*1=\tau.\]

Why convolution identities hold
Associativity groups the same ordered triples \(abc=n\): both \(((f*g)*h)(n)\) and \((f*(g*h))(n)\) equal \(\sum_{abc=n}f(a)g(b)h(c)\). Commutativity swaps the two factors. For coprime \(u,v\), every divisor of \(uv\) uniquely splits into a divisor of \(u\) and a divisor of \(v\), proving that convolution preserves multiplicativity.
For \(n\) with \(r\) distinct prime factors, the divisors contributing nonzero \(\mu\) correspond to subsets of those primes. Consequently
\[\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)=\sum_{S\subseteq[0,r)}(-1)^{|S|}
=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(1-1)=\varepsilon(n).\]
For \(n=1\) the empty product is one; otherwise cancellation gives zero. This proves the inverse identity that the earlier algebra uses. Likewise classify \(1\le a\le n\) by \(d=n/\gcd(a,n)\). Writing \(a=(n/d)b\) leaves exactly the \(\varphi(d)\) values \(1\le b\le d\) coprime to \(d\). Every \(a\) has one such class, so \(\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n\).


GCD counting pattern
If a condition asks for \(\gcd(x,y)=1\), the following identity is a filter:
\[[\gcd(x,y)=1]=\sum_{d\mid x,\ d\mid y}\mu(d).\]
Why does it work? If \(g=\gcd(x,y)\), the right side is \(\sum_{d\mid g}\mu(d)\), which is \(1\) when \(g=1\) and \(0\) otherwise. The pair sum becomes \(\sum_d \mu(d) A_d B_d\), where \(A_d,B_d\) count multiples of \(d\). More generally, group pairs by their gcd, derive a divisor zeta relation, then invert.
Worked example: ordered coprime pairs. Count \((x,y)\) with \(1\le x,y\le4\) and \(\gcd(x,y)=1\). For a fixed divisor \(d\), there are \(\lfloor4/d\rfloor\) choices for each coordinate, so the filter gives
\[\sum_{d=1}^4\mu(d)\lfloor4/d\rfloor^2=16-4-1+0=11.\]
The row counts by \(x=1,2,3,4\) are \(4,2,3,2\), also summing to \(11\). For unordered distinct pairs, first remove the only coprime diagonal \((1,1)\) and then divide by two, giving \(5\). Dividing \(11\) by two first would combine an ordered/unordered error with a diagonal error.
Dynamic translation. Maintain \(C_d\), the number of active values divisible by \(d\). Before inserting \(x\), the number of new coprime unordered pairs is \(\sum_{d\mid x}\mu(d)C_d\). Then increment these counts. For deletion, decrement first and use the same formula on the remaining set. Only square-free divisors matter, so a factorization with \(r\) distinct primes gives \(2^r\) terms. For active values \(\{2,3\}\), inserting \(6\) creates \(2-1-1+0=0\) coprime pairs; inserting \(5\) creates two. This is the reduction behind the first contest exercise.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
4. Divisor zeta/Möbius transforms
For arrays on \([1,N]\), the divisor zeta transform replaces the value at \(j\) by the sum of values stored at its divisors: \(F[j]=\sum_{d\mid j}f[d]\). Direct non-in-place divisor loops cost \(N(1+1/2+\cdots+1/N)=O(N\log N)\); inversion follows from the arithmetic Möbius formula. Prime-wise in-place updates compute the transform and its inverse in \(O(N\log\log N)\). For each prime \(p\), the divisor-zeta update \(f[ip]\mathrel{+}=f[i]\) for \(ip\le N\) must traverse \(i\) upward so prime powers accumulate; its inverse uses the same pairs in downward \(i\) order while subtracting. For example, the \(p=2\) stage sends the contribution at \(1\) first to \(2\), then that accumulated contribution to \(4\). After a set of prime stages, the value at \(x\) has accumulated exactly the divisors obtained by lowering the exponents of those primes; this is the no-overcounting invariant. The multiple zeta transform \(F[d]=\sum_{d\mid j}f[j]\) reverses the divisibility order: for each prime \(p\), apply \(f[i]\mathrel{+}=f[ip]\) with \(i\) decreasing, and invert with subtraction while \(i\) increases. Divisor zeta diagonalizes LCM convolution, while multiple zeta diagonalizes GCD convolution; the more general poset view appears in the transforms chapter.
The word “diagonalizes” is a double count. If \(h[x]=\sum_{\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)=x}f[a]g[b]\), then
\[
\sum_{d\mid x}h[d]
=\sum_{a\mid x}\sum_{b\mid x}f[a]g[b]
=F[x]G[x].
\]
The first equality holds because \(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\mid x\) exactly when both \(a\mid x\) and \(b\mid x\). Reversing all divisibility signs gives the same proof for GCD convolution and the multiple transform.
Example. If \(f[1]=2,f[2]=3,f[3]=5\), then the transformed value at \(6\) is \(f[1]+f[2]+f[3]+f[6]\). This is the integer analogue of a subset zeta transform: “submask” becomes “divisor.” Recognition. If every operation replaces a set by all divisors, every query involves \(\gcd\), or values are bounded while query count is large, transform the entire frequency vector instead of processing elements individually.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
5. Quotient grouping (harmonic lemma)
The value \(q=\lfloor n/l\rfloor\) does not change one index at a time. Once it has value \(q\), it remains constant through
\[r=\left\lfloor n/q\right\rfloor.\]
This works because \(\lfloor n/i\rfloor=q\) exactly when \(n/(q+1)<i\le n/q\). Thus a loop for (l=1; l<=n; l=r+1) has only \(O(\sqrt n)\) iterations. The distinct quotients are precisely the small integers up to \(\sqrt n\) plus values \(\lfloor n/i\rfloor\) for small \(i\).
For two or more floor terms, take the minimum end point: if a summand uses \(\lfloor n/i\rfloor\) and \(\lfloor m/i\rfloor\), then compute the end point for each nonzero current quotient and take their minimum. If the loop continues beyond one numerator, that quotient is zero and remains zero through the loop’s final bound; do not evaluate m/(m/l) when m/l is zero. Pair this with prefix sums of \(\mu\), \(\varphi\), powers, or another arithmetic function.
A standard derivation is
\[\sum_{i=1}^n \left\lfloor\frac ni\right\rfloor
=\sum_{ab\le n}1=\sum_{k\le n}\tau(k),\]
showing how a floor sum and a divisor sum are the same lattice-point count.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
6. Dirichlet inverses and recurrence design
If \(f(1)≠0\) in a coefficient field, its Dirichlet inverse is the function \(g\) for which \(f*g=ε\). The \(n=1\) equation fixes \(g(1)\); every larger \(n\) equation has exactly one unknown term, \(f(1)g(n)\), giving the recurrence
\[g(1)=1/f(1),\qquad
g(n)=-\frac1{f(1)}\sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\d>1}}f(d)g(n/d).\]
In prefix-sum problems, search for an easy convolution identity \(f*g=h\). Summing for \(n≤N\) and swapping divisors yields
\[\sum_{n\le N}h(n)=\sum_{d\le N}f(d)\,G(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).\]
If the \(d=1\) term contains the unknown prefix \(G(N)\), isolate it. Quotient grouping then turns the rest into \(O(\sqrt{N})\) states. This is the bridge to Du Jiao sieve in Chapter 03.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
7. Gaussian integers and two squares
The Gaussian integers \(\mathbb Z[i]\) are numbers \(a+bi\) with integer coordinates. Their norm \(N(a+bi)=a^{2}+b^{2}\) is nonnegative and, crucially, multiplicative: \(N(zw)=N(z)N(w)\). They admit Euclidean division by rounding a complex quotient to nearby integer coordinates. Hence gcd, units, associates, and unique factorization behave much like the integers. Use exact integer arithmetic to test the few rounding candidates; floating point may select the wrong quotient for large coordinates.
For a positive integer \(n\), Fermat’s two-square theorem says \(n\) is a sum of two squares iff every prime \(p=3 \bmod 4\) has even exponent. For \(p=1 \bmod 4\), find a square root of \(-1 \bmod p\) and run Cornacchia/Euclidean descent to obtain \(p=x^{2}+y^{2}\). The local representation of \(p^e\) is then \((x+yi)^e\): it is important to raise the Gaussian integer, not merely the integer coordinates. The other local cases are explicit: \(2^e=N((1+i)^e)\), and a \(3\bmod4\) prime with exponent \(2e\) contributes \(p^{2e}=(p^e)^2+0^2\). Multiply local representations with
\[ (a^{2}+b^{2})(c^{2}+d^{2})=(ac-bd)^{2}+(ad+bc)^{2}, \]
Normalize signs/order only after constructing the result.

Why the two-square criterion is true
For \(z=a+bi\), complex conjugation sends it to \(\bar z=a-bi\), and \(N(z)=z\bar z\). Hence \(N(zw)=N(z)N(w)\). To divide Gaussian integers \(\alpha\) by nonzero \(\beta\), round each coordinate of \(\alpha/\beta\) to a nearest integer. The squared distance is at most \(1/2\), so the remainder has norm at most \(N(\beta)/2\). Euclid and the Bézout argument therefore work in this ring. Its units are the elements of norm one: \(\pm1,\pm i\); associates differ by a unit. As for ordinary integers, Euclid’s divisibility lemma proves unique factorization into irreducible Gaussian integers.
If \(p\equiv3\pmod4\) divides \(a^2+b^2\) and \(p\nmid b\), then \((a/b)^2=-1\) in \(\mathbb F_p\). Euler’s criterion rules this out because \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}=-1\). Thus \(p\mid b\) and also \(p\mid a\). Removing \(p^2\) and repeating proves that such primes have even valuation.
If \(p\equiv1\pmod4\), cyclicity supplies \(t\) with \(t^2=-1\bmod p\). Let \(\delta=\gcd(p,t+i)\) in the Gaussian integers. It is not a unit: otherwise a Bézout equation multiplied by \(t-i\) would force \(p\mid t-i\), contradicting its imaginary coordinate \(-1\). It is not associated to \(p\) either, since \(p\) does not divide the imaginary coordinate of \(t+i\). Because \(\delta\mid p\), its norm divides \(p^2\), and the two excluded possibilities are norm one and norm \(p^2\). Therefore \(N(\delta)=p\). Together with \(2=N(1+i)\) and multiplication of norms, this proves sufficiency.
For \(65=5\cdot13\), multiply \((2+i)(3+2i)=4+7i\), giving \(65=4^2+7^2\). Multiplying coordinates separately would give \(6^2+2^2=40\), which does not preserve norms. This construction finds a representation; counting all representations requires separately tracking conjugate-factor choices and symmetries.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
Contest checklist

Multiplicative is not completely multiplicative: \(\varphi(p²)≠\varphi(p)²\).
Decide whether a divisor formula uses \(f(d)\) or \(f(n/d)\) before coding.
\(\mu(n)=0\) whenever a prime square divides \(n\).
Frequency transforms require a bounded value domain; factorization-based inclusion–exclusion may be better for sparse large values.
Quotient blocks must use 64-bit division; for multiple floors, update the end point for each one.
Pollard–Rho factor lists contain repetitions; compress them before enumerating divisors or inclusion–exclusion subsets.

TipEditorial guidance: all upper bounds





Let \(B(i)=\sum_{d\le i}\mu(d)\lfloor i/d\rfloor^n\) and \(B(0)=0\), for the positive array length \(n\). The floor changes from \(i-1\) to \(i\) only when \(d\mid i\), so \(B(i)-B(i-1)=\sum_{d\mid i}\mu(d)((i/d)^n-(i/d-1)^n)\). Precompute powers, add these differences over all \(i=dt\le k\), then prefix sum. Cost is \(O(k\log n+k\log k)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(k)\) memory. For \(n=3,k=4\), the counts are \(1,7,25,55\). Apply the statement’s final XOR/output aggregation only after reducing each count as specified. Recomputing a full inversion for every upper bound would be too slow.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
Exercises with solutions

1. A multiplicativity trap — concept check
Compute \(\tau(12)\), \((\mu*\mathbf1)(12)\), and \(\varphi(12)\) from prime powers. Why is \(\tau(12)\ne\tau(6)\tau(2)\)?






TipHint and solution





Since \(12=2^2\cdot3\), \(\tau(12)=3\cdot2=6\) and \(\varphi(12)=(4-2)(3-1)=4\). The square-free divisor signs give \(1-1-1+1=0\). But \(\tau(6)\tau(2)=4\cdot2=8\); multiplying values requires coprime arguments, whereas \(6,2\) share a prime.





2. Recover an arithmetic function — derivation
Suppose \(\sum_{d\mid n}f(d)=n^2\) for every positive \(n\). Find \(f(p^e)\) and \(f(12)\).






TipHint and solution





At a prime power, subtract the equations at \(p^e\) and \(p^{e-1}\): \(f(p^e)=p^{2e}-p^{2e-2}\) for \(e\ge1\), with \(f(1)=1\). Inversion says \(f=\mu*\operatorname{id}^2\), hence it is multiplicative. Thus \(f(12)=(16-4)(9-1)=96\). It counts ordered pairs of residues modulo \(n\) whose coordinates and \(n\) have joint gcd one, by excluding pairs both divisible by each prime.





3. Equal gcd with a fixed value — modelling
For positive integers \(m,k\), count \(1\le x\le m\) with \(\gcd(x,k)=d\). Express the answer using only square-free divisors.






TipHint and solution





If \(d\nmid k\), the answer is zero. Otherwise write \(x=dy\); we need \(y\le\lfloor m/d\rfloor\) and \(\gcd(y,k/d)=1\). Apply the filter: \(\sum_{e\mid k/d}\mu(e)\lfloor m/(de)\rfloor\). For \(m=10,k=12,d=2\), it is \(5-2-1+0=2\), represented by \(x=2,10\). Enumerating only square-free \(e\) takes \(O(2^{\omega(k/d)})\) terms after factorization, where \(\omega\) counts distinct primes.





4. Regroup a floor sum — synthesis
Derive \(\sum_{i=1}^N i\lfloor N/i\rfloor=\sum_{n=1}^N\sigma_1(n)\) and obtain an \(O(\sqrt N)\) arithmetic-operation algorithm.






TipHint and solution





Each left summand gives weight \(i\) to every pair \((i,j)\) with \(ij\le N\). Grouping by \(n=ij\) sums all divisors \(i\) of \(n\), giving \(\sigma_1(n)\). On a quotient block \([l,r]\) with quotient \(q\), the contribution is \(q(l+r)(r-l+1)/2\). The division is exact in integers; divide an even factor before modular reduction when two is not a unit. For \(N=5\), the value is \(5+4+3+4+5=21\).

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
Summary and reference sheet
Prime-power values determine a multiplicative function, but shared primes prevent naive multiplication. Dirichlet convolution enumerates factorizations \(n=ab\); \(\mathbf1*\mu=\varepsilon\) follows from cancellation over prime subsets. The gcd filter converts exact coprimality into weighted counts of multiples. Divisor zeta uses increasing prime-power updates; multiple zeta uses decreasing updates. Their inverses reverse those directions.
A linear sieve costs \(O(N)\) arithmetic operations and storage; direct divisor sums cost \(O(N\log N)\), prime-wise transforms \(O(N\log\log N)\), and floor quotient grouping uses \(O(\sqrt N)\) blocks. Factorization of isolated 64-bit values has a deterministic primality contract and a heuristic randomized splitting runtime. Positive two-square representations exist exactly when every \(3\bmod4\) prime has even valuation.
