title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
text:
Prerequisites and learning objectives
Prerequisite: arithmetic with integers and fractions. The notation reference collects conventions used later. After this chapter you should be able to translate a quantified claim, choose an appropriate proof method, derive Bézout’s identity, and justify a counting formula or state invariant without relying on small-case evidence.

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
text:
Definitions and notation
The sets \(\mathbb Z\), \(\mathbb Q\), and \(\mathbb R\) contain integers, rational numbers (fractions of integers with nonzero denominator), and real numbers. Write \(\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for nonnegative integers. A set has no repeated elements; a sequence has order and may repeat. The empty set is \(\varnothing\), and \(|S|\) is the number of elements of a finite set \(S\).
The interval \([0,n)\) means the integers \(0,\ldots,n-1\) when used for indices. An indexed sum \(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_i\) adds one term for each such index. An empty sum is zero; an empty product is one. These conventions make recurrences work at size zero: there is one empty sequence, even though it contains no elements.
A function \(f:A\to B\) assigns one output in \(B\) to each input in \(A\). It is injective if different inputs have different outputs, surjective if every output is reached, and bijective if both hold. A bijection proves \(|A|=|B|\) for finite sets because it pairs their elements one for one.
An indicator \([P]\) is \(1\) if a proposition \(P\) is true and \(0\) otherwise. For example, \(\sum_{i=1}^{10}[2\mid i]=5\) counts even integers in that range. The symbol \(a\mid b\) means \(b=ak\) for some integer \(k\); its negation is \(a\nmid b\). The floor \(\lfloor x\rfloor\) is the greatest integer at most \(x\), so \(\lfloor-3/2\rfloor=-2\), which differs from truncation toward zero.

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
section: Logic: what exactly must be proved?
text:
Logic: what exactly must be proved?
The statement \(P\Rightarrow Q\) means every instance satisfying \(P\) also satisfies \(Q\). Its converse \(Q\Rightarrow P\) is a different claim. The notation \(P\Longleftrightarrow Q\) requires both directions. A reduction claiming that feasible solutions correspond must prove both directions unless it explicitly needs only a bound.
The quantifiers \(\forall\) and \(\exists\) mean “for every” and “there exists.” Their order matters. For every integer \(x\) there exists an integer \(y>x\); there does not exist one integer \(y\) larger than every integer \(x\). To disprove a universal claim, one counterexample suffices. To negate “for every \(x\) there exists \(y\) with \(P(x,y)\),” say “there exists \(x\) for which every \(y\) fails \(P(x,y)\).”
Worked failure: an invalid converse. If a positive integer is divisible by \(6\), it is divisible by \(3\). The reverse implication fails at \(3\). Thus checking a necessary condition can reject impossible instances, but passing it does not construct a solution.
For implication proofs, the contrapositive \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\) is equivalent to \(P\Rightarrow Q\). For example, to prove that \(n^2\) even forces \(n\) even, take odd \(n=2k+1\). Then \(n^2=2(2k^2+2k)+1\) is odd. A proof by contradiction instead assumes the claim is false and derives an impossibility.

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
text:
Induction: a recurrence for correctness
To prove \(P(n)\) for all integers \(n\ge n_0\), prove the base \(P(n_0)\) and prove \(P(n)\Rightarrow P(n+1)\). The base starts a chain that reaches every allowed index. In strong induction, the step may use all smaller valid indices. Both are natural for dynamic programming: the mathematical dependency graph must reach already proved states.
Worked example: a sum. Let \(S_n=1+\cdots+n\), with \(S_0=0\). We claim \(S_n=n(n+1)/2\). It holds at \(0\). Assuming it at \(n\),
\[S_{n+1}=S_n+(n+1)
=\frac{n(n+1)}2+(n+1)
=\frac{(n+1)(n+2)}2.\]
Each equality uses the definition, the induction hypothesis, or ordinary algebra. This proof is over the integers/rationals. When computing modulo \(m\), divide the even integer factor by \(2\) before reduction; \(2\) need not have an inverse modulo \(m\).
Worked example: prime factorization exists. A prime is an integer \(p\ge2\) whose only positive divisors are \(1,p\). By strong induction, every \(n\ge2\) is a product of primes. If \(n\) is prime, we are done. Otherwise \(n=ab\) with \(2\le a,b<n\), so the induction hypotheses factor both \(a\) and \(b\). This proves existence, not yet uniqueness; uniqueness follows below.
Failed induction. “All objects in every set have the same color” has a true one-element base. Comparing the first \(n\) and last \(n\) elements of an \((n+1)\)-element set would transfer color through their overlap only when \(n\ge2\). The step from one to two has empty overlap. An induction step must work at the first boundary, not only for large indices.

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
section: Invariants, potential functions, and extremal choice
text:
Invariants, potential functions, and extremal choice
An invariant is a property preserved by every allowed transition. Prove it initially and after one arbitrary transition. A potential function assigns a value to a state that moves in a controlled direction. A nonnegative integer potential that strictly decreases proves termination; a real-valued decrease alone need not, as \(1,1/2,1/4,\ldots\) illustrates.
Worked impossibility and construction. On a binary board, one move flips exactly two cells. The parity of the number of ones is invariant: a move changes it by \(-2,0,\) or \(2\). Hence a board with one one cannot become all zero. Even parity is only a necessary condition until the allowed pairs are specified. If the allowed-pair graph is connected, it is also sufficient: take a spanning tree, process leaves upward, and flip a leaf with its parent exactly when the leaf is one. Cleared leaves never change again. The root is finally zero because total parity is even. This gives an \(O(V+E)\) construction using a graph traversal, where \(V\) counts cells and \(E\) allowed pairs.
An extremal argument selects a smallest, largest, or otherwise optimal object and exploits what it cannot do. Every finite nonempty set of integers has a minimum. Every nonempty set of nonnegative integers has a minimum even if infinite.
Worked example: a tree has a leaf. In a finite tree with at least two vertices, take a longest simple path. An endpoint cannot have another neighbor: a neighbor off the path extends it, while a neighbor elsewhere on the path creates a cycle. Thus each endpoint has degree one. This is why repeatedly removing leaves supports induction in the matrix-tree theorem.

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
section: Euclid and Bézout: deriving a central algebraic tool
text:
Euclid and Bézout: deriving a central algebraic tool
For nonnegative \(a,b\), not both zero, their greatest common divisor \(g=\gcd(a,b)\) is the greatest positive integer dividing both. Division with remainder gives \(a=qb+r\) with \(0\le r<b\) when \(b>0\). A number divides both \(a,b\) exactly when it divides both \(b,r=a-qb\). Therefore \(\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(b,r)\). The positive remainders decrease, so Euclid’s algorithm terminates, and its last nonzero remainder is \(g\).
Every remainder is an integer linear combination of \(a,b\): the starting values are, and subtracting \(q\) times one combination from another preserves that property. Consequently there exist integers \(u,v\) such that
\[au+bv=g.\]
This is Bézout’s identity. For \(a=30,b=18\), the remainders are \(12,6,0\), and back substitution gives \(6=18-(30-18)=2\cdot18-30\). It follows that \(30x+18y=6\) has \((x,y)=(-1,2)\) as one solution.
For arbitrary integer \(c\), the equation \(ax+by=c\) has integer solutions iff \(g\mid c\). Necessity holds because \(g\) divides every left side; sufficiency comes from multiplying Bézout’s coefficients by \(c/g\). When \(a,b>0\), all solutions from one \((x_0,y_0)\) are
\[x=x_0+\frac bg t,\qquad y=y_0-\frac ag t,\qquad t\in\mathbb Z.\]
To prove completeness, subtract two solutions: \((a/g)\Delta x=-(b/g)\Delta y\). The coefficients \(a/g,b/g\) are coprime. Bézout then implies \(b/g\mid\Delta x\), which forces exactly the parameterization above. Zero coefficients are handled directly; if both coefficients are zero, solvability is exactly \(c=0\).
Euclid uses \(O(\log\max(a,b))\) integer divisions for positive inputs: in two remainder steps the larger argument at least halves. This counts arithmetic operations; large-integer division has its own bit cost.
Why prime factorization is unique. If prime \(p\) divides \(ab\) but not \(a\), then \(\gcd(p,a)=1\). Multiply a Bézout equation for \(p,a\) by \(b\) to conclude \(p\mid b\). Thus a prime appearing in one factorization must appear in any other factorization of the same integer. Cancel that prime and repeat. This proves uniqueness up to the order of the factors.

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
text:
Double counting and bijections
Before rearranging a sum, name the objects represented by its terms. In a finite undirected graph, count incidences \((v,e)\) where vertex \(v\) is an endpoint of edge \(e\). Summing by vertex gives \(\sum_v\deg(v)\); summing by edge gives \(2|E|\). Thus the two expressions agree. Here edges have two distinct endpoints; with loops, define degree by endpoint occurrences instead.
For subsets, let \(\binom nk\) count \(k\)-element subsets of an \(n\)-element set; it is zero when \(k<0\) or \(k>n\). Count ordered lists of \(k\) distinct elements: there are \(n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)\). Each subset has exactly \(k!\) orderings, so
\[\binom nk=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!},\qquad 0\le k\le n.\]
The quotient is exact in the integers. The factorial \(n!\) is the product of \(1,\ldots,n\), with \(0!=1\). Choosing whether a distinguished element is present also gives \(\binom nk=\binom{n-1}k+\binom{n-1}{k-1}\) for \(n\ge1\).
Worked example: choose a team and captain. From \(n\ge1\) people choose a nonempty subset and distinguish one member. Choosing size first gives \(\sum_{k=1}^n k\binom nk\). Choosing the captain first gives \(n\) choices, then every other person independently joins or does not: \(2^{n-1}\) choices. Therefore \(\sum_k k\binom nk=n2^{n-1}\). For \(n=3\), \(3+6+3=12=3\cdot4\). The power of two counts subsets, not permutations.

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
text:
Contest translation and checklist
Use a library routine only after the reduction has an input/output contract. Keep four statements separate: the model is correct, every solution is represented, the algorithm finds the required result, and the resource bound fits the constraints. Exhaustive tests can refute any of these claims on a small case; passing tests does not replace the proof for arbitrary inputs.

What is the domain, including empty and zero cases?
Is the proposed condition necessary, sufficient, or both?
Which object does one summand or DP state represent?
What is preserved by a transition, and what ensures termination?
Are counted fibers all the same size before dividing?
Does the complexity count arithmetic operations or actual machine work?

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
text:
Exercises, hints, and solutions

1. Quantifiers and a counterexample — concept check
Negate “every pair of nonzero residues modulo \(m\) has a nonzero product.” Find the smallest \(m\ge2\) where the original claim fails.






TipHint and solution





Seek two nonzero factors of the modulus. The negation says that there exist two nonzero residues whose product is zero. Modulo \(4\), \(2\cdot2=0\); modulo \(2\) and \(3\), direct multiplication shows no such pair. The answer is \(4\). This is the first warning that a nonzero element need not be invertible.





2. Count the same marked subset twice — derivation
For \(n\ge2\), derive \(\sum_{k=0}^n k(k-1)\binom nk=n(n-1)2^{n-2}\).






TipHint and solution





Mark an ordered pair of distinct members in the chosen subset. For a \(k\)-element subset there are \(k(k-1)\) such pairs. Alternatively choose the ordered marked pair first in \(n(n-1)\) ways, then choose any of the remaining \(n-2\) elements. Both counts describe exactly the same objects. For \(n=3\), the left side is \(2\cdot3+6\cdot1=12\).





3. All bounded solutions — modelling
Find all nonnegative integer pairs satisfying \(6x+9y=45\) and \(x\le6\).






TipHint and solution





Divide by \(3\). The equation \(2x+3y=15\) has one solution \((0,5)\). Every solution is \(x=3t,y=5-2t\). Bounds imply \(0\le t\le2\). The pairs are \((0,5),(3,3),(6,1)\). Guessing one solution would miss two; the parameterization proves completeness.





4. Flip graph — synthesis
Extend the two-cell flip model to a graph that may be disconnected. Give a necessary and sufficient condition for reaching all zero and a construction.






TipHint and solution





Each move stays inside one connected component, so parity in every component is invariant. Even parity in each component is sufficient by the spanning-tree leaf procedure applied independently. An isolated vertex must already be zero. Components plus the construction cost \(O(V+E)\), with at most \(V-1\) tree-edge flips overall when the graph is nonempty. This proof combines an obstruction with a construction, which is stronger than either alone.

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
text:
Summary and reference sheet
An implication needs one direction; an equivalence needs two. Induction needs a valid base and a step at every boundary. An invariant proves preservation; a decreasing nonnegative integer potential proves termination. A bijection or double count proves equality by describing the same finite objects twice.
For integers \(a,b\) not both zero, Bézout gives \(au+bv=\gcd(a,b)\). Thus \(ax+by=c\) is solvable exactly when the gcd divides \(c\). Binomial coefficients count unordered subsets; factorial division is exact over integers and needs separate justification modulo a modulus.
Continue with modular algebra. Later, combinatorics, linear algebra, and probability develop the other former entrance diagnostics from their mathematical definitions.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
This chapter turns congruences into algorithms. The recurring contest signal is that values are huge but only their residue, multiplicative order, or compatibility across several moduli matters. A congruence is an equality after we deliberately forget multiples of a modulus; it is not ordinary arithmetic with a mysterious % attached. Work through the sections in order; the final four topics assume factorization from Chapter 02.
For every division below, first ask one question: is the denominator a unit in this ring? In modular arithmetic, that question is the difference between a valid derivation and a plausible-looking wrong answer.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
Prerequisites and learning objectives
Read proofs and Bézout. This chapter teaches you to derive linear-congruence and CRT conditions, distinguish rings from fields, prove exponent-period facts, and select a root or logarithm algorithm with an explicit domain. Factorization is treated as supplied data when needed; Chapter 02 explains how to obtain it.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
Definitions and notation
Throughout, \(m\ge1\) is an integer modulus, \(p\) is prime, and exponents in algorithmic queries are nonnegative unless stated otherwise. A residue class modulo \(m\) contains all integers with the same remainder; its representative is chosen in \([0,m)\). Modulo one there is just one class, so return zero directly rather than passing it to field algorithms.
A commutative ring supports addition, subtraction, and multiplication with their familiar associative, commutative, and distributive laws, and identities \(0,1\). A unit has a multiplicative inverse. A field is a nonzero commutative ring where every nonzero element is a unit. The ring \(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\) records residues; it is a field exactly when \(m\) is prime. A group has an associative operation, an identity, and inverses for all elements; the units of any ring form a group under multiplication.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
1. Congruences as algebra
For a positive modulus \(m\), write \(a ≡ b \pmod{m}\) when \(m \mid (a-b)\): \(a\) and \(b\) leave the same remainder after division by \(m\). Thus \(17≡5\pmod {12}\), and replacing one by the other cannot change a later sum or product modulo \(12\). Addition and multiplication descend to residue classes, but division is conditional: \(a\) has an inverse modulo \(m\) exactly when \(\gcd(a,m)=1\). Extended Euclid gives integers \(x,y\) with
\[ax+my=\gcd(a,m).\]
This identity explains division: when \(g=1\), it reads \(ax+my=1\), so \(ax≡1\) and \(x\) is the inverse of \(a\). More generally, the values of \(ax\) modulo \(m\) are exactly the multiples of \(g=\gcd(a,m)\). Therefore \(ax ≡ b \pmod{m}\) has no solution if \(g∤b\); otherwise divide by \(g\), invert \(a/g\) modulo \(m/g\), and obtain one residue class modulo \(m/g\) (hence \(g\) solutions modulo \(m\)).
Example. \(6x≡8\pmod {14}\) becomes \(3x≡4\pmod7\), so \(x≡6\pmod7\). Modulo \(14\) this means the two solutions \(6\) and \(13\). By contrast, \(6x≡5\pmod {14}\) is impossible because every left side is even modulo \(14\).
Recognition. A repeated step on a cycle, synchronized clocks, or an equation with a coefficient that may not be invertible is a linear congruence, not “ordinary modular division.”

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
2. CRT, including non-coprime moduli
To merge \(x≡a \pmod{m}\) and \(x≡b \pmod{n}\), start from the first statement: every such integer has the form \(x=a+mt\). Substituting it into the second gives
\[mt\equiv b-a\pmod n.\]
It is solvable iff \(\gcd(m,n) \mid b-a\); all solutions form one class modulo \(\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)\). This is a consistency check, not an optional optimization. For example, \(x≡1\pmod6\) and \(x≡3\pmod8\) are compatible because \(2\mid(3-1)\); substituting gives \(6t≡2\pmod8\), then \(t≡3\pmod4\), hence \(x≡19\pmod {24}\). The pair \(x≡1\pmod6\), \(x≡2\pmod8\) is impossible: their parities already disagree. Fold constraints one at a time, normalize each merged residue, and guard the LCM against overflow.
For pairwise coprime prime powers, CRT is a ring isomorphism \(\mathbb Z/(\prod_i p_i^{e_i})\mathbb Z \cong
\prod_i \mathbb Z/(p_i^{e_i})\mathbb Z\). This is why composite-modulus equations should often be solved locally and recombined.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
3. Finite fields and multiplicative order
For prime \(p\), every nonzero residue is invertible, so the nonzero residues form a multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^\times\). This group happens to be cyclic: there is a generator \(g\) whose powers list every nonzero residue once, and its order is \(p-1\). Consequently:

Fermat: \(a^{p-1}=1\) for \(a≠0\).
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a) \mid p-1\).
A nonzero polynomial of degree \(d\) over a field has at most \(d\) roots.
\(x^{k}=a\) can be converted into a linear congruence in exponents after choosing a primitive root.

For composite moduli, nonzero does not imply invertible, polynomial root bounds may fail, and the unit group need not be cyclic. Always identify where primality is used.
The order of \(a\) is the first positive exponent \(d\) for which \(a^d=1\); it is the length of the cycle \(1,a,a^2,\ldots\). For example, \(2\) modulo \(7\) has order \(3\) because \(2,4,1\) repeat. Assuming \(\gcd(a,m)=1\), start at \(\varphi(m)\) (or the Carmichael exponent \(\lambda(m)\)) and remove a prime factor \(q\) whenever \(a^{\operatorname{ord}/q}=1\). A primitive root has order \(\varphi(m)\); for \(m\ge2\), primitive roots exist exactly for \(m\in\{2,4,p^{k},2p^{k}\}\) with odd prime \(p\) and \(k\ge1\). Some sources add \(m=1\) by a vacuous convention; it has no relevance to modular algorithms.
To understand the classification, lift a generator modulo odd \(p\) to one modulo \(p^2\). Among its \(p\) lifts, at most one has \((p-1)\)st power one modulo \(p^2\): expanding \((g+tp)^{p-1}\) makes the next digit a nonconstant linear function of \(t\). Choose another lift. The valuation formula proved in the next section shows its order modulo \(p^k\) is \(p^{k-1}(p-1)\). CRT identifies units modulo \(2p^k\) with those modulo \(p^k\). Conversely, two distinct odd-prime components, or an odd-prime component and a factor four, have even-sized unit groups: no element of their product can have order equal to the product of the sizes, because its order divides their smaller lcm. Modulo \(2^k\) for \(k\ge3\), the four distinct roots \(1,-1,1+2^{k-1},-1+2^{k-1}\) of \(x^2=1\) rule out cyclicity, since a cyclic even-order group has exactly two such elements. Moduli two and four are checked directly.

Why the group and root facts hold
A nonzero degree-\(d\) polynomial over a field has at most \(d\) distinct roots. A root \(r\) permits division by the monic polynomial \(x-r\), leaving zero remainder. Every other root is a root of the quotient because \(x-r\) is nonzero there and can be cancelled. Induct on the degree. Modulo \(8\), however, the degree-two polynomial \(x^2-1\) has four roots \(1,3,5,7\): field hypotheses matter.
For a unit \(a\) of order \(d\), the powers \(1,a,\ldots,a^{d-1}\) are distinct. Every element in a finite group belongs to a block obtained by multiplying these \(d\) elements by some \(b\). Two blocks coincide or are disjoint: one common element lets us cancel and express one multiplier through the other. Thus \(d\) divides the group size. If \(a^e=1\), division of \(e\) by \(d\) shows its remainder must be zero, so \(d\mid e\).
Here is a proof of cyclicity. Let \(G\) be a finite subgroup of the nonzero elements of a field, and let \(D\) be the lcm of its element orders. For each prime power \(q^e\) dividing \(D\) exactly, some element has order divisible by \(q^e\); raising it to the other factor of its order gives an element of order \(q^e\). Products of commuting elements of coprime orders have order equal to the product: a common power of the two elements has order dividing both, so must be the identity. Repeating this constructs an element of order \(D\). Every element of \(G\) is a root of \(x^D-1\), so \(|G|\le D\) by the root bound; the constructed cyclic subgroup has \(D\) elements, so \(D\le |G|\). Equality proves a generator exists. For \(\mathbb F_p^\times\), its order is \(p-1\).
The Euler totient \(\varphi(m)\) counts units modulo \(m\). Multiplication by a unit permutes them; multiplying all entries and cancelling their product proves \(a^{\varphi(m)}=1\). The Carmichael exponent \(\lambda(m)\) is the lcm of all unit orders, hence the least positive exponent giving one for every unit. It divides \(\varphi(m)\), so using \(\varphi(m)\) is always a valid alternative when a smaller period is unnecessary.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
4. Valuations and lifting
The \(p\)-adic valuation \(v_p(n)\) is the exponent of \(p\) in the prime factorization of a nonzero integer \(n\): for instance \(v_2(40)=3\). It is useful to set \(v_p(0)=+\infty\) when comparing valuations of sums. It turns a question about a large product into a question about addition of exponents:
\[v_p(ab)=v_p(a)+v_p(b),\qquad
v_p(n!)=\sum_{j\ge1}\left\lfloor n/p^j\right\rfloor.\]
For sums, \(v_p(a+b)≥\min(v_p(a),v_p(b))\), with equality if the two valuations differ: factor out the smaller power, and the remaining sum is nonzero modulo \(p\). LTE supplies sharper forms when cancellation needs to be measured. The most used one is: for an odd prime \(p\), positive integer \(n\), distinct integers \(x,y\), \(p\mid(x-y)\), and \(p\nmid xy\),
\[v_p(x^{n}-y^{n})=v_p(x-y)+v_p(n).\]
Why the factorial sum holds. There are \(\lfloor n/p\rfloor\) multiples contributing at least one \(p\), \(\lfloor n/p^2\rfloor\) contributing an additional \(p\), and so on. Each integer of valuation \(e\) is counted exactly \(e\) times; stop once \(p^j>n\).
Proof sketch for the stated LTE form. Write \(x=y+p^t u\) with \(t=v_p(x-y)\ge1\) and \(p\nmid u\). For positive \(s\) coprime to \(p\), the binomial expansion of \(x^s-y^s\) has first term \(s y^{s-1}p^t u\) of valuation \(t\) and all other terms of larger valuation. For exponent \(p\), the first term has valuation \(t+1\), intermediate terms have valuation at least \(2t+1\), and the last has valuation \(pt>t+1\) for odd \(p\). Thus exponent \(p\) raises the valuation by one. Write \(n=p^e s\) and repeat. The odd-prime hypothesis prevents a tie at \(p=2,t=1\).
Use valuations when divisibility by a huge power or the number of trailing prime factors is asked. For binomial coefficients,
\[v_p\binom nk=\sum_{j\ge1}\left(\lfloor n/p^{j}\rfloor-\lfloor k/p^{j}\rfloor-\lfloor(n-k)/p^{j}\rfloor\right),\]
equivalently the number of carries when adding \(k\) and \(n-k\) in base \(p\) (Kummer).
For an integer polynomial \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\), Hensel lifting upgrades a root modulo \(p^{k}\) to modulo \(p^{k+1}\). We only need to decide its next base-\(p\) digit, so try \(r'=r+t p^{k}\) with \(t\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\). If \(f(r)≡0\pmod {p^k}\), the first-order expansion gives
\[\frac{f(r)}{p^k}+t f'(r)\equiv0\pmod p.\]
The quotient is an integer because \(r\) was already a root modulo \(p^k\). If \(f'(r)\not\equiv0\pmod p\), this linear equation has one \(t\), hence one lift. If the derivative vanishes, it has either no solution or every \(t\) is a solution, giving zero or \(p\) lifts—never assume uniqueness.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
5. Discrete logarithms
Given \(a^{x}≡b \pmod{m}\) with \(a\) a unit, baby-step giant-step (BSGS) searches an exponent by writing the representative \(0\le x<\operatorname{ord}(a)\) as \(x=q+nj\), where \(0\le q<n\) and \(n=\lceil\sqrt{\operatorname{ord}(a)}\rceil\). Then \(a^q=b(a^{-n})^j\). Store all small “baby” powers \(a^q\) and scan the “giant” right sides; an equality gives \(x=q+nj\). Retain the smallest baby exponent for each stored value and verify every reported candidate. If the order is not known, taking \(n=\lceil\sqrt m\rceil\) is safe for a unit modulo \(m\), since the order is at most \(\varphi(m)<m\). This group version needs \(\gcd(a,m)=1\) and costs \(O(\sqrt{\operatorname{ord}(a)})\) time and memory when the order is used. It is a meet-in-the-middle search, not a logarithm in the numerical sense. If giant steps are scanned by increasing \(j\), the table retains the smallest \(q\) for each value, and candidates \(q+nj\ge\operatorname{ord}(a)\) are discarded, the first verified collision is the smallest nonnegative solution. Other scan or hash conventions should collect and minimize the normalized candidates.
The search succeeds only when \(b\) belongs to the cyclic subgroup generated by \(a\). For example, modulo \(7\) the powers of \(2\) are \(1,2,4\); therefore \(2^x\equiv3\pmod 7\) has no solution even though both sides are units.
When \(\gcd(a,m)>1\), ordinary BSGS cannot invert \(a\). The extension maintains \(k a^{x-t}\equiv b\pmod m\) for the still-unexamined exponents \(x\ge t\); initially \(k=1,t=0\). First test \(k=b\) for \(x=t\). For \(x>t\), set \(g=\gcd(a,m)\): if \(g\nmid b\), no remaining exponent works. Otherwise divide \(m,b\) by \(g\), update \(k\leftarrow k(a/g)\bmod m\) using the old \(g\), and increase \(t\). These are integer divisions of the equation, so the invariant is preserved. When the reduced modulus becomes one, the smallest remaining exponent works. When \(\gcd(a,m)=1\), \(k\) is also a unit: any prime shared with the original base has by then been removed from the modulus. Solve \(a^{x-t}=b/k\) using ordinary BSGS. Always check exponent zero first, including \(a=0\); the convention here is \(a^0=1\) even for zero. The stripping phase takes at most \(O(\log m)\) steps.
Pohlig–Hellman is better when the known order \(L=\prod_i q_i^{e_i}\) has small prime factors. Raise \(a,b\) to \(L/q_i^{e_i}\) to project to order \(q_i^{e_i}\). If the low \(j\) base-\(q_i\) digits of the logarithm are known, divide away their contribution and raise to \(q_i^{e_i-1-j}\); this leaves a logarithm in the subgroup of order \(q_i\), revealing the next digit. CRT recombines the exponent residues. BSGS for each digit gives \(O(\sum_i e_i(\log L+\sqrt{q_i}))\) group operations and reusable \(O(\max_i\sqrt{q_i})\) table space, excluding factorization. The largest prime factor matters, but the digit and exponentiation costs also count.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
6. Modular roots
For odd prime \(p\) and \(a\ne0\), a quadratic residue is a value \(a\) for which some \(x\) satisfies \(x^2=a\). Euler’s criterion gives \(a^{(p-1)/2}\equiv1\pmod p\) exactly for residues, and \(-1\) for non-residues. Tonelli–Shanks writes \(p-1=q\cdot2^{s}\) with odd \(q\), finds a quadratic non-residue, then cancels the current error inside the \(2\)-power subgroup. Given a non-residue, it runs in \(O(\log p+s^{2})\) modular multiplications; random sampling finds one in expected constant trials.
Euler’s criterion follows from a generator \(g\): \(a=g^t\) is a square iff \(t\) is even, and \(g^{(p-1)/2}=-1\) because it has order two. Thus the criterion has no false positives in an odd prime field.
For the Tonelli–Shanks invariant, put \(r=a^{(q+1)/2}\), \(t=a^q\), \(c=z^q\), and \(M=s\), where \(z\) is a non-residue. Then \(r^2=at\), \(c\) has order \(2^M\), and \(t\) has order dividing \(2^{M-1}\) when \(a\) is a square. If \(t\ne1\), find the least \(i\) with \(t^{2^i}=1\); then \(1\le i<M\). Put \(b=c^{2^{M-i-1}}\) and replace \((r,t,c,M)\) by \((rb,tb^2,b^2,i)\). The relation \(r^2=at\) is preserved. Both \(t\) and \(b^2\) have \(2^{i-1}\)st power \(-1\), so their product has order dividing \(2^{i-1}\); \(c\) now has order \(2^i\). Thus the invariant holds with a strictly smaller \(M\), and termination at \(t=1\) gives a root. The repeated squarings over decreasing \(M\) cost \(O(s^2)\). Sampling a non-residue adds expected \(O(\log p)\) multiplications, since half the nonzero field elements are non-residues.
For example, \(a=10,p=13\) has \(q=3,s=2\), and \(z=2\) is a non-residue. Initially \(r=9,t=12,c=8\). The least \(i\) is one, so \(b=8\) and the new \(r=7,t=1\). The roots are \(7\) and \(6\); their squares are \(10\) modulo \(13\).
For the excluded prime \(p=2\), the nonzero multiplicative group has one element, and both field elements \(0\) and \(1\) are their own square roots. Euler’s criterion and Tonelli–Shanks are not needed there.
For a positive integer \(k\), first separate \(a=0\) in \(x^{k}=a \pmod{p}\): its only root in a field is \(x=0\). For nonzero \(a\), write values as powers of a primitive root: \(g^{kt}=a\). A discrete logarithm converts this to \(kt≡\log_g(a) \pmod{p-1}\). It has \(\gcd(k,p-1)\) solutions if compatible. Specialized root algorithms avoid a full discrete log; use them when constraints exceed BSGS.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
section: 7. Exponent towers and efficient k-th roots
text:
7. Exponent towers and efficient k-th roots
Euler reduction \(a^{e} \bmod m = a^{e \bmod \varphi(m)} \bmod m\) is valid without qualification only when \(\gcd(a,m)=1\): otherwise reducing a large exponent can turn a multiple of a prime into a nonmultiple. For example, \(2^4≡0\pmod4\) but \(2^{4\bmod\varphi(4)}=2^0≡1\pmod4\). For a tower, recurse through the Carmichael chain \(m, \lambda(m), \lambda(\lambda(m)), \ldots\), but a residue alone is not enough: the caller must also know whether the true exponent exceeds a requested small cap. Compute that fact with saturating arithmetic instead of inferring it from the reduced residue. For a prime-power modulus \(p^r\), first separate \(e=0\), which gives \(1\). If \(p^r\mid a\) and \(e>0\), the residue is \(0\). Otherwise write \(a=p^v u\) with \(p\nmid u\) and \(0\le v<r\). If \(v=0\), reduce the exponent modulo \(\lambda(p^r)\). If \(v>0\), then \(a^e\equiv0\pmod{p^r}\) as soon as \(e\ge\lceil r/v\rceil\); below that threshold the exponent is small enough to retain exactly. Solve this independently for every \(p^r\mid m\) and combine the residues by CRT. This local rule is the reason the extra “is the exponent large enough?” information is necessary.
For \(x^k=a\bmod p\) with \(a\ne0\), existence is equivalent to \(a^{(p-1)/g}=1\), where \(g=\gcd(k,p-1)\). Indeed, writing \(a=u^b\) for a generator \(u\), both conditions say \(g\mid b\). If \(g=1\), invert \(k\) modulo \(p-1\) and return \(a^{k^{-1}\bmod(p-1)}\). If \(g>1\), the general discrete-log reduction is valid, but one must not assume the relevant subgroup is smooth: \(g\) may contain a large prime. Specialized root extraction needs its own proved contract; it is not obtained merely by splitting off the gcd.

Worked synthesis: a composite-modulus exponent
Compute \(6^{\,2^{10}}\bmod72\). Factor \(72=8\cdot9\). Modulo \(8\), the base has valuation \(v_2(6)=1\), so any exponent at least three gives zero. Modulo \(9\), \(v_3(6)=1\), so any exponent at least two gives zero. Since \(2^{10}\) exceeds both caps, CRT gives zero modulo \(72\) without storing the power of six. The tempting reduction modulo \(\varphi(8)=4\) changes the exponent to zero and would incorrectly return one modulo \(8\). The missing information is the exponent’s size relative to the valuation threshold.
For a height-\(h\) tower of nonnegative integer bases, define \(0^0=1\) locally if zero bases are allowed. A capped evaluator returns \(\min(E,C)\), where \(E\) is the true exponent and \(C\) the requested cap. Repeated multiplication stops as soon as the cap is reached; for base at least two, only \(O(\log C)\) multiplications are needed at a level. Bases zero and one need explicit branches. Combine these size certificates with modular recursion; the work depends on the tower height and the factorization/period chain, not on writing the enormous tower value.

Contest translation: algorithm contracts








Task

Linear congruence

One modular power per attempted factor removal

A unit and an order bound \(L\)

Sorting rather than hashing BSGS entries adds a logarithmic lookup/sort factor. Finding a primitive root requires the factorization of \(p-1\) and tests \(g^{(p-1)/q}\ne1\) for every distinct prime \(q\mid p-1\); these tests suffice because every proper divisor of \(p-1\) divides at least one \((p-1)/q\). The cost includes the number of candidates tried.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
Contest checklist and pitfalls

Normalize negative residues; C++ % may be negative.
Never use Fermat inversion unless the modulus is prime and the denominator nonzero.
Protect multiplication and LCM with __int128; check promised bounds before casting back.
CRT consistency is a divisibility test, not pairwise coprimality.
Distinguish a primitive root of the whole multiplicative group from an \(n\)th root of unity.
In BSGS, clarify whether the smallest solution is required and handle \(x=0\), \(a=0\), and non-coprime cases.
Hensel’s derivative-zero branch and \(p=2\) require separate analysis.

text:
Ordered practice
Levels are curriculum-relative: Foundation, Advanced, Mastery, Capstone. Try each problem before opening its hints.

1. Throne — AtCoder ABC186 E

Level: Foundation · Language: English/Japanese
Trains: linear congruences, solvability, extended Euclid.
Editorial: official contest editorial



Hint 1 — recognition

After \(x\) moves the position condition is one congruence in \(x\).



Hint 2 — reduction

Solve \(Kx ≡ -S \pmod{N}\) and test the gcd condition.



Hint 3 — algorithm

Divide all three quantities by \(\gcd(K,N)\), then use an extended-Euclid inverse.



2. Power Pair — AtCoder ABC212 G

Level: Advanced · Language: English/Japanese
Prerequisites: cyclic \(\mathbb F_p^\times\), Euler \(\varphi\), divisor enumeration.
Editorial: official contest editorial



Hint 1

Classify each nonzero \(x\) by its multiplicative order.



Hint 2

An element of order \(d\) reaches exactly the subgroup it generates; count elements of each order.



Hint 3

Sum a divisor expression involving \(\varphi(d)\) over \(d\mid(P-1)\) and remember \((0,0)\).



3. Moodular Arithmetic — Codeforces 603B

Level: Mastery · Language: English/Russian
Trains: functional graphs induced by multiplication and multiplicative order.
Editorial: official Round 334 tutorial



Hint 1

The equation links values of the function along orbits of \(x→kx\).



Hint 2

Handle \(k=0,1\) separately; otherwise the nonzero residues split into equal cycles.



Hint 3

The cycle length is \(\operatorname{ord}_p(k)\); count free choices per orbit and the forced behavior at zero.



4. GCD Table — Codeforces 338D

Level: Capstone · Language: English/Russian
Trains: converting gcd requirements into congruences; generalized CRT with overflow constraints.
Editorial: official problem analysis



Hint 1

Seek a row equal to a common multiple of every requested gcd.



Hint 2

The starting column must satisfy one congruence modulo each \(a_i\); merge them even though the moduli overlap.



Hint 3

Construct a bounded common multiple, CRT the column constraints, then explicitly verify every gcd and table boundary.



5. Product Transformation — Codeforces 852F

Level: Capstone · Language: English/Russian
Trains: multiplicative order, binomial exponent structure, computation modulo a prime order.
Editorial: official Bubble Cup X booklet, Problem F



Hint 1

Write each array entry as a power of \(a\) and inspect how one transformation changes the exponent vector.



Hint 2

Pascal’s recurrence shows that the final exponents are prefix sums of one row of binomial coefficients.



Hint 3

Reduce exponents modulo the multiplicative order, which the statement guarantees is prime. Compute the order from the supplied base and modulus; use factorial division only where its indices are below that prime.







TipEditorial guidance: transformation as a shift





Write \(A_i=a^{e_i}\), initially \(e_i=1\). One operation sends \(e_i\) to \(e_i+e_{i+1}\), with the final exponent unchanged. If \(S\) shifts the exponent vector one position toward smaller indices and fills the end with zero, then \(S^N=0\) and \(M\) operations give \((I+S)^M\). The binomial theorem yields \(e_i=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(M,N-i)}\binom Mj\) for one-based \(i\). Compute these prefix sums in the prime-order field, then exponentiate the original base modulo \(Q\). If every needed \(j\) is below that prime, the incremental binomial product divides only by those \(j\); it does not require \(M!\) to be invertible. For indices crossing the characteristic, use the Lucas/prime-power contracts.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
Exercises with solutions

1. Roots can branch — concept check
Lift all roots of \(x^2=1\) modulo \(4\) to modulus \(8\). Why does the simple-root Hensel rule not apply?






TipHint and solution





The roots modulo four are \(1,3\). Their candidate lifts are \(1,5\) and \(3,7\); all four square to one modulo eight. The derivative \(2x\) vanishes modulo two, so each existing root can have either zero or two lifts. By contrast, \(x^2=3\) has a root modulo two but none modulo four.





2. Root counting through exponents — derivation
Find all solutions of \(x^4=4\) modulo \(7\), and explain why there are exactly two.






TipHint and solution





The primitive root \(3\) has powers \(1,3,2,6,4,5\). Thus \(4=3^4\), and \(4t\equiv4\pmod6\) gives \(t\equiv1\pmod3\): \(t=1,4\). The roots are \(3,4\). The count is \(\gcd(4,6)=2\); zero is not a root.





3. Synchronization with a deadline — modelling
A machine is ready at times \(t\equiv1\pmod6\) and another at \(t\equiv3\pmod8\). Find the first common ready time at least \(50\).






TipHint and solution





CRT gives \(t=19+24k\). Impose \(19+24k\ge50\), so \(k\ge\lceil31/24\rceil=2\) and the answer is \(67\). Choosing the normalized CRT residue alone answers a different question. For a time window \([A,B]\), the feasible \(k\) interval is \([\lceil(A-19)/24\rceil,\lfloor(B-19)/24\rfloor]\).





4. Count valid exponents without a logarithm — synthesis
For prime \(p\) and a unit \(a\) of known order \(d\), count integers \(0\le x<X\) satisfying \(a^{kx}=1\), where \(k\ge1\) and \(X\ge0\).






TipHint and solution





The condition is \(d\mid kx\), hence \(d/\gcd(d,k)\mid x\). Let \(D=d/\gcd(d,k)\). For \(X=0\) the count is zero; otherwise it is \(1+\lfloor(X-1)/D\rfloor\). No discrete logarithm is needed because the target is the identity. With \(a=2,p=7,d=3,k=2,X=10\), valid exponents are \(0,3,6,9\).

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
Summary and reference sheet
Division modulo \(m\) means inversion of a unit. Linear congruences are solvable iff their gcd obstruction vanishes; compatible CRT constraints form one class modulo the lcm. Field polynomial root bounds imply cyclicity of finite multiplicative subgroups. Exponents reduce modulo an element’s order only for units. Valuations turn prime-power vanishing into an exponent threshold. Hensel chooses the next digit by a derivative congruence; a zero derivative requires a branching test. Match the required answer—existence, one root, all roots, or the smallest exponent—to the algorithm’s output contract.

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
Ordinary sieves compute every value through \(N\); summatory sieves compute only
\[F(N)=\sum_{n\le N}f(n)\]
when \(N\) is too large to visit. Here “compute only” does not mean magically skip information: it means find a recurrence whose arguments repeat among a small set of floor quotients. The art is choosing the correct structure:

Du Jiao sieve: an easy Dirichlet convolution isolates \(F(N)\).
Min_25 sieve: \(f\) is multiplicative and \(f(p)\) is a low-degree polynomial in \(p\).
Powerful-number sieve: remove an easy function agreeing with \(f\) on primes, leaving support only on numbers whose prime exponents are never one.

Before this chapter, master multiplicative functions, Möbius inversion, and quotient grouping in Chapter 02.

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
Prerequisites and learning objectives
Read multiplicative functions and divisor sums. For weighted prefixes, the discrete-sums chapter supplies polynomial block sums. You should learn to derive a prefix recurrence, prove that its recursive states close under floor division, distinguish a prime-sum sieve from full multiplicative enumeration, and justify a cutoff using the actual time and storage model.

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
Definitions and notation
\(N\ge1\) is the fixed query bound. An arithmetic function \(f\) has prefix \(F(x)=\sum_{1\le n\le x}f(n)\) for integer \(x\ge0\), with \(F(0)=0\). \(f*g\) means Dirichlet convolution. Coefficients lie in a commutative ring; integer formulas are evaluated exactly before reduction unless their denominators are units. In prime enumeration, \(p_i\) is the \(i\)th prime with zero-based index \(p_0=2\). A cutoff \(B\) is an integer preprocessing bound. Operation counts below treat exact coefficient operations as constant time.

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
1. The \(O(\sqrt{N})\) quotient-state space
Every recursive call in these methods should normally be one of the distinct values \(\lfloor N/i\rfloor\). This is a small state space because values below \(\sqrt N\) can occur directly, while every value above it equals \(\lfloor N/i\rfloor\) for some \(i<\sqrt N\). There are fewer than \(2\sqrt N\) values in total. Two common indexing schemes are:

store large values in a hash map and precompute all values up to a cutoff;
map \(v\) to \(v\) itself if \(v≤\sqrt{N}\), otherwise to \(N/v\) in a second array.

For \(N=20\), the distinct states are \(20,10,6,5,4,3,2,1\), rather than twenty different arguments. This is the object being memoized; quotient grouping is what makes a recurrence over all divisors practical.
Never accidentally memoize arbitrary arguments: that can turn an intended \(O(\sqrt{N})\) state set into linear space.
Closure follows from the identity \(\lfloor\lfloor N/a\rfloor/b\rfloor=\lfloor N/(ab)\rfloor\) for positive integers \(a,b\): both sides count how many complete blocks of \(ab\) fit in \(N\). Thus recursively dividing an existing quotient cannot create a new kind of state. The map using a second array is injective on the distinct large quotients: their producing indices are at most \(\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\), and different large quotient blocks have different right endpoints \(N/v\). This is a property of this state set, not of arbitrary integers \(v\).

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
section: 2. Du Jiao sieve from a convolution identity
text:
2. Du Jiao sieve from a convolution identity
Suppose \(h=f*g\) and the prefixes of \(h\) and \(g\) are cheap. We want \(F(N)=\sum_{n\le N}f(n)\). Start by summing the definition of convolution:
\[H(N)=\sum_{n\le N}\sum_{d\mid n}f(n/d)g(d).\]
Writing \(n=dk\) makes the meaning visible: for each possible \(d\), the allowed \(k\) run through \(1,\ldots,\lfloor N/d\rfloor\). Swapping those two sums gives
\[H(N)=\sum_{d\le N}g(d)F(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).\]
If \(g(1)=1\), the \(d=1\) term is exactly \(F(N)\); move every other term to the other side:
\[F(N)=H(N)-\sum_{d=2}^{N}g(d)F(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).\]
If instead \(g(1)\) is another unit, divide the whole equation by \(g(1)\) after isolating \(g(1)F(N)\); without an invertible \(g(1)\) this recurrence is not an algorithmic contract. Commutativity lets you swap the names of \(f,g\) if the other factor has easier prefix sums. The remaining formula appears to have \(N\) terms, but all indices \(\lfloor N/d\rfloor\) repeat. Group a block \(l\le d\le r\) with one quotient \(q\); its total coefficient is \(G(r)-G(l-1)\). That quotient grouping is the speedup, not the recurrence alone.

Mertens and totient prefixes
Let \(M(N)=\sum_{n\le N}\mu(n)\). The identity \(\mu*1=\varepsilon\) says that the convolution prefix \(H(N)\) is \(1\) for every \(N\ge1\). Here \(g=1\), so a block of indices \([l,r]\) has coefficient \(r-l+1\). Substitution gives
\[
M(N)=1-\sum_{l\in\mathcal B_N}
(r_N(l)-l+1)M(\lfloor N/l\rfloor),
\qquad r_N(l)=\left\lfloor\frac{N}{\lfloor N/l\rfloor}\right\rfloor.
\]
Here \(\mathcal B_N\) is the set of quotient-block starts: begin with \(l=2\) and repeatedly replace \(l\) by \(r_N(l)+1\). It is not the set of every integer from \(2\) through \(N\).
Let \(\Phi(N)=\sum_{n\le N}\varphi(n)\). The identity \(\varphi*1=\operatorname{id}\) says its convolution prefix is \(1+2+\cdots+N=T(N)=N(N+1)/2\), giving
\[
\Phi(N)=T(N)-\sum_{l\in\mathcal B_N}
(r_N(l)-l+1)\Phi(\lfloor N/l\rfloor),
\]
with the same definitions of \(\mathcal B_N\) and \(r_N(l)\).
Precompute through \(B\ge\sqrt N\) and memoize only larger quotient states. Such a state is \(x=\lfloor N/k\rfloor\) for \(k\le N/B\). Its quotient loop takes \(O(\sqrt x)\) operations, so all memoized work is at most
\[
O\left(\sum_{k\le N/B}\sqrt{N/k}\right)
=O\left(\sqrt N\sqrt{N/B}\right)
=O(N/\sqrt B).
\]
The middle bound follows by comparing \(\sum_{k\le K}k^{-1/2}\) with its integral, which is at most \(2\sqrt K\) up to a constant. Total time is \(O(B+N/\sqrt B)\) and storage is \(O(B+N/B)\), assuming \(O(1)\) prefix access and memo lookup. Choosing \(B\) near \(N^{2/3}\) balances the terms and gives \(O(N^{2/3})\) time and space for one query. This bound does not automatically amortize across unrelated query bounds.
Worked recurrence. For \(N=6\), \(\mu(1),\ldots,\mu(6)\) are \(1,-1,-1,0,-1,1\). The block formula uses \([2,2],[3,3],[4,6]\): \(M(6)=1-M(3)-M(2)-3M(1)=1-(-1)-0-3=-1\). The corresponding totient formula gives \(\Phi(6)=21-\Phi(3)-\Phi(2)-3\Phi(1)=21-4-2-3=12\). The weights are lengths of blocks, not numbers of distinct quotient values.
The quadratic scale of \(\sum\varphi(n)\) requires wide intermediates. Reduce modulo the problem modulus inside every operation if that is what the statement asks.


Derivation workflow

Name the wanted prefix \(F\).
Find \(g\) so \(h=f*g\) has an elementary prefix.
Sum \(h(n)\) for \(n≤N\), swap \(n=dk\), and isolate \(F(N)\).
Express coefficient sums on \([l,r]\) with prefix formulas.
Confirm every recursive argument is \(\lfloor N/l\rfloor\) and smaller than \(N\).

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
section: 3. Prime-sum sieve: the engine inside Min_25
text:
3. Prime-sum sieve: the engine inside Min_25
Min_25 first solves a narrower problem: quickly find sums over primes, such as \(\sum_{p\le w}p^k\), at every quotient state \(w=\lfloor N/l\rfloor\). Initialize
\[g_k(w)=\sum_{i=2}^{w}i^{k}.\]
At the start, \(g_k(w)\) is the sum over all integers \(2,\ldots,w\). Process primes \(p\) in increasing order. At the \(p\) stage, subtract the composites whose smallest prime factor is \(p\); for every state \(w\ge p^2\) this is
\[g_k(w)\mathrel{-}=p^{k}\left(g_k(\lfloor w/p\rfloor)-S_k(p-1)\right),\]
where \(S_k(p-1)=\sum_{q<p,q prime}q^{k}\). After processing all \(p≤\sqrt{N}\), \(g_k(w)=\sum_{q≤w,q prime}q^{k}\).
Why \(p^2\)? Any composite first removed at this stage has least prime factor \(p\), hence it is \(p\cdot x\) with \(x\ge p\). Just before the \(p\) stage, \(g_k(\lfloor w/p\rfloor)\) consists of two kinds of surviving entries: primes below \(p\), which are deliberately retained as final prime answers, and integers having no prime factor below \(p\). Only the second kind can be a valid cofactor \(x\), so \(S_k(p-1)\) removes the retained small primes. Updating states in descending order prevents the right side from using values already modified by the current prime. After all relevant stages, only prime contributions remain.
Worked sieve. For \(k=0,N=10\), initially \(g_0(10)=9\), counting \(2,\ldots,10\). The \(p=2\) update removes \(4,6,8,10\), leaving five entries. The \(p=3\) update removes \(9\), leaving the four primes \(2,3,5,7\). At \(w=5\), processing prime two before \(w=10\) would change the cofactor data used by larger states; descending order is what preserves the stage invariant.
For \(k=0\) this computes \(\pi(w)\), the number of primes at most \(w\). One array uses \(O(\sqrt N)\) space. An elementary upper bound on update count is \(O(N^{3/4})\): primes at most \(N^{1/4}\) have at most \(2\sqrt N\) states each, while larger primes can update only \(O(N/p^2)\) large states; \(N\sum_{j>N^{1/4}}j^{-2}=O(N^{3/4})\). Using prime-density estimates sharpens this to \(O(N^{3/4}/\log N)\) asymptotically for this prime-sum core, as discussed in the official ABC370 editorial. The simple bound already explains why the prime-sum stage is sublinear.

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
4. Full Min_25 sieve
Min_25 extends that prime-sum engine to a multiplicative function. Assume \(f\) is multiplicative, each \(f(p^{e})\) is computable in \(O(1)\), and the prime values, not necessarily all prime-power values, satisfy
\[f(p)=\sum_{k=0}^{K}c_kp^{k}\]
for small fixed \(K\). Run the prime-sum sieve for each required power \(k\); combine the arrays to obtain
\[G_f(x)=\sum_{p\le x}f(p).\]
The prime-sum sieve gives the contribution of prime numbers. To cover every composite exactly once, enumerate it by its least prime and the exact exponent of that prime. Index primes from \(p_0=2\) and set \(G_f(p_{-1})=0\). Define \(S(x,y)\) as the sum of \(f(n)\) for \(2\le n\le x\) whose least prime is at least \(p_y\). Calls maintain \(p_{y-1}\le x\) (with the \(y=0\) sentinel understood), so its prime-only base contribution is \(G_f(x)-G_f(p_{y-1})\) and is zero when the interval contains no prime. For every possible least prime \(p_i\), enumerate an exponent \(e\ge1\). The term with \(S\) counts numbers \(p_i^e m\) where \(m>1\) has no prime factor at most \(p_i\); the separate term counts pure powers (the prime \(p_i\) itself is already in the base term):
\[
S(x,y)=G_f(x)-G_f(p_{y-1})+
\sum_{\substack{i\ge y\\p_i^2\le x}}
\sum_{\substack{e\ge1\\p_i^{e+1}\le x}}
\left(f(p_i^e)S(\lfloor x/p_i^e\rfloor,i+1)+f(p_i^{e+1})\right).
\]
Finally \(f(1)+S(N,0)=1+S(N,0)\) is the prefix, using the standard convention for a multiplicative function. The shift in the pure-power exponent is deliberate: as \(e=1,2,\ldots\), those terms list \(p_i^2,p_i^3,\ldots\) exactly once, while the cofactor term uses \(p_i^e\) as the exact valuation. The condition \(p_i^{e+1}\le x\) also safely ends the cofactor branch: any permitted nontrivial cofactor is at least \(p_{i+1}>p_i\). This decomposition is unique.
As a hand check, take \(f(n)=1\) and \(x=10\). The base term counts the four primes \(2,3,5,7\). The branch for least prime \(2\) contributes \(6,10\) from \(2\cdot\{3,5\}\) and the pure powers \(4,8\); the branch for least prime \(3\) contributes the pure power \(9\). Together with \(f(1)\) these are all ten integers, each assigned to exactly one least-prime branch.
Keep the enumeration cost separate from the prime-sum cost. Let \(E(N)\) be the number of \((i,e)\) branches actually visited by the displayed recursion from \((N,0)\). With \(O(1)\) local values and prime-prefix access, the cost is \(O((K+1)N^{3/4}+E(N))\) by the elementary prime-stage bound, with \(O((K+1)\sqrt N+\log N)\) storage for arrays and a depth-first stack. The logarithmic stack bound follows because each recursive step divides by at least two. A conservative \(E(N)=O(N)\) bound follows by assigning each call its product of selected prime powers: the strictly increasing prime indices give a unique factorization path for every product, and all products are at most \(N\). Practical enumeration is much smaller on common instances, but this is not a proof that every variant inherits the prime-sum bound. Count these branches when benchmarking the chosen library; optimized Min_25 variants require their own complexity analysis.
Applicability signals. \(N\) is around \(10^{9}–10^{12}\), the statement gives a multiplicative function through its prime powers, and its value at a prime is polynomial (examples: \(\varphi(p)=p-1\), \(\mu(p)=-1\), \(\sigma_k(p)=1+p^{k}\)).
Non-applicable cases. If \(f(p)\) depends on an arbitrary property of \(p\) for which no fast prime prefix exists, standard Min_25 has no base data. If only \(\mu/\varphi\) prefixes are needed, Du Jiao is simpler.

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
5. Powerful-number support
A positive integer is powerful if every prime dividing it has exponent at least two. For example, \(72=2^3\cdot3^2\) is powerful whereas \(12=2^2\cdot3\) is not. The count through \(N\) is \(O(\sqrt N)\) because every powerful integer has the unique representation
\[n=a^2b^3,\qquad b\text{ square-free}.\]
For each prime exponent \(e\ge2\), choose the unique \(e=2u+3v\) with \(v\in\{0,1\}\); the primes with \(v=1\) form \(b\). Consequently \(b\le N^{1/3}\) and \(a\le\sqrt{N/b^3}\). Summing over \(b\) gives \(\sqrt N\sum_b b^{-3/2}=O(\sqrt N)\) candidates. The requirement that \(b\) be square-free is what makes the representation unique.
This sparsity yields another generic strategy. Choose an easy multiplicative \(g\) agreeing with \(f\) on primes, and define
\[h=f*g^{-1}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f=h*g.\]
Because multiplicative functions have value \(1\) at \(1\), the prime-power convolution identity gives \(h(p)=f(p)-g(p)=0\). Multiplicativity then forces \(h(n)=0\) whenever any prime has exponent exactly one: its product over prime-power factors contains \(h(p)=0\). Thus \(h\) is supported on powerful numbers. Let \(G(x)=\sum_{n\le x}g(n)\). In the convolution \(f=h*g\), choosing a divisor \(d\) for the \(h\) factor leaves a \(g\) factor through \(\lfloor N/d\rfloor\); summing those choices gives
\[F(N)=\sum_{d\le N\atop d\text{ powerful}}h(d)G(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).\]
Compute local prime-power coefficients from
\[f(p^{e})=\sum_{j=0}^{e}h(p^{j})g(p^{e-j}),\]
so \(h(1)=1\), \(h(p)=0\), and for \(e≥2\),
\[h(p^{e})=f(p^{e})-\sum_{j=0}^{e-1}h(p^{j})g(p^{e-j}).\]
Enumerate powerful numbers by DFS over increasing primes, choosing exponent zero or at least two; accumulate \(h(d)G(N/d)\). Prune when \(d·p²>N\). Alternatively enumerate the unique \(a²b³\) representation when the coefficient is easier to recover that way.
This method is attractive when \(G(x)\) is elementary or already available and \(h(p^{e})\) is cheap. Complexity is commonly around \(O(\sqrt{N} \operatorname{polylog} N)\) plus the cost of obtaining \(G\) and primes, but must be derived for the exact enumeration.

A common special case: perfect powers
To count integers \(n>1\) representable as \(a^{b}\) with \(a,b>1\), enumerate exponents but remove duplicate representations. If \(n=\prod_i p_i^{e_i}\), its maximal possible exponent is \(\gcd_i e_i\); thus \(n\) is a nontrivial perfect power exactly when this gcd exceeds one. Möbius inversion over exponents, or counting by the maximal exponent, avoids double counting. Integer kth roots must be corrected with exact 128-bit power comparisons—floating- point pow alone is unsafe near \(10^{18}\).


Worked powerful-support transformation
Let \(f(n)=\tau(n)\) and \(g(n)=2^{\omega(n)}\), where \(\omega(n)\) counts distinct prime factors. Both functions equal two at a prime. At \(p^e\), \(g(p^e)=2\) for \(e\ge1\). Local convolution gives \(h(p)=0\), \(h(p^2)=3-2=1\), and \(h(p^3)=4-(2+0+2)=0\). Continuing gives \(h(p^{2j})=1\) and \(h(p^{2j+1})=0\): the local generating-series quotient is
\[
\frac{\sum_{e\ge0}(e+1)t^e}{1+2t+2t^2+\cdots}
=\frac{1/(1-t)^2}{(1+t)/(1-t)}
=\frac1{1-t^2}.
\]
These are formal identities with constant-one denominators, valid over the integers without dividing coefficients. Thus \(h\) is the indicator of squares, and \(\sum_{n\le N}\tau(n)=\sum_{a\le\sqrt N}G(\lfloor N/a^2\rfloor)\). This is an identity, not automatically a fast algorithm: we still need cheap \(G\). Matching on primes makes support sparse but does not supply that prefix. For \(N=4\), \(G(4)=1+2+2+2=7\) and \(G(1)=1\), giving \(8\).

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
Pitfalls

Prove the convolution identity before optimizing it; a swapped divisor argument silently computes the wrong function.
In prime-sum DP, process \(w\) descending and only while \(w≥p²\).
Distinguish “primes \(<p\)” from “primes \(≤p\)” in the base subtraction.
Min_25 recursion must enforce strictly increasing prime factors after choosing the least prime.
Include \(f(1)\) exactly once.
Use 128-bit arithmetic for \(p²\), prime-power growth, polynomial sums, and unmodded answers.
Modular polynomial sums may require division by \(2,6,…\); use integer formulas before reduction if the modulus is not guaranteed coprime to denominators.
Cached values keyed by the actual argument \(x\) may be reused across queries for the same function and coefficient ring. Array slots keyed by \(N/x\) are query-specific and must be rebuilt when \(N\) changes.

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
Ordered practice

1. Relatively Prime Powers — Codeforces 1036F

Level: Mastery · Language: English/Russian
Trains: perfect-power counting, Möbius inversion over exponents, exact integer roots.
Editorial: official Educational Round 50 editorial



Hint 1

Count numbers that are not expressible as a nontrivial perfect power, then complement.



Hint 2

A number may appear under several exponents; classify it by the gcd of exponents in its prime factorization.



Hint 3

Use Möbius inclusion–exclusion on exponents and exact corrected kth roots up to the relevant logarithm.







TipEditorial guidance: many queries





The exponent-inversion formula derives the answer, but the official task has many queries. Precompute all non-square perfect powers through the maximum query: enumerate bases for odd exponents \(3,5,\ldots,\lfloor\log_2 X\rfloor\), discard squares using exact integer square roots, then sort and deduplicate. Every non-square perfect power has an odd exponent at least three in some representation. The largest base range is the cube range, \(X^{1/3}\); the total candidates are \(O(X^{1/3}\log X)\) by a conservative bound. For each query \(n\), squares contribute \(\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor-1\) and a binary search counts precomputed non-squares. The elegant count is \(n-\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor-C(n)\). Exact roots and deduplication matter: \(64\) has several representations but is removed as a square.





2. A Simple Math Problem — Luogu P3768

Level: Capstone · Language: Chinese
Prerequisites: totient convolution, Du Jiao sieve, polynomial block sums.
Editorial: Luogu solution index (Chinese; login required). A complete local reduction is in the capstone guide.



Hint 1

Rewrite the gcd-weighted double sum by extracting the gcd and using a totient identity.



Hint 2

The remaining expression needs prefix sums of a weighted totient function, not plain \(\varphi\).



Hint 3

Derive its convolution recurrence, evaluate polynomial coefficients over quotient blocks, and reduce throughout modulo the given large prime. The exact-integer derivation also works for composite answer moduli if no invalid modular division is introduced.

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
Exercises with solutions

1. Blocks and boundary cases — concept check
List the quotient blocks for \(N=10\), then compute \(M(10)\) from smaller Mertens prefixes.






TipHint and solution





Starting at two, the blocks are \([2,2],[3,3],[4,5],[6,10]\), with quotients \(5,3,2,1\). Since \(M(5)=-2,M(3)=-1,M(2)=0,M(1)=1\), \(M(10)=1-(-2)-(-1)-2\cdot0-5=-1\). At \(N=1\) there are no blocks and \(M(1)=1\).





2. A weighted recurrence — derivation
Let \(f(n)=n^2\varphi(n)\). Find a convolution with an elementary prefix, and write the grouped recurrence for \(F(N)\).






TipHint and solution





Take \(g(n)=n^2\). Then \((f*g)(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d^2\varphi(d)(n/d)^2
=n^2\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n^3\). Thus \(F(N)=\sum_{n\le N}n^3-
\sum_{[l,r],\,l\ge2}(\sum_{d=l}^r d^2)F(\lfloor N/l\rfloor)\). Here \(\sum_{n\le N}n^3=[N(N+1)/2]^2\); square sums provide block weights. At \(N=3\), \(F(3)=1+4+18=23=36-4-9\). All fractions in power-sum formulas are exact integer divisions if the answer modulus does not permit the corresponding inverses.





3. Perfect powers without duplicates — synthesis
Count the integers \(2\le n\le X\) that are nontrivial perfect powers, using exact integer roots and Möbius values of exponents.






TipHint and solution





If the gcd of the prime exponents of \(n\) is \(g\), then \(n\) is an \(e\)th power iff \(e\mid g\). The weight \(-\sum_{e\mid g,\,e\ge2}\mu(e)\) is zero when \(g=1\) and one otherwise. Summing by \(e\) gives
\[-\sum_{e=2}^{\lfloor\log_2 X\rfloor}
\mu(e)\left(\lfloor X^{1/e}\rfloor-1\right).\]
Subtract one to exclude base one. At \(X=16\), the terms are \(3+1+0=4\), representing \(4,8,9,16\). Each root may be found by binary search with capped integer powers; one safe baseline uses \(O(\log X\log\log X)\) arithmetic operations per root and \(O(\log X)\) roots. A faster integer-root library must still correct rounding exactly.

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
Summary and reference sheet
The closed state set is \(\{\lfloor N/i\rfloor:1\le i\le N\}\). Du Jiao isolates a prefix from \(h=f*g\) when \(g(1)\) is a unit and the other prefixes are cheap; one-query cost is \(O(B+N/\sqrt B)\) for \(B\ge\sqrt N\). Prime-sum sieving removes composites at their unique least-prime stage and updates quotient values downward. Full multiplicative enumeration additionally chooses the exact least-prime exponent; its branch count is a separate cost. Matching functions on primes confines their convolution quotient to powerful numbers, but a cheap prefix for the matched function remains essential. Every method must include the value at one exactly once.

title: 04 · Practice — Advanced Combinatorics
text:
Concept checks with solutions

A. Named rooms and unnamed teams
Split four labelled people into two nonempty teams. How many answers are there if the teams are unnamed? What changes if the teams are named red and blue?






TipHint





Count assignments to named teams, then examine the number of names for each unlabelled partition.









NoteSolution





There are \(2^4-2=14\) assignments using both names. Each unlabelled partition has exactly two namings, so the answers are \(7\) and \(14\). Empty teams would break this simple correspondence if the requested number of nonempty blocks were not fixed. This is \(S(4,2)=2S(3,2)+S(3,1)=7\).





B. Forbidden diagonal
Derive the number of permutations of four labels with no fixed point.






TipHint





Any selection of diagonal cells is a nonattacking rook placement.









NoteSolution





Here \(r_k=\binom4k\). Thus the answer is \(24-4\cdot6+6\cdot2-4\cdot1+1=9\). For general \(n\), the same reasoning gives \(\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk(n-k)!\). The cancellation proof of IE justifies every sign; no modular division is needed.





C. Exactly one shared value
Let \(f,g:[2]\to[3]\) each be injective. Count ordered pairs for which exactly one aligned position has \(f(i)=g(i)\).






TipHint





Use marked counts \(b_1,b_2\), or first fix \(f\) and the shared position.









NoteSolution





There are six choices for \(f\). For either chosen shared position, the other value of \(g\) must avoid both the shared value and the other value of \(f\); exactly one of the three target names remains. Hence the answer is \(6\cdot2=12\). Alternatively \(b_1=6\cdot2\cdot2=24\), \(b_2=6\), and \(a_1=b_1-2b_2=12\).

title: 05 · Practice — Group Actions
text:
List binary necklaces of length three. Why is \(2^3/3\) meaningless as a count?






TipHint





Separate constant strings from strings with one minority color.









NoteSolution





Representatives are 000, 001, 011, 111, with orbit sizes 1, 3, 3, 1. Their sizes sum to 8, but there is no common orbit size to divide by. Burnside gives \((8+2+2)/3=4\).






Count square bead colorings with exactly two red and two blue beads up to rotation. Then add reflection symmetry.






TipHint





The half-turn fixes two such colorings; quarter-turns fix none.









NoteSolution





The identity fixes \(\binom42=6\). Rotation Burnside gives \((6+2)/4=2\). Representatives have adjacent or opposite red beads. Both are preserved as classes under reflection, so the bracelet count is also two. Counting all \(2^{z(g)}\) fixed colorings would ignore the prescribed multiplicities.






A group of size six has Burnside numerator 42. Recover its orbit count modulo four without inverting six. Generalize the method.






TipHint





Preserve the numerator modulo the product of the divisor and target modulus.









NoteSolution





\(42\bmod24=18\), and \(18/6=3\equiv7\pmod4\). In general retain the numerator modulo \(gm\) then divide its representative by \(g\). Keeping only modulo \(m\) loses information: residues 2 could represent numerator 6 or 18, whose quotients differ modulo 4.

title: 06 · Practice — Polynomial Algorithms
text:
Solved exercises

A. Samples are not a degree bound
Recover a polynomial of degree at most two from values 1, 6, 17 at 0, 1, 2. Give a different polynomial with the same samples when the bound is removed.






TipHint





The second finite difference determines twice the quadratic coefficient.









NoteSolution





Writing \(f=a+bx+cx^2\) gives \(a=1\), \(b+c=5\), \(2b+4c=16\), hence \(c=3,b=2\). Thus \(f=1+2x+3x^2\). The polynomial \(f+x(x-1)(x-2)\) has the same samples but degree three. These computations require rational arithmetic or a field in which 2 is a unit; in characteristic two the sample points 0 and 2 coincide.





B. A false CRT shortcut
An integer convolution coefficient is known only to lie in \([0,100]\). Can its residue modulo 17 determine its residue modulo 10?






TipHint





Find two bounded numbers agreeing modulo 17.









NoteSolution





No: 1 and 18 agree modulo 17 but differ modulo 10. Auxiliary CRT moduli must have product greater than 100 for unambiguous reconstruction on this interval. Garner’s algorithm changes representation, not this information limit.





C. Sum of pair differences
Two multisets contain nonnegative integers at most \(D\). Derive all counts of ordered pairs \((a,b)\) with difference \(a-b=d\) for \(-D\le d\le D\).






TipHint





Reverse the second frequency array and solve its convolution index equation.









NoteSolution





Let \(u_i\) count first-multiset values \(i\) and \(v_{D-j}\) count second-multiset values \(j\). Index \(i+D-j=D+d\) counts exactly the desired pairs, so answer \(d\) is \((u*v)_{D+d}\). The range 0…2D includes every difference. Complexity is \(O(M(D+1))\) after frequency construction; multiply occurrence counts, not mere presence flags. Diagonal pairs are included when the multisets coincide unless the problem explicitly excludes reusing one occurrence.

title: 07 · Practice — Formal Power Series
text:
Over the rationals, find the normalized logarithm of \(A=2+2x\) through degree three. What is its exponential?






TipHint





The logarithmic derivative ignores a constant multiplicative factor.









NoteSolution





\(A'/A=1/(1+x)=1-x+x^2+\cdots\), so normalized \(\log A=x-x^2/2+x^3/3\). Its exponential is \(1+x\pmod{x^4}\), not \(2+2x\). Recovering \(A\) requires remembering its constant factor separately.






How many roots does \(B^2=0\pmod{x^5}\) have over \(\mathbb F_5\)?






TipHint





Use the first nonzero coefficient rather than solving five equations.









NoteSolution





A nonzero square has valuation twice the valuation of its root, so \(v(B)\ge3\). Precisely the polynomials \(b_3x^3+b_4x^4\) work, giving \(5^2=25\) roots including zero. This count is in the truncated ring, not the infinite domain \(\mathbb F_5[[x]]\).






Suppose events observed at time \(n\) split uniquely by their first occurrence: \(g_n=\sum_{i=0}^nf_i h_{n-i}\) with \(h_0=1\). Given \(G=1/(1-2x)\) and \(H=1/(1-x)\), find all \(f_n\).






TipHint





Interpret the convolution as a product before selecting an FPS operation.









NoteSolution





\(FH=G\) and \(H\) is a unit, so \(F=(1-x)/(1-2x)\). Thus \(f_0=1\), and for \(n\ge1\), \(f_n=2^n-2^{n-1}=2^{n-1}\). The decomposition must be unique; allowing several candidate first occurrences would overcount and invalidate the product equation. For arbitrary prefixes, one inverse and one convolution compute the answer in \(O(M(n))\).

text:
Count objects of total size four whose parts have sizes one or two, first when order matters and then when it does not.






TipHint





Compare \(1/(1-x-x^2)\) with \(1/((1-x)(1-x^2))\).









NoteSolution





Ordered sequences are 1111, 112, 121, 211, 22: five. Unordered objects are 1111, 112, 22: three. The first GF chooses a sequence of parts, while the second independently chooses the multiplicity of each part size. Coefficients through degree four are \((1,1,2,3,5)\) and \((1,1,2,2,3)\) respectively.






Find the first four coefficients of \((2+x)/(1-x-x^2)\) and state the recurrence.






TipHint





Compare coefficients in \((1-x-x^2)A=2+x\) before using the recurrence.









NoteSolution





\(a_0=2\) and \(a_1-a_0=1\), so \(a_1=3\). For \(n\ge2\), \(a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}\). The requested prefix is \(2,3,5,8\). For a huge \(n\), use Bostan–Mori with this numerator and denominator; replacing the numerator by the Fibonacci numerator would change the sequence.






Let \(T=x/(1-T)\) count nonempty plane rooted trees by vertices. Count ordered pairs of such trees with a total of five vertices.






TipHint





Use Lagrange with \(n=5,k=2\), or convolve the small tree counts.









NoteSolution





\([x^5]T^2=\frac25[t^3](1-t)^{-5}=\frac25\binom73=14\). The independent check is \(T=x+x^2+2x^3+5x^4+\cdots\), giving \(1\cdot5+1\cdot2+2\cdot1+5\cdot1=14\). Modulo five the displayed division cannot be used directly; the integer answer may be reduced afterward, or the convolution may be computed there.
