Hint 3

For \(A,B\ge1\), the answer simplifies to \(\binom{A+B-2}{A-1}\left[{N-1\atop A+B-2}\right]\). Obtain the Stirling coefficient from the product \(x(x+1)\cdots(x+N-2)\) using a balanced product tree. Handle \(N=1\) with the empty product.







NoteWhy the simplification works





Cut at the global maximum. On each side, break the permutation at its records (reading the right side backwards). Each record starts a block with its largest element first; viewing the block cyclically is a permutation cycle. The remaining \(N-1\) labels therefore form \(A+B-2\) cycles. Choose which \(A-1\) cycles belong on the left; record order reconstructs the two sides uniquely. This gives the binomial factor and the first-kind Stirling coefficient. If either \(A\) or \(B\) is zero the answer is zero for a nonempty permutation.

title: 10 — Linear Algebra over Finite Fields
text: Linear algebra appears whenever constraints are linear, path choices form an XOR space, spanning trees must be counted, or a long recurrence must be compressed. The common idea is to replace many objects by coordinates in a vector space and then use reversible row operations. Always identify the scalar domain first: real numbers, \(\mathbb F_p\), and \(\mathbb F_2\) have different numerical and structural hazards.

title: 10 — Linear Algebra over Finite Fields
text:
Prerequisites and learning objectives
Read proofs and invariants and fields and units. The recurrence sections also use polynomial division. After this chapter you should be able to count solutions from rank, prove an XOR representation count, translate a tree count into a determinant, and explain why a finite-dimensional transition produces a linear recurrence. Your library supplies elimination and polynomial arithmetic; the task here is to establish what those operations mean and when they are valid.

title: 10 — Linear Algebra over Finite Fields
text:
1. Vectors, coordinates, and reversible equations
Fix a field \(K\). A vector in \(K^c\) is a list of \(c\) field elements; addition and scalar multiplication act coordinate by coordinate. A linear combination of \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) is \(\sum_i a_i v_i\) with \(a_i\in K\). Their span is the set of all such combinations. A list is independent if the only combination equal to zero has every coefficient zero. A basis is an independent list that spans the space in question. Its length is the dimension.
For example, \((1,0)\) and \((1,1)\) form a basis of \(K^2\): the vector \((x,y)\) is uniquely \((x-y)(1,0)+y(1,1)\). The word “uniquely” matters. If two coefficient lists represented the same vector, subtracting them would produce a nonzero dependence. A basis is therefore a lossless coordinate system, much like compressing a state to exactly its independent parameters.
A matrix \(A\in K^{r\times c}\) describes the linear map \(x\mapsto Ax\). Its kernel is \(\{x:Ax=0\}\); its image is \(\{Ax:x\in K^c\}\). The image dimension is the rank. The equation \(Ax=b\) asks whether \(b\) belongs to the image and, if it does, for all its preimages.

Elimination and the rank–nullity count
Over a field, row operations preserve the solution set because they merely replace one equation by an equivalent linear combination of equations. Maintain a pivot row; for each column choose a nonzero entry, swap it to that row, normalize, and eliminate. These operations are reversible: undo the swap, multiply back by the nonzero scalar, or subtract the row previously added. After processing a column, each pivot column has one leading entry and all later rows are zero in previous pivot columns. This is the invariant that ensures no equation is lost and each pivot settles one new variable. A pivot in the coefficient matrix records one independent equation, so \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\) is the number of such pivots. For a system with \(r\) equations and \(c\) unknowns, a zero row with a nonzero augmented entry means inconsistency; otherwise the augmented matrix has the same rank as \(A\) and there are \(c-\operatorname{rank}(A)\) free variables. Over \(\mathbb F_q\), that means exactly \(q^{\,c-\operatorname{rank}(A)}\) solutions; over an infinite field it describes a solution affine space of that dimension. To justify the count, choose the \(c-\operatorname{rank}(A)\) nonpivot variables freely and solve pivot variables backwards; each choice has exactly one completion. Thus \(\dim\ker A=c-\operatorname{rank}(A)\), the rank–nullity identity. If \(x_0\) solves \(Ax=b\), every solution is \(x_0+z\) with \(z\in\ker A\), since \(A(x-x_0)=0\). Such a translated subspace is called an affine space.






NoteExample: constraints versus variables



Over \(\mathbb F_5\), the equations \(x+y+z=2\) and \(2x+2y+2z=4\) have rank one. Choose \(y,z\) arbitrarily and set \(x=2-y-z\): there are \(25\) solutions. Replacing the second right side by \(3\) makes the system inconsistent, not rank two: subtraction leaves \(0=4\) in \(\mathbb F_5\).


For example, over \(\mathbb F_5\), \(x+y=1\), \(2x+3y=0\) becomes \(y=3,x=3\) after subtracting twice the first row. The integer solution is irrelevant: the field is part of the question. Dense elimination costs \(O(rc\min(r,c))\). For determinant, do not normalize: each row swap negates the answer, multiply by the pivot, then eliminate below using the current entry divided by the pivot. Composite moduli are not fields: a nonzero pivot may be noninvertible. Use prime-factor methods, fraction-free elimination, or exact integer algorithms instead. For instance, \(2x=2\) modulo \(6\) has solutions \(x=1,4\); dividing by the nonzero residue \(2\) would discard one. Rank-based field counts do not apply to this ring.


What the determinant measures
For an \(n\times n\) matrix, define
\[\det A=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)
\prod_{i=1}^n A_{i,\sigma(i)}.\]
Here \(S_n\) consists of permutations of \(1,\ldots,n\), and the sign is \((-1)\) to the number of inversions. A summand chooses one entry from each row and column. Swapping rows reverses the sign; adding a multiple of another row does not change the determinant because terms with repeated rows cancel. Triangular matrices have determinant equal to their diagonal product. These facts explain the elimination contract above. Over a field, \(\det A\ne0\) exactly when every column has a pivot, equivalently when \(Ax=b\) has a unique solution for every \(b\). The permutation definition also makes sense over any commutative ring, although division-based elimination may not. The determinant of the empty matrix is \(1\).

title: 10 — Linear Algebra over Finite Fields
section: 2. XOR basis as elimination over \(\mathbb F_2\)
text:
2. XOR basis as elimination over \(\mathbb F_2\)
A set of machine words is a vector set whose coordinates are bits, with XOR as vector addition. Keep at most one pivot per highest bit. Inserting a word means XORing away known highest bits; if nothing remains it was already a linear combination of earlier words, otherwise it adds one independent direction.
Insertion costs \(O(B)\). If rank is \(r\), the span has \(2^{r}\) distinct values. For representation counts from \(n\) input vectors, every reachable value has \(2^{n-r}\) representations. To obtain the zero-indexed \(k\)-th smallest distinct XOR, reduce to a basis in which every pivot bit occurs in only its own vector, order those vectors by increasing pivot bit, and XOR the vectors selected by the bits of \(k\). A merely triangular or arbitrarily ordered basis does not give numeric order.
Why the representation count is uniform: map a choice vector in \(\mathbb F_2^n\) to the XOR it selects. This map has rank \(r\), so its kernel has \(2^{n-r}\) elements; every nonempty fiber is a translate of that kernel. For words \(1,2,3\), the rank is \(2\) and each of \(0,1,2,3\) has two representations. Zero comes from the empty subset and from all three words.
For sorted enumeration require \(0\le k<2^r\). In a reduced basis, compare two coefficient masks at their highest different bit. That selects the highest pivot at which their numeric XORs differ; lower basis vectors cannot change it. Thus the order of coefficient masks equals numeric order. As a failure example, triangular vectors \(1,3\) in increasing pivot order enumerate \(0,1,3,2\), not sorted order; reducing \(3\) by \(1\) repairs them to \(1,2\).
Graph recognition: assign each vertex an XOR distance from a DFS root. Every non-tree edge yields a cycle XOR dist[u] ^ w ^ dist[v]. If \(s,t\) lie in the same undirected connected component, all XORs of walks from \(s\) to \(t\) are dist[s]^dist[t] plus the span of that component’s cycle XORs.
To prove this, XOR the edges of a walk with the fixed tree path; every vertex then has even incidence, so the remaining edges decompose into cycles. Each cycle is a combination of fundamental cycles from non-tree edges. Conversely, walk to any such cycle along the tree, traverse it, and return along the same tree edges; the detour contributes exactly the cycle XOR because its connector appears twice. This proves equality for walks in an undirected component. It does not prove equality for simple paths: a triangle attached at a single articulation to the \(s\)–\(t\) path can alter a walk’s XOR, but a simple path cannot visit the triangle and return through that articulation.
With \(m\) edges, \(n\) vertices, and \(B\) bits, build the component bases in \(O((n+m)B)\) time and \(O(n+B\cdot\text{components})\) auxiliary space. Do not reuse one component’s cycles for endpoints in another component.

title: 10 — Linear Algebra over Finite Fields
text:
3. Kirchhoff’s matrix-tree theorem
For a weighted undirected graph, form the Laplacian
\[L_{ii}=\sum_{j\ne i}w_{ij},\qquad L_{ij}=-w_{ij}\quad(i\ne j).\]
The diagonal is the total edge weight leaving a vertex; an off-diagonal entry is the negative edge weight connecting its two vertices (with parallel-edge weights added first). Delete any one row and the corresponding column. The determinant of the resulting \((n-1)\times(n-1)\) cofactor equals the total weight of spanning trees, where a tree’s weight is the product of its edge weights.
Why it works: orient edges arbitrarily and let \(B\) be the incidence matrix. Each column of \(B\) has \(+1\) at one endpoint and \(-1\) at the other; \(W\) is diagonal with the edge weights. Then \(L=BWB^{T}\) because one edge contributes its weight to both diagonal positions and its negative to the two off-diagonal positions. Delete the root row from \(B\) to obtain \(\bar B\). The determinant-of-product expansion, called Cauchy–Binet, gives
\[\det(\bar B W\bar B^T)
=\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq E\\|S|=n-1}}
\det(\bar B_{[:,S]})^2\prod_{e\in S}w_e.\]
This identity follows by expanding determinants: terms that choose a repeated intermediate column cancel in opposite-sign pairs, leaving subsets of distinct columns and their two determinant factors. A cyclic edge set has dependent incidence columns. For a disconnected set, summing the rows of a component not containing the deleted root gives zero, so its determinant also vanishes. For a tree, remove a nonroot leaf and expand along its single incident entry; induction down to the empty matrix gives determinant \(\pm1\). Exactly the spanning trees therefore survive, each with its edge-product weight. Directed arborescences require a directional convention. With \(L_{ii}=\sum_{i\to j,\ j\ne i}w_{ij}\) and, for \(i\ne j\), \(L_{ij}=-\sum_{\text{edges }i\to j}w_{ij}\), the root cofactor counts trees whose edges point toward the root. To count trees pointing away from the root, use the indegree convention \(L_{ii}=\sum_{j\to i,\ j\ne i}w_{ji}\), \(L_{ij}=-\sum_{\text{edges }j\to i}w_{ji}\). On the one-edge graph \(r\to v\), deleting the row and column of \(r\) gives determinant \(1\) only under the indegree convention, as required for the unique tree pointing away from \(r\). This two-vertex test catches a transposed convention.
Complexity is \(O(n^{3})\) with dense elimination. Parallel edge weights add. Self-loops do not contribute. Under a modulus, the determinant counts modulo that modulus.
For a triangle with unit edge weights, deleting one row and column leaves \(\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\), whose determinant is \(3\). These are exactly the three spanning trees obtained by deleting one edge.
For triangle edge weights \(a,b,c\), the same calculation gives \(ab+ac+bc\): with \((a,b,c)=(2,3,5)\) the weighted count is \(31\). A zero determinant modulo a prime can mean cancellation of a positive integer count modulo that prime; it is not a certificate that the original graph is disconnected.

title: 10 — Linear Algebra over Finite Fields
text:
4. Linear recurrences and characteristic polynomials
Let \(k\ge1\) and let the recurrence \(s_n=c_1s_{n-1}+\cdots+c_ks_{n-k}\) hold for every \(n\ge k\), with initial values \(s_0,\ldots,s_{k-1}\) in a commutative ring. Then the polynomial \(x^{k}-c_1x^{k-1}-\cdots-c_k\) annihilates the sequence: replace every \(x^k\) by the prescribed combination of lower powers. Reduce \(x^{N}\) modulo this polynomial; the remainder coefficients tell exactly how to combine \(s_0,\ldots,s_{k-1}\) to obtain \(s_N\). Binary exponentiation with polynomial reduction costs \(O(k^{2}\log N)\) (Kitamasa); NTT-based methods or Bostan–Mori improve large \(k\).
Here is why reduction computes sequence values, rather than merely a useful formal remainder. Define \(\Lambda(x^j)=s_j\) and extend by linearity. For every \(j\ge0\), the recurrence says \(\Lambda(x^j(x^k-c_1x^{k-1}-\cdots-c_k))=0\). If \(x^N=Q(x)C(x)+R(x)\) with \(\deg R<k\), applying \(\Lambda\) leaves \(s_N=\Lambda(R)\). Division by the monic \(C\) uses no inverse, so this argument works even modulo a composite number. Binary exponentiation maintains that its accumulated polynomial is congruent to the processed power of \(x\) modulo \(C\); multiply and reduce after each step. Memory is \(O(k)\) with naive products.
For Fibonacci, the characteristic polynomial is \(x^2-x-1\). Since \(x^5\equiv5x+3\pmod{x^2-x-1}\), every Fibonacci-type sequence obeys \(s_5=3s_0+5s_1\). This is what “the remainder coefficients tell how to combine initial terms” means concretely.

Discovering a recurrence: the discrepancy idea
For a field-valued sequence, Berlekamp–Massey maintains a shortest recurrence consistent with the prefix already read. Its discrepancy is the observed next term minus the term predicted by the current recurrence. Zero discrepancy extends the verified prefix. A nonzero discrepancy supplies a new independent constraint; subtract a suitably shifted saved recurrence whose discrepancy is nonzero, scaled by the ratio of discrepancies, to cancel it. The shift ensures earlier constraints remain satisfied. The saved state comes from the last increase of the necessary order. This explains both the field-division requirement and why the algorithm is more than guessing a recurrence by fitting a few coefficients.
Its library contract is \(O(T^2)\) field operations and \(O(T)\) space for a prefix of \(T\) terms (often bounded as \(O(TL)\) for linear complexity \(L\)). If an infinite sequence is known to have shortest recurrence order \(L\), valid from index \(L\), then \(2L\) initial terms suffice to identify it. One justification for uniqueness is that a sequence generated by an order-at-most-\(L\) recurrence has a rational generating function with denominator degree at most \(L\) and numerator degree below \(L\). Two such functions agreeing through degree \(2L-1\) have a cross-multiplied numerator of degree below \(2L\) with \(2L\) initial zero coefficients, hence are equal. The all-zero sequence has order zero. No finite prefix proves an arbitrary unknown future obeys the inferred rule: \(0,0,0,0,1,\ldots\) defeats an inference from the first four terms.


Matrices and Cayley–Hamilton
The characteristic polynomial is \(\chi_A(x)=\det(xI-A)\); the minimal polynomial is the monic polynomial of least degree with \(m_A(A)=0\). Cayley–Hamilton states \(\chi_A(A)=0\). To see the mechanism, use the cofactor identity \((xI-A)\operatorname{adj}(xI-A)=\chi_A(x)I\) and compare powers of \(x\). The coefficient equations telescope after multiplying by successive powers of \(A\), leaving \(\chi_A(A)=0\); this avoids an unjustified substitution into matrices whose coefficients might not commute.
Consequently, multiplying by \(u^TA^j\) and \(v\) shows \(u^TA^nv\) obeys a recurrence of order at most the matrix dimension. Some observations see fewer directions: for \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,3)\) and \(u=v=(1,0)^T\), the observed sequence is \(2^n\), of order one although \(\chi_A=(x-2)(x-3)\).

title: 10 — Linear Algebra over Finite Fields
text:
5. Characteristic polynomial and black-box methods
For dense matrices over a field, a similarity transformation \(A\mapsto S^{-1}AS\) preserves \(\det(xI-A)\). Hessenberg reduction uses paired row/column operations to zero entries below the first subdiagonal in \(O(n^3)\) operations. Unlike ordinary row elimination, the inverse column operation is necessary to preserve the characteristic polynomial. For an upper Hessenberg matrix \(H\), let \(D_i=\det(xI_i-H_{1:i,1:i})\), with \(D_0=1\). Expanding its final column gives
\[D_i=(x-h_{ii})D_{i-1}
-\sum_{k=1}^{i-1}h_{ki}
\left(\prod_{j=k}^{i-1}h_{j+1,j}\right)D_{k-1}.\]
Each non-diagonal choice forces the intervening subdiagonal chain, leaving the leading minor of size \(k-1\); this is why there are no missing minors. Naive polynomial accumulation costs \(O(n^3)\) altogether. Determinant interpolation at \(n+1\) distinct field points instead costs \(O(n^4)\) with naive determinants and needs a field large enough to supply those points.
For a huge sparse matrix, dense elimination wastes work on zeroes. Wiedemann chooses random vectors \(u,v\), generates \(a_i=u^T A^i v\), and applies Berlekamp–Massey. With enough terms, this recovers the scalar sequence’s minimal polynomial exactly; random projection makes it equal to the matrix’s minimal polynomial with high probability, with a bound that depends on the field and invariant factors. Applications include sparse linear systems and determinants after random diagonal preconditioning.
Assumptions and failure modes:

It is randomized; a projection can miss invariant factors. Repeat independently.
A small fixed field may need an extension field and a proved projection strategy. Changing the prime changes the input problem; several primes help integer reconstruction only when that is the actual goal.
One sparse matrix-vector multiply must be fast; otherwise dense elimination is safer.
Recovering a determinant requires more than the scalar recurrence: use a proven preconditioning recipe and account for the preconditioner’s determinant.

Generating \(2n\) terms costs \(O(n\,\mathcal V+n^2)\) field operations, where \(\mathcal V\) is one matrix-vector multiplication cost and the \(n^2\) term allows naive BM. A returned annihilator can be tested on additional vectors, but such random checks have an error probability; a deterministic certificate requires checking its action on a spanning set. This optional section is a decision guide for black-box methods, not a replacement for a specified preconditioned solver.

title: 10 — Linear Algebra over Finite Fields
text:
6. Common pitfalls

Division modulo a composite number silently invalidates Gaussian elimination.
Floating-point partial pivoting helps numerical stability but does not repair an ill-conditioned model; “largest pivot” has no algebraic meaning in a finite field.
A determinant changes sign on every row swap.
A graph XOR basis uses cycle values, not raw edge weights.
Kirchhoff counts multigraph edges separately; collapsing them without adding weights changes the answer.
Berlekamp–Massey coefficient sign conventions differ among templates. Verify on Fibonacci before a contest.

title: 10 — Linear Algebra over Finite Fields
text:
7. Practice, in order

Application — Xor Sum 3, AtCoder ABC141 F. XOR basis with an objective transformation.


Hints


Bits set in the XOR of all numbers contribute a fixed amount.
Mask those bits away from every vector.
Maximize a subset XOR on the remaining bits and relate the two colors.


Synthesis — Spices, AtCoder ABC236 F. Minimum-weight basis and an exchange argument.


Hints


Being able to create every mask means selecting a full-rank basis.
Sort candidates by cost.
Insert a vector exactly when it raises the XOR-basis rank (matroid greedy).


Synthesis — Xor-matic Number of the Graph, CF 724G. Cycle space and aggregate counting.


Hints


DFS XOR distances make each non-tree edge a cycle vector.
For a bit represented in the cycle basis, exactly half of span values contain it.
Otherwise its contribution depends only on endpoint distance bits; sum per component.

title: 10 — Linear Algebra over Finite Fields
text:
Exercises and solution workshop

1. Concept check: a fiber count
Over \(\mathbb F_3\), how many triples satisfy \(x+y+z=1\) and \(x+2y=0\)? Hint: choose one coordinate freely.






NoteSolution





The second equation gives \(x=y\), and the first gives \(z=1+y\) modulo \(3\). There are three solutions, corresponding to \(y=0,1,2\). The two rows are independent, so this also checks \(3^{3-2}=3\). The solutions form a translate of the kernel, not a subspace: the zero vector is not among them.





2. Application: a partition objective
Given nonnegative \(B\)-bit words, divide them into two groups and maximize the sum of the two group XORs. Derive the reduction used in ABC141 F. Hint: let \(T\) be the XOR of all inputs and inspect one bit of \(X+(T\mathbin{\oplus}X)\).






NoteSolution





At a set bit of \(T\), exactly one group has the bit, giving a fixed contribution. At an unset bit, both groups agree and contribute twice that bit of \(X\). Hence the objective is \(T+2(X\mathbin{\&}\neg T)\), with the complement restricted to the \(B\) input bits. Mask every input by \(\neg T\) and maximize subset XOR by a basis, greedily improving the answer from high pivot to low. This costs \(O(nB)\) time and \(O(B)\) space. For \(3,6,5\), \(T=0\) and maximum subset XOR is \(6\), giving \(12\). Maximizing the unmasked \(X\) would optimize irrelevant fixed bits. If both groups must be nonempty and \(n\ge2\), an optimum with positive masked XOR is already proper; if the maximum is zero, all partitions attain \(T\) and any proper one suffices.





3. Synthesis: minimum-price spanning choices
Prove that sorting vectors by nonnegative cost and accepting a vector exactly when it raises rank produces a cheapest basis of their span. Hint: exchange one vector of an optimal basis when greedy accepts its next vector.






NoteSolution





Maintain an optimal basis containing the accepted greedy prefix. Express the next accepted vector \(v\) in that basis. At least one vector \(w\) with nonzero coefficient lies outside the prefix, since \(v\) is independent of the prefix. Replacing \(w\) by \(v\) preserves a basis: the expression solves for \(w\) in the new basis. Every vector processed before \(v\) already lies in the prefix span, so such a \(w\) cannot have been an earlier rejected vector. Its cost is at least the cost of \(v\). The exchange preserves optimality and extends the invariant. Sorting plus insertion costs \(O(n\log n+nB)\) for XOR vectors. For costs \(c_1=4,c_2=5,c_3=3\), accept \(3\) then \(1\), costing \(7\); raw numeric order would instead choose the more expensive pair \(1,2\).





4. Advanced: weighted graph versus modular certificate
A triangle has edge weights \(2,3,5\). Count its weighted trees modulo \(31\). Does the answer certify disconnection? Hint: enumerate the deleted edge.






NoteSolution





The three weights are \(2\cdot3\), \(2\cdot5\), and \(3\cdot5\), totaling \(31\), so the modular determinant is zero although the graph is connected. Exact nonnegative weights and residue-field computations answer different questions. This is why a determinant used as a randomized existence certificate needs its own error analysis; see algebraic graph methods.

title: 12 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text: This chapter collects methods that turn an apparently huge integer range into a small algebraic object: a polynomial, a Euclidean recursion, or a continued fraction. They are especially valuable in ICPC because the statement rarely names the method. The recurring question is: what structure stays small even though the input range is huge?

title: 12 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
Prerequisites and learning objectives
Read Bézout and units and polynomials. Bernoulli preprocessing also uses formal power series; interpolation does not. Learn to prove degree bounds, evaluate huge polynomial sums, count lattice points without enumeration, and convert rational and quadratic constraints into integer recurrences. Symbols \(n,d\) are nonnegative integers unless stated otherwise; inequalities concern ordered integers, not residues.

title: 12 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
1. Polynomial interpolation
Over a field \(K\), a polynomial of degree at most \(d\) is determined by its values at \(d+1\) distinct sample points: if two such polynomials agree there, their difference has more roots than its degree and must be zero. Lagrange interpolation constructs the unique polynomial explicitly:
\[P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{d} y_i\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{x-x_j}{x_i-x_j}.\]
The factor for index \(i\) is \(1\) at \(x_i\) and \(0\) at all other samples, so the sum assigns the requested value at each point. At arbitrary points this costs \(O(d^2)\) for one query. When \(x_i=i\), prefix/suffix products and factorials reduce one query to \(O(d)\) after \(O(d)\) preprocessing:
\[\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{x-j}{i-j}
=\frac{\prod_{j<i}(x-j)\prod_{j>i}(x-j)}{i!(-1)^{d-i}(d-i)!}.\]
Preconditions are not cosmetic: sample points must be distinct and their differences invertible. In \(\mathbb F_p\), the points \(0,\ldots,d\) therefore require \(d<p\). For many arbitrary queries use a product tree and multipoint evaluation.
The unit-difference condition also licenses interpolation over a commutative ring, but the field root-bound proof does not: \(x^2-1\) has four roots \(1,3,5,7\) modulo 8. Over a field, the root bound follows by dividing out one factor \((x-a)\) for each distinct root.






NoteExample: reconstructing a quadratic



Suppose \(P(0)=1,P(1)=2,P(2)=5\) and \(\deg P\le2\) over \(\mathbb Q\). At \(x=4\), the Lagrange basis values are \(3,-8,6\), so \(P(4)=3-16+30=17\). The polynomial is \(x^2+1\). Without the degree bound, adding \(x(x-1)(x-2)\) preserves all three samples but changes the answer.


For consecutive evaluation, prefix product \(L_i=\prod_{0\le j<i}(x-j)\) and suffix product \(R_i=\prod_{i<j\le d}(x-j)\) omit exactly the forbidden factor. Multiply \(y_iL_iR_i\) by inverse factorials and \((-1)^{d-i}\). If \(x\) equals a sample point, return that sample directly. For \(d<p\), reduce a huge integer query modulo \(p\) only after proving the desired function is represented by this polynomial.

title: 12 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
2. Finite differences and polynomial sums
Define \(\Delta P(x)=P(x+1)-P(x)\) over any coefficient ring. It is the discrete analogue of a derivative: the leading \(x^d\) terms cancel, so the degree drops by at least one. It drops by exactly one when the leading coefficient times \(d\) is nonzero; this can fail in small characteristic, as \(\Delta(x^p)=1\) over \(\mathbb F_p\). When \(1,\ldots,d\) are units, repeated differences give the Newton expansion
\[P(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{d} \Delta^k P(0){x\choose k}.\]
For example, \(\Delta(x^2)=2x+1\) and \(\Delta^2(x^2)=2\). This Newton basis is ideal when values are consecutive or arguments shift repeatedly. Over a characteristic-zero field (more generally a \(\mathbb Q\)-algebra), or when \(1,\ldots,d+1\) are units in the coefficient ring, it also proves that if \(P\) has degree \(d\), then
\[S(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}P(i)\]
has degree \(d+1\), because \(\Delta S=P\) and its leading coefficient is the leading coefficient of \(P\) divided by \(d+1\). Therefore evaluate \(S(0),\ldots,S(d+1)\) directly and interpolate at huge \(n\). More generally, the needed condition is that all denominators in this Newton/interpolation basis are units. In small characteristic, \(S\) may not be representable by a polynomial of the expected degree, so the ordinary consecutive-point method is not licensed.
Here is the basis derivation. When \(1,\ldots,d\) are units, define \(\binom{x}{k}=x(x-1)\cdots(x-k+1)/k!\). Pascal’s identity gives \(\Delta\binom{x}{k}=\binom{x}{k-1}\) for \(k\ge1\). These polynomials have distinct degrees and unit leading coefficients and therefore form a basis through degree \(d\). In \(P=\sum_k a_k\binom{x}{k}\), apply \(\Delta^j\) and set \(x=0\): only \(a_j\) survives. Thus \(a_j=\Delta^jP(0)\). Summation is then telescoping:
\[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\binom{i}{k}
=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\left(\binom{i+1}{k+1}-\binom{i}{k+1}\right)
=\binom{n}{k+1}.\]
For \(P(x)=x^2\), the difference coefficients are \(0,1,2\); hence \(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}i^2=\binom n2+2\binom n3=n(n-1)(2n-1)/6\). At \(n=4\), this is \(1+4+9=14\). The identity is exact over integers, but evaluating it modulo 2 or 3 needs integer cancellation, not division by 6.
Recognition signal: fixed exponent/degree, enormous upper bound, modular answer. Do not interpolate if the degree depends on \(n\) or if sample denominators vanish modulo the chosen prime.

title: 12 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
3. Floor sum via Euclidean descent
Define
\[F(n,m,a,b)=\sum_{0\le i<n}\left\lfloor\frac{ai+b}{m}\right\rfloor,\]
with nonnegative inputs and \(m>0\). First strip quotient parts. Writing \(a=q_am+a'\) and \(b=q_bm+b'\) separates full multiples of \(m\), whose floors are ordinary arithmetic progressions:
\[a=q_am+a',\quad b=q_bm+b'.\]
Exactly,
\[
F(n,m,a,b)=q_a\frac{n(n-1)}2+q_bn+F(n,m,a',b').
\]
Now consider the normalized remainder with \(0\le a,b<m\). The sum counts lattice points \((i,j)\) with \(0\le i<n\) and \(1\le j\le(ai+b)/m\). Let \(y=an+b\), the numerator one step beyond the final \(i\); this is the boundary used by the half-open rectangle. If \(y<m\), no point reaches the first horizontal level and the remainder is zero. Otherwise \(a>0\); put \(q=\lfloor y/m\rfloor\) and \(r=y\bmod m\). On horizontal row \(1\le j\le q\), substitute \(t=n-i\) in \(jm\le ai+b=y-at\); the number of points on that row is \(\lfloor((q-j)m+r)/a\rfloor\). Summing and reindexing \(q-j=0,\ldots,q-1\) swaps the axes and yields
\[F(n,m,a,b)=F(\lfloor y/m\rfloor,a,m,y\bmod m)\]
after the parameter update \((n,m,a,b)\leftarrow(\lfloor y/m\rfloor,a,m,y\bmod m)\). Normalize again at the start of the next iteration: the new numerator coefficient is the old modulus and may be at least the new denominator. For example, \(F(4,7,3,2)=0+0+1+1=2\), and the update gives \(F(2,3,7,0)\); stripping \(7=2\cdot3+1\) gives \(2+F(2,3,1,0)=2\). This is the Euclidean algorithm geometrically, so there are \(O(\log m)\) iterations.
The horizontal count is between zero and \(n\): for \(j\ge1\), \(y-jm<an\) because \(b<m\). A top row may be empty; for \(F(1,2,1,1)\), \(y=2\) but the only actual floor is zero. The empty row makes the half-open update uniform. Maintain original answer = accumulated stripped terms + current F. Both normalization and axis swap preserve this invariant. Stop on \(n=0\), or after normalization when \(an+b<m\); if \(a=0\), the latter holds automatically. The logarithmic bound counts arithmetic operations.
Use __int128 when its range covers the proven product bounds. For negative \(a\) or \(b\), use mathematical floor division to normalize them; C++ truncation is not floor division. A library routine can have overflow semantics different from exact mathematics; the AtCoder contract returns modulo \(2^{64}\) on overflow.
Applications include counting lattice points, sums of residues, Beatty sequences, and recursively counting points constrained by rational lines.
The residue sum follows from \(u=m\lfloor u/m\rfloor+(u\bmod m)\):
\[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(ai+b)\bmod m
=a\frac{n(n-1)}2+bn-mF(n,m,a,b).\]
For \((4,7,3,2)\) the residues \(2,5,1,4\) sum to \(12=18+8-14\). For \((n,m,a,b)=(3,5,-1,0)\) the floors are \(0,-1,-1\) and residues \(0,4,3\). Truncating division toward zero breaks this normalization.

title: 12 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
4. Continued fractions
Euclid’s quotients form the finite simple continued fraction of a positive rational number, and the same process gives an infinite expansion for an irrational number \(\alpha\):
\[\alpha=[a_0;a_1,\ldots].\]
This means \(a_0+1/(a_1+1/(a_2+\cdots))\), with \(a_0=\lfloor\alpha\rfloor\) and subsequent \(a_i\) positive integers. Invert the fractional part repeatedly to find the quotients. For rationals, stop at an integer; choose the final coefficient greater than one unless there is only one coefficient. A finite truncation is a convergent. For example, \(13/5=[2;1,1,2]\).
Convergents satisfy
\[P_i=a_iP_{i-1}+P_{i-2},\qquad Q_i=a_iQ_{i-1}+Q_{i-2},\]
starting with \((P[-2],P[-1])=(0,1)\) and \((Q[-2],Q[-1])=(1,0)\). Substitution in the nested fractions proves these recurrences. They give \(2/1,3/1,5/2,13/5\) for the example. The determinant \(D_i=P_iQ_{i-1}-P_{i-1}Q_i\) obeys \(D_i=-D_{i-1}\), so \(D_i=\pm1\); in particular every convergent is reduced. For the tail \(t=[a_{i+1};a_{i+2},\ldots]>1\),
\[\alpha=\frac{tP_i+P_{i-1}}{tQ_i+Q_{i-1}},\qquad
\left|\alpha-\frac{P_i}{Q_i}\right|
=\frac1{Q_i(tQ_i+Q_{i-1})}.\]
This explains alternating sides and rapidly decreasing errors. The adjacent determinant also makes these integer vectors a basis of \(\mathbb Z^2\); expressing a competing \((p,q)\) in this basis is the mechanism behind the best-approximation theorem below. Its specified error measure is essential. For an irrational \(\alpha\), its convergents are best approximations of the second kind: no fraction \(p/q\) with \(0<q<Q_i\) has a smaller value of \(|q\alpha-p|\) than \(|Q_i\alpha-P_i|\). (For a rational input, the final convergent is the number itself.) The recurrence is just the record of successive Euclidean quotients, so it also supplies the Bezout-like identity below. For other bounded-denominator objectives, the optimum may be a convergent or an intermediate (semiconvergent), so derive the relevant comparison rather than citing “best approximation” without a definition. Adjacent convergents obey \(P_iQ_{i-1}-P_{i-1}Q_i=\pm1\), a built-in error check.
Use continued fractions for rational approximation, modular inequalities, and Pell equations. Intermediate fractions replace the next quotient by \(1\le t\le a_i\): \((tP_{i-1}+P_{i-2})/(tQ_{i-1}+Q_{i-2})\). For approximating \(13/5\) with denominator at most 3 in absolute error, \(8/3\) beats the convergent \(5/2\), since \(1/15<1/10\). An optimum need not be a convergent. Rational Euclid takes logarithmically many arithmetic steps. Compare by exact cross products with a proved width bound or big integers; 128 bits do not cover arbitrary input lengths.

title: 12 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
5. Pell equations
For nonsquare \(D>0\), Pell’s equation is
\[x^{2}-Dy^{2}=1.\]
The continued fraction of \(\sqrt D\) is periodic. The first convergent satisfying the equation gives the fundamental solution \((x_1,y_1)\) with \(x_1,y_1>0\). Multiplication of numbers \(x+y\sqrt D\) preserves \(x^2-Dy^2\), proving powers remain solutions. The stronger theorem is that every solution with \(x>0,y>0\) follows from
\[(x_k+y_k\sqrt D)=(x_1+y_1\sqrt D)^{k},\]
or the recurrence
\[x'=x_1x+Dy_1y,\qquad y'=x_1y+y_1x.\]
The converse needs descent. Write \(\varepsilon=x_1+y_1\sqrt D>1\) for the least positive norm-one unit. Given another \(u=x+y\sqrt D>1\), choose \(k\) with \(1\le v=u\varepsilon^{-k}<\varepsilon\). Since \(\varepsilon^{-1}=x_1-y_1\sqrt D\), \(v\) still has integer coefficients and norm one. They are \((v+v^{-1})/2>0\) and \((v-v^{-1})/(2\sqrt D)\ge0\). Unless \(v=1\), this contradicts minimality of \(\varepsilon\). Thus \(u=\varepsilon^k\); norm preservation alone would not establish completeness.
For \(D=2\), \([1;2,2,\ldots]\) gives fundamental pair \((3,2)\), then \((17,12)\) and \((99,70)\). Searching convergents suffices because a Pell solution satisfies \(|x/y-\sqrt D|=1/(y^2(x/y+\sqrt D))<1/(2y^2)\), and the continued-fraction approximation criterion says a reduced fraction this close must be a convergent. Periodicity and existence of a solution are classical quadratic-surd theorems, separate from the power-generation argument. The integer expansion maintains \((\sqrt D+m)/d\) with \(d\mid D-m^2\):
\[m'=da-m,\quad d'=(D-m'^2)/d,\quad
a'=\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor\sqrt D\rfloor+m'}{d'}\right\rfloor.\]
Start with \(m=0,d=1,a=\lfloor\sqrt D\rfloor\). Bounded reduced surd states yield periodicity. This avoids cumulative floating-point error; the number of convergents is not uniformly \(O(\log D)\), and the fundamental solution may have many more bits than \(D\).
For \(x^{2}-Dy^{2}=N\), existence and seed generation are subtler; do not assume the \(N=1\) theorem transfers unchanged. Contest tasks often bound the search enough to find seeds and then advance each orbit by the fundamental unit.
Values grow exponentially. Use big integers or stop with division-based overflow checks before multiplication.

title: 12 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
section: 6. Linear Diophantine equations and CRT viewpoint
text:
6. Linear Diophantine equations and CRT viewpoint
For \((a,b)\ne(0,0)\), the equation \(ax+by=c\) has an integer solution iff \(g=\gcd(a,b)\) divides \(c\): the left side is always a multiple of \(g\), and Bézout constructs one whenever that necessary condition holds. Extended Euclid finds \(u,v\) with \(au+bv=g\); scale by \(c/g\). All solutions are
\[x=x_0+k\frac bg,\qquad y=y_0-k\frac ag.\]
To prove completeness, subtract solutions: \(a\Delta x=-b\Delta y\). For nonzero coefficients, coprimality of \(a/g,b/g\) implies \(b/g\) divides \(\Delta x\), and substitution determines \(\Delta y\). If one coefficient is zero, its nonzero partner fixes one variable and the other is free, consistently with the formula. Here \(g>0\) and \(k\) ranges over all integers.
If \(a=b=0\), all integer pairs solve the equation when \(c=0\), and none solve when \(c\ne0\); keep that degenerate case outside an extended-gcd routine.
Intersect this parameterization with sign or interval constraints using correct floor/ceiling division. A congruence \(ax\equiv c\pmod m\) is the same equation \(ax+my=c\); after dividing by \(\gcd(a,m)\), invert in the reduced modulus.
For \(6x+9y=30\), take \((x_0,y_0)=(2,2)\) to obtain \(x=2+3k,y=2-2k\). Nonnegativity requires \(\lceil-2/3\rceil\le k\le1\), yielding \((2,2),(5,0)\). A linear objective becomes linear in \(k\), so its minimum on a bounded feasible interval is at an endpoint; zero slope makes all points tie. Check separately whether the feasible interval is empty or unbounded.
For nonlinear-looking determinant constraints such as \(ad-bc=k\), fixing two variables often reduces the rest to Bézout. For quadratic forms, factorization, modular obstructions, descent, or Pell reduction may apply.

title: 12 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
7. Stern–Brocot and modular extrema
Start with boundaries \(a/b=0/1\) and \(c/d=1/0\), the latter denoting infinity. Their mediant is \((a+c)/(b+d)\). Boundaries maintain \(bc-ad=1\), so the mediant is reduced and lies strictly between them. For a target in this interval, replace the lower or upper boundary by the mediant according to its side. The determinant invariant is preserved. To see that every positive reduced \(p/q\) is reached, write it uniquely as \((ua+vc)/(ub+vd)\) with positive integers \(u,v\) while it is strictly between the boundaries. Comparing with the mediant subtracts the smaller of \(u,v\) from the larger. Euclid eventually gives \(u=v=1\). The strict interval choices also prove uniqueness: this is the Stern–Brocot tree.
Repeated same-side updates can be batched: replacing the lower bound \(t\) times gives \((a+tc)/(b+td)\). Solve the exact denominator and target inequalities for the largest legal integer \(t\), observing whether the target bound is strict. The run lengths relate to continued-fraction quotients, with initial/final adjustments depending on the sentinel and endpoint conventions. Use the inequalities as the contract, not a memorized unqualified run sequence.
Functions such as \(\min_{0\le i<n} (ai+b) \bmod m\) use the same Euclidean geometry as floor_sum: quotient away full multiples, then swap axes after the first wrap. Keep half-open interval conventions consistent.
An alternative derived contract avoids a new recursive template. For a proposed threshold \(0\le t<m\), write \(ai+b=qm+r\) with \(0\le r<m\). Then
\[[r<t]=1+\left\lfloor\frac{ai+b}{m}\right\rfloor
-\left\lfloor\frac{ai+b+m-t}{m}\right\rfloor.\]
Thus the count below \(t\) is \(n+F(n,m,a,b)-F(n,m,a,b+m-t)\). For \(n>0\), binary-search the first \(t\in[1,m]\) whose count is positive and return \(t-1\). This costs \(O(\log^2m)\) arithmetic operations. Direct Euclidean minimum algorithms can remove a logarithm, but need their own interval invariant. For \(n=0\) there is no minimum.

title: 12 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
8. Bernoulli numbers and Faulhaber sums
Bernoulli numbers are defined by
\[\frac{x}{e^{x}-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}B_k\frac{x^{k}}{k!}.\]
With the convention \(i^0=1\) even at \(i=0\), they give for \(d\ge0\)
\[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}i^{d}=\frac1{d+1}\sum_{j=0}^{d}{d+1\choose j}B_j n^{d+1-j}.\]
To derive the formula, count the exponential weight of each summand:
\[\sum_{d\ge0}\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}i^d\right)\frac{x^d}{d!}
=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}e^{ix}
=\frac{e^{nx}-1}{e^x-1}
=\frac{e^{nx}-1}{x}\frac{x}{e^x-1}.\]
The coefficient of \(x^d\), multiplied by \(d!\), chooses degree \(j\) from the Bernoulli factor and degree \(d-j\) from the other factor; this yields the displayed binomial coefficient. The proof is over \(\mathbb Q[[x]]\), or truncated over a ring where the denominators through \(d+1\) are units. The first terms are \(B_0=1,B_1=-1/2,B_2=1/6\), giving sums \(n\), \(n(n-1)/2\), and \(n(n-1)(2n-1)/6\). The formal quotient \(x/(e^x-1)\) means the inverse of \((e^x-1)/x\), whose constant term is 1; it is not inversion of a zero-constant series. To obtain degree \(d\), form the exponential through degree \(d+1\).
This computes all power-sum formulas through one FPS inversion and factorial scaling. Check the \(B_1\) sign convention and require all denominators through \(d+1\) to be invertible. For one degree and one query, consecutive-point interpolation is often simpler; Bernoulli preprocessing wins for many degrees.

title: 12 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
9. Pitfalls

C++ % and / on negatives do not implement Euclidean remainder/floor division.
Lagrange denominators vanish if the interpolation degree reaches the modulus.
Inferring “it is polynomial” from samples is not a proof; establish a degree bound.
\(a*n+b\) can overflow before the floor sum shrinks it.
Pell recurrences need all seed orbits for generalized equations.
Extended-GCD coefficients may overflow even if the final normalized answer fits.

title: 12 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
10. Practice, in order

Advanced — The Sum of the k-th Powers, CF 622F. Consecutive-point interpolation.


Hints


The prefix sum is a polynomial in \(n\) of degree \(k+1\).
Evaluate it at \(0,\ldots,k+1\) directly.
Use prefix/suffix Lagrange products for one huge query.


Advanced — S = 1, AtCoder ABC340 F. Bézout and determinant construction.


Hints


Rewrite the required area as an equation of the form \(Xb-Ya=±2\).
Check the gcd divisibility condition.
Scale extended-Euclid coefficients and map signs carefully.


Mastery — Cowmpany Cowmpensation, CF 995F. Tree DP whose answer is polynomial.


Hints


First solve for small color bounds with a tree DP.
Prove each subtree’s count is a polynomial and bound its degree by subtree size.
Evaluate enough consecutive points, then interpolate at \(D\).


Mastery — Sum of Min of Mod of Linear, AtCoder ARC182 E. Floor sums inside a modular-minimum decomposition. Official English editorial.

title: 12 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
Exercises with solutions

1. Concept check: polynomiality before interpolation
Compute \(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(i^2+1)\) as a polynomial and evaluate at \(n=4\). Why do four sampled values suffice? Hint: summation raises the degree by one over \(\mathbb Q\).






NoteSolution





The answer is \(n+n(n-1)(2n-1)/6\), degree three, and its value at 4 is 18. The degree proof licenses four samples; four samples alone do not prove the function is cubic. Modulo a prime \(p>3\), these rational coefficients and the four consecutive sample differences are valid units. For smaller moduli, evaluate the integer formula by exact cancellation or use a different basis.





2. Application: a residue threshold
Among \(i=0,1,2,3\), how many residues \((3i+2)\bmod7\) are below 3? Derive the general threshold count rather than enumerate a large \(n\). Hint: compare floors before and after adding \(m-t\).






NoteSolution





The residues \(2,5,1,4\) give two. The general formula is \(n+F(n,m,a,b)-F(n,m,a,b+m-t)\); here it is \(4+2-4=2\). For \(t=0\) it gives zero, and for \(t=m\) it gives \(n\), checking both boundaries. Two floor sums cost \(O(\log m)\) arithmetic operations, even for negative \(a,b\) after mathematical floor normalization.





3. Advanced: an interval Diophantine optimum
Find nonnegative integers satisfying \(6x+9y=30\) that minimize \(2x+5y\). Hint: optimize the single integer parameter, not both original variables.






NoteSolution





\(x=2+3k,y=2-2k\), with \(k=0,1\). The objective is \(14-4k\), so choose \(k=1\) and obtain \((5,0)\) with cost 10. Extended Euclid and interval intersection cost \(O(\log\max(|a|,|b|))\) arithmetic steps in the general case. Verify the original equation and bounds after mapping coordinates.





4. Synthesis: square triangular numbers
Find the first three positive integers that are both a square and a triangular number, where the \(n\)th triangular number is \(n(n+1)/2\). Hint: complete the square in \(n(n+1)=2m^2\).






NoteSolution





Multiply by 4 and add 1: \((2n+1)^2-8m^2=1\). The fundamental solution for \(D=8\) is \((x,m)=(3,1)\), and multiplying by \(3+\sqrt8\) produces \((17,6),(99,35)\). Thus \(n=(x-1)/2\) is \(1,8,49\), and the numbers are \(1,36,1225\). All generated \(x\) stay odd. Conversely every positive solution of the original problem gives a positive Pell solution, so the fundamental-unit descent proves completeness. Enumerating \(n\) up to the largest answer ignores the exponentially spaced structure; generate units with big integers instead.

title: 14 — Modular Combinatorics and q-Analogues
text:
This chapter begins where the familiar formula
\[\binom nk=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}\]
stops being a legal modular computation. A factorial table modulo a prime \(p\) only supports division while every denominator is nonzero, hence while the relevant factorial arguments are below \(p\). The two warning signs are \(n\ge p\) and a composite modulus. The cure is to separate the powers of each prime (which are not invertible) from the remaining unit part (which is).
The notation \(v_p(x)\) means “the exponent of \(p\) in \(x\)”; for example, \(v_2(40)=3\). It is the bookkeeper that tells us exactly when a binomial coefficient becomes zero modulo a prime power.

title: 14 — Modular Combinatorics and q-Analogues
text:
Prerequisites and learning objectives
Read units, valuations, and CRT, binomial counting, and, for subspaces, linear algebra. The advanced practice also uses convolution and Stirling transforms. Learn to compute binomials when factorials vanish, distinguish divisibility from residue value, derive a subspace count by counting bases, and recognize when a q-product is a polynomial whose displayed divisions are illegal.
Throughout, \(n\ge0\) and \(0\le k\le n\) are integers; set \(\binom nk=0\) outside that range. A prime is denoted \(p\), its power modulus \(Q=p^e\) with \(e\ge1\), and a vector-space field size \(q\). For a nonzero integer \(a\), \(v_p(a)\) counts its factors of \(p\); \(v_p(0)=+\infty\) if needed, but the factorial arguments below are always nonnegative and their factorials nonzero. All divisions by factorials in exact counting occur over integers or rationals first; modular inverses are a separate computational step.

title: 14 — Modular Combinatorics and q-Analogues
text:
1. Lucas and Kummer
For prime \(p\), write \(n=\sum n_i p^{i}\) and \(k=\sum k_i p^{i}\), where each digit is in \([0,p)\). Lucas gives
\[\binom nk\equiv\prod_i\binom{n_i}{k_i}\pmod p.\]
Here is the proof. In \(\mathbb F_p[x]\), the middle coefficients of \((1+x)^p\) are divisible by \(p\): for \(0<j<p\), the numerator of \(\binom pj\) has one factor \(p\) and its denominator has none. Thus \((1+x)^p=1+x^p\), and iterating gives
\[(1+x)^n=\prod_i((1+x)^{p^i})^{n_i}
=\prod_i(1+x^{p^i})^{n_i}.\]
To obtain \(x^k\), choose \(x^{k_i p^i}\) from factor \(i\). Each chosen digit is less than \(p\), so this representation is unique and carries never occur in this expansion. The coefficient is the product in Lucas’s formula. Thus one huge binomial coefficient becomes a product of tiny digit-level ones. For example, \(5=(101)_2\) and \(2=(010)_2\), so Lucas includes \(\binom 0 1=0\) and therefore \(\binom52\equiv0\pmod2\).
Kummer says \(v_p\binom nk\) is the number of carries in base \(p\) when adding \(k\) and \(n-k\). It supplies more information than the yes/no answer modulo \(p\): a carry count of \(c\) says the coefficient is divisible by \(p^c\). In the example above, \(2+(5-2)=(10)_2+(11)_2=(101)_2\) has one carry, agreeing with \(v_2\binom52=1\). A digit with \(k_i>n_i\) detects that some borrowing is necessary, but borrows can propagate through further positions. For example, \(8-1=(1000)_2-(0001)_2\) has three borrows, although only one original digit satisfies \(k_i>n_i\). Accordingly \(v_2\binom81=3\). Lucas is the value theorem; Kummer is the divisibility theorem.
For the derivation, let \(s_p(n)\) be the sum of base-\(p\) digits. Counting how many multiples of \(p,p^2,\ldots\) occur in \(n!\) gives
\[v_p(n!)=\sum_{j\ge1}\lfloor n/p^j\rfloor
=\sum_i n_i(1+p+\cdots+p^{i-1})
=\frac{n-s_p(n)}{p-1}.\]
Subtract the factorial valuations to obtain
\[v_p\binom nk=\frac{s_p(k)+s_p(n-k)-s_p(n)}{p-1}.\]
Each carry replaces \(p\) units in one digit by one in the next, decreasing the digit sum by \(p-1\); count every carry, including propagated ones. This proves Kummer. With a table through \(p-1\), Lucas queries cost \(O(\log_p(n+1))\) after \(O(p)\) preprocessing and memory. That table is impractical for a huge prime; computing small digit binomials by products instead costs the sum of the smaller digit arguments. Lucas changes the scale but does not guarantee a fast digit-binomial routine.

title: 14 — Modular Combinatorics and q-Analogues
text:
2. Prime powers and composite moduli
For \(Q=p^{e}\), first use Legendre’s formula
\[v_p(n!)=\sum_{j\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac n{p^j}\right\rfloor.\]
Then represent a factorial as \(n!=p^vU(n)\), where \(U(n)\) is not divisible by \(p\) and is therefore invertible modulo \(p^e\). Compute this p-free factorial by multiplying only terms not divisible by \(p\) in complete blocks, then recursing on \(\lfloor n/p\rfloor\): the recursive call accounts for the factors left after removing one \(p\) from every multiple of \(p\). This is the reason a prime-power factorial routine is more than a factorial table. Then
\[\binom nk=p^{v_p(n!)-v_p(k!)-v_p((n-k)!)}
U(n)U(k)^{-1}U(n-k)^{-1}\pmod {p^e}.\]
If the exponent is at least \(e\), the answer is zero modulo \(p^e\). Otherwise all inverted parts are units and the displayed expression is valid. For a composite modulus \(m\), factor \(m\) into coprime prime powers, solve one local problem per factor, and use CRT to select the unique residue modulo \(m\) with those local residues. Never cancel numerator and denominator directly in \(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\): a nonzero residue can still be a non-unit, such as \(2\) modulo \(6\).

The exact unit-factorial recurrence
Define \(U(n)=n!/p^{v_p(n!)}\) as an integer, then reduce it modulo \(Q\). Let \(A(t)=\prod_{1\le j\le t,\ p\nmid j}j\pmod Q\) for \(0\le t\le Q\). The factors in \(n!\) not divisible by \(p\) contribute a product \(V(n)\). Each multiple \(pj\) contributes the p-free part of \(j\), so
\[U(n)=V(n)U(\lfloor n/p\rfloor),\qquad
V(n)\equiv A(Q)^{\lfloor n/Q\rfloor}A(n\bmod Q)\pmod Q.\]
The second equality groups full periods of length \(Q\): corresponding factors are congruent, and divisibility by \(p\) repeats. Stop at \(U(0)=1\). The recursion invariant is that every factor has had its entire p-power removed, including factors recursively contributed by multiples of \(p\). A full table costs \(O(Q)\) time and memory. With modular binary exponentiation at each level, a query costs \(O(\log_p(n+1)\log(n+1))\) modular operations; special formulas for the period product improve this but are not required. For huge \(Q\) this preprocessing is unavailable: use a problem-specific bound, factorwise products for small \(k\), or an independently specified prime-power routine. Factoring a composite answer modulus has its own cost and contract.






NoteExample: a nonzero binomial despite zero factorials



Compute \(\binom62\) modulo 8. The factorial valuations are \(4,1,3\), so the net exponent is zero. The exact unit factorials are \(U(6)=45\), \(U(2)=1\), \(U(4)=3\). Hence the residue is \(5\cdot1^{-1}\cdot3^{-1}
\equiv5\cdot3=7\pmod8\), agreeing with 15. Ordinary factorial residues would contain zeros and nonunits and could not be divided. For \(\binom42=6\), the valuation is one and the remaining unit residue is 3, giving \(2\cdot3=6\) modulo 8. Valuation alone would not identify the unit.

title: 14 — Modular Combinatorics and q-Analogues
text:
3. Gaussian binomial coefficients
Here \(q\) is either a formal variable or the size of a finite field. When \(q\) is a prime power, the Gaussian (or q-) binomial coefficient counts \(r\)-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb F_q^{n}\):
\[\binom nr_q=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}\frac{q^{n-i}-1}{q^{r-i}-1}.\]
Assume \(0\le r\le n\), with value 1 for \(r=0\); set it to zero for out-of-range \(r\). Field size \(q\) is a positive prime power; the answer modulus, if any, is another number. The product first states an exact integer count, not a formula for arbitrary modular division.
To see the product, count ordered independent vectors in two ways. The first vector has \(q^n-1\) choices, the next has \(q^n-q\) choices, and so on; divide by the number \((q^r-1)(q^r-q)\cdots(q^r-q^{r-1})\) of ordered bases of one fixed \(r\)-subspace. The same polynomial is the inversion generating polynomial for binary strings with \(r\) ones, and the area generating polynomial for partitions inside an \(r\times(n-r)\) rectangle. Thus \(\binom42_q=
1+q+2q^2+q^3+q^4\) records how many such objects have each statistic value.
To connect binary strings, define an inversion as a pair of positions with a 1 before a 0. Splitting by the first bit: a leading 0 leaves a length-\(n-1\) string with \(r\) ones; a leading 1 leaves \(r-1\) ones and adds \(n-r\) inversions. This gives the same recurrence below and the same boundary values, proving the polynomial identity by induction. Record, for each successive 1, how many zeros follow it; these counts form a nonincreasing list bounded by \(n-r\). Its Ferrers rows form a partition inside an \(r\times(n-r)\) rectangle, and their sum is the inversion count. For \(n=4,r=2\), the strings \(0011,0101,0110,1001,1010,1100\) have respectively \(0,1,2,2,3,4\) inversions. At \(q=2\), their weighted total is 35, the number of 2-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb F_2^4\); the six strings themselves are not the 35 subspaces.
The recurrence
\[\binom nr_q=\binom{n-1}r_q+q^{n-r}\binom{n-1}{r-1}_q\]
remains valid even when the product formula appears to divide by zero. Fix a hyperplane \(H\cong\mathbb F_q^{n-1}\). An \(r\)-subspace is either contained in \(H\), giving the first term, or meets \(H\) in an \((r-1)\)-subspace; the latter case has \(q^{n-r}\) extensions, giving the second term. It is often the safest way to compute a whole table. To justify the extensions, fix \(W=U\cap H\) of dimension \(r-1\). In the quotient vector space \(V/W\), an extension \(U/W\) is a line outside the hyperplane \(H/W\). There are \(q^{n-r+1}-q^{n-r}\) vectors outside that hyperplane, and each line contains \(q-1\) such nonzero vectors. Division gives \(q^{n-r}\) lines. The recurrence with the boundary values computes a table through \(n,r\) in \(O(nr)\) ring operations with \(O(r)\) rolling memory, assuming powers of \(q\) are available; evaluate rows in an order preserving both prior-row entries. For a fixed numerical \(q\) modulo a prime \(P\), precompute q-integers and q-factorials only while their factors are invertible. If some \(q^i-1\) vanishes modulo \(P\), ordinary division is invalid even though the Gaussian binomial itself remains defined. Use the division-free recurrence, a proved q-Lucas theorem when its hypotheses match, or cancel cyclotomic-factor exponents before evaluation.
Define the q-integer \([i]_q=1+q+\cdots+q^{i-1}\) directly as a polynomial. At \(q=1\), it is \(i\), although the expression \((q^i-1)/(q-1)\) is \(0/0\). Thus at \(q=1\) the q-factorial method reduces to ordinary factorials when \(1,\ldots,n\) are units, and the Gaussian coefficient equals \(\binom nr\). When \(q\ne1\) and \(q-1\) is a unit, a q-integer vanishes exactly when \(q^i=1\). For example at \(q=2\) modulo 7, \([3]_q=7\) vanishes; the Gaussian polynomial \(\binom32_q=1+q+q^2\) is still defined and evaluates to zero. Do not “cancel zeros” after evaluation. The optional q-Lucas/cyclotomic methods require their own hypotheses; the division-free recurrence is the complete safe contract taught here.

title: 14 — Modular Combinatorics and q-Analogues
text:
4. Small characteristic
Factorial-scaled EGF formulas require \(1,\ldots,N\) to be invertible. When \(N\ge p\), use base-\(p\) digit structure, recurrences that avoid division, or algorithms specifically designed for small characteristic. This affects Stirling rows, Bell numbers, FPS integration, and q-factorials—not just \({n\choose k}\).
For example, over \(\mathbb F_2\), the derivative of every polynomial has zero coefficient at \(x\): differentiating \(a_2x^2\) gives \(2a_2x=0\). Thus there is no formal antiderivative of \(x\). A failed division by 2 can signify nonexistence, not merely a missing trick for computing an otherwise unique answer. Conversely a Gaussian binomial has an integer polynomial definition and survives a failed product denominator. Determine which situation you are in before choosing a fallback.

title: 14 — Modular Combinatorics and q-Analogues
section: 5. Rank distributions as a counting model
text:
5. Rank distributions as a counting model
How many \(a\times b\) matrices over \(\mathbb F_q\) have rank \(r\)? Their column space is an \(r\)-subspace of \(\mathbb F_q^a\), with \(\binom ar_q\) choices. For a fixed basis of that space, the \(b\) columns form an \(r\times b\) coordinate matrix of full row rank. Choose its \(r\) independent rows successively, giving
\[N_{a,b}(r)=\binom ar_q\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(q^b-q^i),
\qquad 0\le r\le\min(a,b).\]
Changing the chosen basis is not another matrix choice: coordinates transform with it, so fixing one basis for each subspace counts each matrix once. For binary \(2\times2\) matrices, ranks 0,1,2 occur \(1,9,6\) times, totaling \(16=2^4\). This is the bridge from subspaces to random linear maps and XOR sequence counting. A naive rank sum/table can still be too slow; the advanced problems require compressing the products or recognizing a convolution.

title: 14 — Modular Combinatorics and q-Analogues
text:
Decision checklist

Prime modulus and \(n<p\): factorial tables.
Small prime and huge \(n\): Lucas; use Kummer to reason about zeros.
Prime power: valuation plus unit factorial.
General composite modulus: prime powers plus generalized CRT.
q-analogue: identify whether it counts subspaces, inversions, or partitions.

Before coding, write down the modulus factorization, the largest factorial argument, and every quantity you intend to invert. Those three lines usually choose the method and expose an invalid factorial-table solution immediately.

title: 14 — Modular Combinatorics and q-Analogues
text:
Exercises with hints and solutions

1. Concept check: a Lucas value and a carry chain
Find \(\binom{10}{3}\bmod3\) and \(v_2\binom81\) without forming factorials. Hint: write base-3 digits for the first and count every carry in the second.






NoteSolution





\(10=(101)_3\) and \(3=(010)_3\), so the middle Lucas factor is \(\binom01=0\); the result is 0, agreeing with 120. In binary, \(1+7=(001)_2+(111)_2=(1000)_2\) carries at all three low positions, giving valuation 3. Counting only original-digit violations misses the propagation through the zero digits of 8.





2. Application: assemble a composite residue
Compute \(\binom62\) modulo 72 using prime powers. Hint: \(72=8\cdot9\).






NoteSolution





Modulo 8 the worked example gives 7. Modulo 9, valuations of \(6!,2!,4!\) are \(2,0,1\), so the binomial has one factor 3. Unit factorials are \(U(6)=80\equiv8\), \(U(2)=2\), \(U(4)=8\). Their unit ratio is \(8\cdot5\cdot8\equiv5\pmod9\), giving \(3\cdot5\equiv6\). Now write \(x=7+8t\). Modulo 9, \(7-t=6\) yields \(t=1\pmod9\), hence \(x=15\pmod{72}\). The CRT moduli are coprime even though 72 is composite.





3. Advanced: subspaces avoiding a vector
In \(\mathbb F_q^n\), fix a nonzero vector \(v\). How many \(r\)-subspaces do not contain \(v\)? Hint: first count those containing its one-dimensional span.






NoteSolution





Subspaces containing \(\langle v\rangle\) correspond bijectively to \((r-1)\)-subspaces of \(V/\langle v\rangle\), so the count avoiding \(v\) is \(\binom nr_q-\binom{n-1}{r-1}_q=q^r\binom{n-1}r_q\). For the latter identity, project an avoiding subspace to the quotient: its image is an \(r\)-subspace, and its lifts are graphs of the \(q^r\) linear maps from that subspace to \(\langle v\rangle\), after fixing a complementary hyperplane. For \(q=2,n=3,r=1\), there are \(7-1=6\) lines avoiding \(v\). For \(r=0\) the zero subspace always avoids a nonzero vector.





4. Synthesis: forbid an even zero-XOR subset
Among subsets of \(\mathbb F_2^N\), count those with no nonempty even-sized subset of XOR zero. Derive a count by cardinality. Hint: append one parity bit to every chosen vector.






NoteSolution





Map \(x\) to \((x,1)\in\mathbb F_2^{N+1}\). A dependence among these vectors is exactly an even zero-XOR subset. For \(r\) previously independent augmented vectors, their span has \(2^r\) elements. If \(r\ge1\), exactly half have last coordinate one: the last-coordinate map is a nonzero linear functional, so its two fibers both have size \(2^{r-1}\). The next allowed vector therefore has \(2^N-2^{r-1}\) choices. The first has \(2^N\) choices. For cardinality \(s\ge1\) the unordered count is
\[\frac{2^N\prod_{r=1}^{s-1}(2^N-2^{r-1})}{s!},
\qquad 1\le s\le N+1.\]
Add one for the empty set. Division by \(s!\) is exact over integers; the ARC146 C modulus and indexing bounds also make it a unit. Prefix products and inverse factorials evaluate all cardinalities in \(O(N)\) field operations. For \(N=2\), the counts are \(1,4,6,4\), totaling 15; the full four-element set is the only forbidden subset of the four-vector universe.





5. Synthesis: nonzero forbidden XOR versus zero
Count ordered length-\(m\) sequences in \(\mathbb F_2^k\) with no nonempty subsequence XOR equal to a specified \(x\). Derive a rank-sum expression for \(x\ne0\) and a separate formula for \(x=0\). Hint: use the preceding avoiding subspace count and full-row-rank coordinate matrices.






NoteSolution





For \(x\ne0\), the condition is \(x\) outside the span. The exact count is
\[\sum_{r=0}^{\min(m,k-1)}2^r\binom{k-1}r_2
\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(2^m-2^i).\]
Each term chooses an avoiding \(r\)-subspace and a sequence spanning it. For \(x=0\), the empty subsequence is excluded, so the vectors must be independent: the count is \(\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}(2^k-2^i)\) when \(m\le k\), otherwise zero. Treating zero as an ordinary forbidden span vector would wrongly return zero for every instance. For \(k=1,x=1\), only the all-zero sequence survives; for \(k=1,x=0\), only the length-one sequence (1) survives among positive lengths. These formulas are the mathematical reduction, not a complete multi-query algorithm for CF1603 F’s largest bounds: its product/rank-sum evaluations need batch preprocessing and further algebraic simplification. Use the official contest tutorial linked on its statement for that optimization.

title: 16 — Set Power Series
text:
A DP table indexed by subsets often describes objects whose labels must be used exactly once. Team partitions, graph components, and collections of disjoint structures all have this form. Ordinary polynomial multiplication remembers only a size; set power series remember precisely which labels were used. This extra information makes connected-component extraction possible even when different vertex subsets have different internal graphs.
Prerequisites: partitions and counting, subset transforms, and the exp/log analogy from formal series. You should know how subset zeta and Möbius transforms respectively sum over subsets and undo that sum.
The objectives are to derive fast subset convolution, prove the connected-component identities, identify exactly when factorial division is legal, and implement the mathematical contracts using your own transform library.

title: 16 — Set Power Series
section: Definitions: a polynomial whose labels cannot repeat
text:
Definitions: a polynomial whose labels cannot repeat
Let \(U=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and let \(R\) be a commutative ring with identity. A set series is a table \(f[S]\in R\) for every \(S\subseteq U\). For \(S\subseteq U\), write \(x^S=\prod_{i\in S}x_i\); this is a monomial, not an ordinary integer power. We impose \(x_i^2=0\) for each label. The resulting algebra is
\[R[x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}]/(x_0^2,\ldots,x_{n-1}^2).\]
Multiplying \(x^Ax^B\) returns \(x^{A\cup B}\) if \(A,B\) are disjoint, and zero otherwise. For example, \(x^{\{0,1\}}x^{\{1,2\}}=0\), but \(x^{\{0\}}x^{\{1,2\}}=x^{\{0,1,2\}}\). The empty-set coefficient is the constant term. The multiplicative identity has coefficient one at the empty set and zero elsewhere.
Suppose \(f[T]\) counts a first structure on labels \(T\), and \(g[S\setminus T]\) counts a second structure on the remaining labels. Summing over the choice of the first label set gives subset convolution:
\[ (f*g)[S]=\sum_{T\subseteq S}f[T]g[S\setminus T]. \]
Every label is assigned to exactly one of the two structures. Over all masks, the naive cost is \(\sum_S2^{|S|}=3^n\): each label is outside \(S\), in the first part, or in the second part.
Example. On \(\{0,1\}\), suppose \(f[\{0\}]=2\), \(f[\{1\}]=3\), \(g[\{0\}]=5\), \(g[\{1\}]=7\), with all other coefficients zero. Then \((f*g)[\{0,1\}]=2\cdot7+3\cdot5=29\). An ordinary size polynomial would also combine two structures using the same label, which is forbidden here.

title: 16 — Set Power Series
section: Ranked convolution and the overlap invariant
text:
Ranked convolution and the overlap invariant
Separate a series by cardinality before applying the subset zeta transform:
\[\widehat f_k[S]=\sum_{\substack{A\subseteq S\\|A|=k}}f[A],
\qquad 0\le k\le n.\]
For each \(S\), multiply the rank polynomials and retain ranks \(0\) through \(n\):
\[H_k[S]=\sum_{i=0}^k\widehat f_i[S]\widehat g_{k-i}[S]
=\sum_{\substack{A,B\subseteq S\\|A|+|B|=k}}f[A]g[B].\]
These pairs may overlap. Now Möbius-invert each rank layer. For a fixed pair \((A,B)\), its contribution to inverted entry \(S\) is multiplied by
\[\sum_{A\cup B\subseteq T\subseteq S}(-1)^{|S\setminus T|}
=\begin{cases}1,&A\cup B=S,\\0,&A\cup B\ne S.\end{cases}\]
Indeed, every element of \(S\setminus(A\cup B)\) can be included or excluded, producing \((1-1)^{|S\setminus(A\cup B)|}\). Thus the inverted layer is
\[h_k[S]=\sum_{\substack{A\cup B=S\\|A|+|B|=k}}f[A]g[B].\]
Finally take \(k=|S|\). Since \(|A|+|B|=|A\cup B|+|A\cap B|\), this equality forces \(A\cap B=\varnothing\). Therefore \(h_{|S|}[S]=(f*g)[S]\).






WarningDo not clear intermediate overlap layers



Input layers above \(|S|\) are zero. Product layers above \(|S|\) can be necessary: Möbius inversion needs them to cancel overlaps. On \(U=\{0,1\}\), let \(f[\{0\}]=g[\{0\}]=1\). Then \(H_2[\{0\}]=H_2[U]=1\). Inversion subtracts the first from the second and correctly returns zero. Clearing \(H_2[\{0\}]\) prematurely creates a false disjoint pair on \(U\).


There are \(n+1\) zeta/inverse transforms, each costing \(O(n2^n)\) additions/subtractions, and \(O(n^2)\) rank products for each mask. The total is \(O(n^22^n)\) ring operations and \(O(n2^n)\) coefficient storage. A ring with subtraction suffices; factorials and field division play no role in this multiplication algorithm. OR convolution differs: it keeps overlap and does not enforce \(|A|+|B|=|S|\).

title: 16 — Set Power Series
text:
Functions of a set series
Let \(g[\varnothing]=0\). Any product of more than \(n\) copies of \(g\) must repeat a label, so \(g^{n+1}=0\). This property is nilpotence. It makes substitution into an infinite formal series finite.
When \(1,2,\ldots,n\) are units in \(R\), define
\[\exp(g)=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{g^k}{k!},\qquad
\log(1+g)=\sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^{k-1}\frac{g^k}{k}.\]
Over \(\mathbb F_p\), the sufficient local condition is \(p>n\). The usual finite formal identities show these operations are inverse. We will also derive partition recurrences that work without dividing by these integers.
What does \(g^k/k!\) count? A term of \(g^k[S]\) chooses an ordered list of \(k\) disjoint nonempty blocks covering \(S\), with weight equal to the product of their \(g\)-values. Each unordered partition has exactly \(k!\) orders, because its nonempty blocks have distinct label sets. Hence
\[[x^S]\exp(g)=\sum_{\pi\text{ a partition of }S}\prod_{B\in\pi}g[B].\]
The empty set has one partition with no blocks; its product is one. This finite partition sum makes sense over any commutative ring even when the displayed factorial quotients do not.
Three-label example. If \(g[B]=1\) for every nonempty \(B\), the contributions on three labels are one one-block partition, three two-block partitions, and one three-block partition. The answer is five. If singleton blocks have weight \(a\) and larger blocks have weight zero, the answer on any \(S\) is \(a^{|S|}\): only the singleton partition survives.

Connected objects and a division-free recurrence
Let \(A[S]\) count all objects on \(S\) and \(C[S]\) count connected ones. Assume every object has a unique partition into nonempty connected components, and the allowed choices and weights factor across that partition. Then \(A=\exp(C)\), so \(C=\log(A)\) where the quotient formulas are legal.
For a formula valid over any coefficient ring, choose the least label \(v\in S\). Its component has one uniquely determined label set \(T\) containing \(v\). Therefore
\[A[S]=\sum_{\substack{T\subseteq S\\v\in T}}C[T]A[S\setminus T],
\qquad
C[S]=A[S]-\sum_{\substack{T\subsetneq S\\v\in T}}C[T]A[S\setminus T].\]
Use \(A[\varnothing]=1\) and process nonempty masks by increasing size. The second formula isolates the term \(T=S\). Each object appears once because its component containing \(v\) is unique. Enumerating these transitions costs \(O(3^n)\) operations and \(O(2^n)\) storage.
Graph example. For all simple graphs on a fixed vertex subset, \(A[S]=2^{\binom{|S|}{2}}\). Two vertices have \(A=2\), so \(C=2-1=1\). Three vertices have \(A=8\): subtract the all-singleton graph and three graphs with a connected pair plus an isolated vertex, leaving \(C=8-1-3=4\). They are the three paths and the triangle.

title: 16 — Set Power Series
section: Fast exp, inverse, and log without factorial division
text:
Fast exp, inverse, and log without factorial division
The special relation \(x_i^2=0\) supplies a short recurrence. Split off one label, writing a series as \(f=f_0+x_{n-1}f_1\), where both parts use only the other \(n-1\) labels. The coefficient \(f_1[S]\) equals the old coefficient at \(S\cup\{n-1\}\).
For \(g[\varnothing]=0\), let \(E_0\) be its partition exponential on the smaller universe. The distinguished label belongs to exactly one component; choosing its other labels gives
\[E(g_0+x_{n-1}g_1)=E(g_0)+x_{n-1}\bigl(E(g_0)*g_1\bigr).\]
Compute \(E(g_0)\) recursively and perform one subset convolution. With the ranked multiplier the recurrence is \(T(n)=T(n-1)+O(n^22^n)\), giving \(T(n)=O(n^22^n)\). This operation equals the factorial exponential wherever that formula exists and supplies its combinatorial extension otherwise.
An ordinary multiplicative inverse requires only that \(f[\varnothing]\) be a unit. If \(u=f_0^{-1}\), direct multiplication and \(x_{n-1}^2=0\) give
\[f^{-1}=u-x_{n-1}(u*u*f_1).\]
This is another \(O(n^22^n)\) recursion. Finally, for \(A[\varnothing]=1\), connected extraction obeys
\[L(A_0+x_{n-1}A_1)=L(A_0)+x_{n-1}(A_0^{-1}*A_1).\]
This follows by inverting the exponential split: \(A_1=A_0*C_1\). Recompute smaller inverses if desired; the geometric sum of their \(O(k^22^k)\) costs is still \(O(n^22^n)\). The resulting \(L\) is the inverse of the partition exponential over any ring, and agrees with the displayed formal logarithm when its denominators are units. It is not permission to evaluate \(1/k\) in small characteristic.

title: 16 — Set Power Series
text:
Composition and power projection
For an ordinary polynomial \(F(z)=\sum_{k=0}^m a_kz^k\), substitution \(F(g)=\sum_{k=0}^{\min(m,n)}a_kg^k\) is defined whenever \(g[\varnothing]=0\). Successive subset multiplications give the explicit bound \(O(n^32^n)\) when \(m\le n\). More specialized composition algorithms improve this; do not infer their cost from a single convolution. For an EGF \(\sum F_kz^k/k!\), use unit factorials or interpret coefficients by the corresponding weighted partition sums.
Power projection reverses the question. Given weights \(w[S]\), compute
\[b_k=\sum_{S\subseteq U}w[S]\,[x^S]g^k\qquad(0\le k\le n).\]
For fixed \(g\), composition is a linear map from \((a_k)\) to the subset table. Its transpose maps \(w\) to \((b_k)\), because
\[\sum_S w[S]\,[x^S]F(g)=\sum_k a_kb_k.\]
This equality explains the word “transpose” without an extra combinatorial assumption. Computing successive powers gives the same \(O(n^32^n)\) baseline. A transposed implementation of a faster linear composition circuit can share its asymptotic operation count; that is an additional library contract, not an unexplained property of the basic multiplier.

title: 16 — Set Power Series
text:
Contest translation: coloured bipartite graphs
For Lights Out on Connected Graph, ARC105 F, assign a bit \(s_v\) to whether vertex \(v\) is flipped an odd number of times. An edge \(uv\) becomes blue exactly when \(s_u+s_v=1\) in \(\mathbb F_2\). Thus the retained graph must be bipartite, and the problem asks for connected bipartite spanning subgraphs.
The count easier to obtain is coloured bipartite subgraphs. For every vertex set \(S\) and every colour class \(T\subseteq S\), choose any subset of original edges crossing \(T,S\setminus T\). If \(e(T,S\setminus T)\) is their number, set
\[A[S]=\sum_{T\subseteq S}2^{e(T,S\setminus T)}.\]
Each summand counts graphs with that particular two-colouring. A bipartite graph with \(k\) components has \(2^k\) colourings, including a factor two for an isolated vertex. Therefore \(C=L(A)\) counts connected graphs with a colouring, and the answer for nonempty \(U\) is \(C[U]/2\). The modulus \(998244353\) makes two a unit. Summing first and dividing all \(A[S]\) by two would be wrong for disconnected graphs.
For the official limit \(n\le17\), a practical baseline uses \(O(3^n)\) cut terms and the distinguished-component recurrence; ranked multiplication can accelerate the latter. Precompute induced-edge counts \(e(S)\) so crossing counts are \(e(S)-e(T)-e(S\setminus T)\). The partition coefficient is maintained exactly throughout, rather than deduplicating colourings afterward.

title: 16 — Set Power Series
text:
Problem-solving checklist

Must the two objects use disjoint labels, or is overlap allowed?
What does the empty-set coefficient mean?
Are components uniquely determined and weights multiplicative?
Are you counting uncoloured objects, coloured objects, or objects with an extra mark?
Are divisions legal, or should you use the distinguished-component recurrence?
Have intermediate product ranks survived until Möbius inversion?

title: 16 — Set Power Series
text:
Exercises with hints and solutions

Partition check. Give weight two to a singleton and weight three to a pair. What is the partition exponential on two labels?
Hint: list partitions. Solution: the singleton partition contributes \(2\cdot2=4\) and the one-block partition contributes 3, so the answer is 7.
Characteristic trap. Over \(\mathbb F_2\), let \(g=x_0+x_1\). Why is “compute \(g^2/2\)” invalid, and what is the partition exponential’s two-label coefficient?
Hint: ordered and unordered partitions are different computations. Solution: \(g^2=2x_0x_1=0\), and two has no inverse. The unique partition into two singleton blocks still has weight one, so the division-free answer is one.
Connected extraction. How many connected simple graphs exist on three labelled vertices?
Hint: subtract component partitions from eight. Solution: one empty graph and three single-edge graphs are disconnected, giving four. This also checks the earlier recurrence.
Coloured failure. For a two-vertex graph with one possible edge, compute \(A\) and \(C\) for the coloured bipartite model.
Hint: the empty graph has four colourings. Solution: \(A[U]=4+2=6\), each singleton has \(A=2\), and \(C[U]=6-2\cdot2=2\). Dividing \(C[U]\) by two yields the unique connected graph. Dividing \(A[U]\) by two instead yields three, not the two uncoloured graphs.
Projection model. If \(g\) has coefficient one on singletons and zero elsewhere, and \(w\) selects the full universe, determine every \(b_k\).
Hint: count ordered singleton blocks. Solution: only \(k=n\) can cover \(U\); its coefficient is \(n!\). Hence \(b_n=n!\) and the other \(b_k\) vanish, with the arithmetic interpreted in the coefficient ring.

For a sustained modelling exercise, attempt ARC105 F before reading the reduction above. Chapter 19 supplies a synthesis check on the complete four-vertex graph.
